en: The *prāṇa* (out-breath) is indeed his *upāṃśu* cup;
the *vyāna* (diffused breath) is the *upāṃśusavana* stone; and the *udāna* (up-breath) is the *antaryāma* cup. Now, as to why it is called "upāṃśu."
The cup named Aṃśu is indeed Prajāpati;
this [cup] is his breath. Because it is his breath, it is therefore called Upāṃśu.
He draws it from outside the filter.

He thus places this breath in him turned away; that breath of his, being turned away, flows out, and he purifies it with the *aṃśu* cups, thinking, "May it become pure. He purifies it with six [cups]; for there are six seasons;
it is by means of the seasons that he thus purifies it. 4.1.1 [4]
Regarding this they say: "When he purifies with the *aṃśu* cups while [the other cups are] silent, all the *soma* juices are purified by the filter; but by what means are his *aṃśu* shoots purified?
He pours them down together.
"O Soma, that which is your invincible, watchful name—unto that Soma of yours, O Soma, svāhā!
Thus, by means of the *svāhā* call alone, his stalks become purified. Indeed, this cup is everything, for it is the form of all the pressings. 4.1.1. [6]

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack by the Asuras and Rakṣasas. They said, "Let us complete the sacrifice; if the Asuras and Rakṣasas should attack us, our sacrifice shall remain completed. 4.1.1 [7]
They completed the entire sacrifice at the morning pressing itself: by means of this very cup (graha) they established it through the Yajus;
in the first chant (stotra) they did so through the Sāman; and in the first recitation (śastra) they did so through the Ṛc. Once it was thus completed, from that point onward...

They proceeded with the sacrifice; even now this same sacrifice concludes in this very manner: through the *graha* it is completed from the perspective of the *Yajus*, in the first *stotra* from the perspective of the *Sāman*, and in the first *śastra* from the perspective of the *Ṛc*. Once it has been thus concluded, he proceeds with the sacrifice from that point onward. 4.1.1. [8]
He presses eight times;
for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī—thus it is the morning pressing that is being performed. 4.1.1.[9]

He draws it with the formula, "Flow clear for Vācaspati! Vācaspati is indeed the breath; this cup is the breath, therefore he says, "Flow clear for Vācaspati. With the words, "By the shoots of the bull, purified by the hands," he purifies it with the shoots of Soma;
therefore he says, "By the shoots of the bull. "Purified by the hands": the hands are indeed the *gabhasti*s; [he purifies it] with the two hands.
He purifies it for him. 4.1.1.[10] Then he presses eleven times;
for the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the midday [pressing] belongs to the Triṣṭubh.
This very midday pressing is thus performed.
He draws [the cup], saying: "O god, purify yourself for the gods! For he is indeed a god who purifies himself for the gods.
"You are the portion of those," for he is indeed their portion.
Then he presses twelve times;
for the Jagatī consists of twelve syllables, and the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī; thus the third pressing is thereby performed. 4.1.1.[13]

He takes it up [with the words], "Make our nourishments honey-sweet. He thereby places essence within him; he thus makes it palatable for the gods. Therefore, when this [victim] has been slain, it does not putrefy. Then, when he offers it, he thereby brings it to completion. 4.1.1. [14]

"Eight times each," they say, "one should press [the Soma] for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); the Gāyatrī indeed has eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the Brahman; thus he indeed becomes possessed of spiritual luster. 4.1.1. [15]
That [Soma] has been pressed twenty-four times;
for there are twenty-four half-months in a year, and Prajāpati is the year, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati. Thus, it is as great as the sacrifice itself, as much as its measure.
He thus establishes it as exactly that much.
"One who desires cattle should press [the Soma] five times fivefold," they say; for cattle are fivefold.
Verily, he wins cattle. There are five seasons in the year;
the year is Prajāpati; Prajāpati is the sacrifice. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is, so much does he thereby complete.
This is the deliberation; however, it is performed in the other way. 4.1.1. [17]
Having taken it, he wipes it, thinking, "Lest it drip. He does not set it down, for this is its vital breath (*prāṇa*);
therefore, this vital breath moves about without being set down. However, if he should practice sorcery, then he should set it down, saying, "Thee for so-and-so!"
"I settle the breath," he says; thus, there is nothing therein that he does not release, and by that means both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer live long.
Furthermore, one may indeed place it [the fire] upon him.
"Into the breath of so-and-so I place you," he says; thus there is nothing in him that remains unsituated, and by that he does not disturb the vital breaths.
Being as it were within, he performs the act with the words, "Svāhā! 4.1.1 [19].

The gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Asuras and Rakṣasas should strike down this cup of ours before we have offered it. While still standing between [the fire and the cup], they offered it with the *svāhā* call; and having already been offered, they offered it into the fire. In the same way, he [the sacrificer] now [does so].
While remaining within this very space, he offers with the *svāhā* utterance; thus, he offers that which is already offered into the fire. 4.1.1 [20].
Then he steps out, saying:
"I follow the wide atmosphere. Indeed, it is the atmosphere that he follows.

The Rakṣas roams about rootless and severed on both sides, just as this person here is rootless and severed on both sides as he moves through the intermediate space. This Yajus is indeed the Brahman that slays the Rakṣases;
by means of this Brahman, he makes the intermediate space free from fear and free from destruction. 4.1.1 [21]
Then he chooses a boon.
For the gods indeed strongly desire the offering of this cup; they fulfill this boon for him [with the thought], "May they offer this cup quickly. Therefore, he chooses a boon. 4.1.1. [22]
He offers with the formula, "Thou art self-made. This cup is indeed his vital breath; it is made by itself and born of itself.

Therefore he says, "Thou art self-made. "For all powers, celestial and terrestrial"—for he is born of himself for the sake of all these creatures. "May Tvaṣṭṛ fashion thy mind"—the mind is indeed Prajāpati.

"May Prajāpati accept you"—this is what he thereby says. "Svāhā! To thee, O auspicious one, to Sūrya!"—thus he makes the utterance of *svāhā* for the lower [deity], while [the other] is the higher deity.
Indeed, he has offered this in yonder world.

He who shines yonder is indeed everything; thus he makes him the most excellent of all. Now, if he were to make a lower deity [the object of the *svāhā*], the *svāhā*-utterance would come after [the deity];
for that sun is indeed higher than this [deity]. Therefore, he makes the *svāhā*-utterance first and the deity last. 4.1.1. [24]
Then, having offered the oblation, he wipes the ladle upwards;
he thereby bestows life-breath upon him directed away from himself.
Then, with his hand turned upwards, he wipes towards the east on the middle enclosing-stick.
"By saying, 'For the gods who drink the rays of light, thee,' he places that breath in him turned away from himself.
Indeed, he has offered this in yonder orb which shines;
those who are its rays are the gods."
These [Marīcipas] he thereby gratifies; these gods, being gratified, carry him to the heavenly world.
Of this very cup, there is neither an invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) nor an offering verse (*yājyā*); one offers it with a mantra, for by this means his cup is [offered]. 4.1.1. [26]

By this, he becomes possessed of an invitatory verse (*anuvākyavān*) and by this, possessed of an offering verse (*yājyavān*). Now, if he should practice sorcery (*abhicaret*), he should take that stalk of his which is stuck to his arms, his chest, or his garment, and offer it [into the fire] with the mantra: "O divine stalk, for whomsoever I invoke you—that is the truth!
By this downward-flowing breaking, may he be struck—*phaṭ*! Just as one who is being struck might run away, even so does this [stalk].
If [the Soma] spills while being poured, it will likewise not remain for him who runs or runs after it;
therefore, he deposits it for the one for whom he acts in this manner. He deposits it with the formula, "For breath thee," for this [Soma] is indeed his breath.
Some, however, deposit it in the southern half.
"For he moves along this direction," so they say;
however, one should not do so. One should place it in the northern half [of the altar], for there is no other [direction] beyond this oblation.
He places it with the words, "For breath thee! for this is indeed his breath. 4.1.1. [28]
Then he takes up the Upāṃśusavana stone;

he does not touch it with the fringes of the cloth nor with the strainer, for it is as if it were already cleansed by water; but if a stalk of soma should cling to it, he removes it with his hand alone.
Having destroyed [the stalk], he should set it down facing upwards with the formula, "For the vyāna, thee! for this [cup] is indeed his vyāna.
4.1.2.[1] Verily, the upāṃśu cup is his prāṇa; the upāṃśusavana stone is his vyāna; and the antaryāma cup is his udāna. 4.1.2.[2]
Now, as for why it is called the Antaryāma:
that which is the prāṇa is the udāna, and that is the vyāna; by drawing [the cup] silently (upāṃśu), he thereby places that very outward-turned breath within him.
By drawing the Antaryāma cup, he places that very udāna breath within him facing inward; thus this udāna of his is within the inner self (antarātman).
Because it is within his inner self, and because by means of it these creatures go forth, therefore it is called Antaryāma. 4.1.2. [3]
He draws it from within the strainer;
he thus places the udāna-breath in him facing inward.
This udāna of his is established within the inner self. By this same means, his upāṃśu cup also becomes drawn from within the strainer; it is the same.

For these two, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups, are indeed the out-breath (prāṇa) and the up-breath (udāna); by means of these, he does not miss this [sacrifice] even among the other cups. Now, as to why he purifies the Soma with a filter.

When Soma indeed defeated his own domestic priest Bṛhaspati, he gave him back; with that [gift], he was appeased. When he had given him back, there remained a surplus of evil against him, since he surely intended to injure the Brahman. 4.1.2. [5]
The gods purified him with a filter;
he, being fit for sacrifice and purified, became the oblation for the gods.
In the same way, this [sacrificer] now purifies him with a filter; he, being fit for sacrifice and purified, becomes the oblation for the gods. 4.1.2. [6]
Now, as for the fact that the cups are drawn with the *upayāma* formula:

this earth is indeed Aditi; her is that introductory oblation (*prāyaṇīya-havis*), and that is the rice-pap (*caru*) for Āditya. That is truly like a preliminary to the Soma-pressing; for she, this Earth, desired a share in the pressing among the gods.
"Even so, let there be a share for me also in the pressed [soma].
Then the gods said, "This sacrifice has been assigned to the deities; let the cups be drawn by you alone."
"Let them be offered to the deities," he said; "So be it. This, then, is his portion at this pressing.
Now, as for the fact that the cups are drawn with the *upayāma* formula:
this earth, indeed, is the *upayāma*; for it is this earth that holds fast this food.

From animals, from humans, and from trees—from this world, indeed, the gods go upwards, for the gods are in heaven. 4.1.2. [9] Now, as to why the draughts (grahas) are drawn with the *upayāma* formula: they are thus drawn by means of this very earth; and when he deposits them in the womb, it is in this [earth].

Or rather, he is the source of all this; from her indeed these creatures were born. 4.1.2.[10] The officiating priests carry him, Soma, who has become semen; for if semen is shed outside the womb, it surely perishes. But when he places it in the womb, he places it in her very self. 4.1.2.[11]
These two, indeed, are his cups: the out-breath (prāṇa) and the up-breath (udāna).

Of these two, he offers one after sunrise and the other before sunrise, for the sake of distinguishing the out-breath and the up-breath; thus he distinguishes the out-breath and the up-breath. Therefore, although these two are indeed alike, [they are distinguished].
They do not call them by different names, saying "prāṇa" and "udāna.
Indeed, day and night are his two cups;
of these two, he offers one when the sun has risen and the other before it has risen.
By explaining it in terms of either one of the two, day and night, he explains it as day and night itself.
4.1.2.[13] The Upāṃśu cup, being [the nature of] day, he offers at night; thus he places the day within the night. Therefore, even...
In the *sutamiśrā* [offering], something like a remnant is manifested.
[He offers] the *santamantaryāma* at night; he offers it when the sun has risen. He thereby places this night within the day; by that, indeed—
The sun, rising with laughter, does not burn these creatures; therefore, these creatures are protected. 4.1.2.
[15] Now, therefore, he draws [the cup], saying:
"Thou art taken with a support"—the significance of the support has already been stated—and "Restrain within."
"O Maghavan, drink the Soma!"—Maghavan is indeed Indra, and Indra is the leader of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "O Maghavan.
"Drink the Soma!"—this means "protect the Soma. "Increase wealth, O sacrificer!"—wealth is indeed cattle;
thus he means "protect the cattle. "Sacrifice, O sacrificer!"—the *iṣ* (sacrificial food) is indeed offspring.

Thus do those who are ever-sacrificing perform this; these very creatures, as sacrificers, move about praising and toiling. 4.1.2 [16] "I place you between heaven and earth; I place the wide atmosphere between; in harmony with the lower gods."

And by saying "by others," he indeed makes this [cup] belong to the All-gods (vaiśvadeva). Because these creatures move about in the intermediate space, both breathing out and breathing in, by means of it, it belongs to the All-gods.
[He says,] "O Maghavan, rejoice in the Antaryāma! Maghavan is indeed Indra; Indra is the leader of the sacrifice. Therefore, he says this.
"O Maghavan!"—now, when he draws [the cup] with "within, within," he thereby says, "Place it within yourself.
Having drawn it, he wipes it around; he does so lest it should drip away. He does not set it down, for this is his upward breath (*udāna*).
Therefore, this *udāna* breath moves about as something non-existent; however, if he were to practice sorcery, he should then set it down with the formula:
"I set down your *udāna*, O so-and-so! 4.1.2 [18].
If he should set down the *upāṃśu* cup...

Then he should set it down; if he does not set down the *upāṃśu* cup, he should not set this one down; if he covers the *upāṃśu* cup, he should also cover this one; if he does not cover the *upāṃśu* cup, he should not cover this one; as is the ritual action for the *upāṃśu*, so it is for this one—the procedure is the same.
For these two, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups, are indeed the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (udāna). Now,
the Carakas offer them with two separate mantras, for these two of his are the out-breath and in-breath, possessing distinct powers.

"Those who say, 'We shall perform the out-breathing and the in-breathing,' should not do so; for they indeed cause confusion of the sacrificer's out-breathing and in-breathing. Or rather, he should offer this silently. 4.1.2.
[20] Now, as to why he offers with a silent mantra.

Thus, this [libation] of his also becomes offered with a mantra; why then should he offer it silently? For these two are the same, namely the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma, for they are the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (udāna). He offers the Upāṃśu with the very same mantra [with which he previously offered].
With that very mantra he offers this oblation: "Thou art self-fashioned for all divine and earthly powers; may the mind attend thee, svāhā!
O auspicious one, [be] for Sūrya!"—thus has been stated the connection of the Yajus. 4.1.2. [22]
Then, having offered the oblation, he wipes the cup downwards;
for while elsewhere, having offered to the Upāṃśu, one wipes upwards, here he wipes downwards, thereby placing the out-breath (udāna) within him directed inwardly.
He places [it]. 4.1.2.[23] Then, with his hand lowered, he wipes it westward on the middle enclosing-stick; this indeed is the *upāṃśu*.

Having offered, he wipes along the middle enclosing-stick from west to east with his hand turned upwards; then, with his hand turned downwards, he wipes it along the middle enclosing-stick from east to west.

Thus he bestows the out-breath (*udāna*) upon him in a westerly direction. "For the gods who drink the rays of light (*marīcipa*)," he says; the significance of this is the same as before. 4.1.2. [24]
Having stepped back toward it, he deposits it with the formula, "For the upward breath (udāna) thee! For this [cup] is indeed his upward breath. He deposits them so that they touch one another;
he thereby causes the out-breath (prāṇa) and the upward breath (udāna) to touch, and he joins together the out-breath and the upward breath. 4.1.2 [25]
Or they lie there motionless until the third pressing; therefore these humans sleep.
Then at the third pressing they are employed again; therefore these humans, having slept, wake up.
The moving and non-moving beings are sharpened; this is according to the form of the sacrifice itself. Indeed, the sacrifice is fashioned like a bird:
its two wings are the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups, and its body is the Upāṃśusavana stone.
These [stones], indeed, lie there motionless.

The sacrifice is extended up to the third pressing; indeed, it is because it is extended that these birds fly with their wings spread apart and not drawn together. At the third pressing, they are joined together again;
therefore, these birds fly with their wings drawn together.
This is indeed according to the form of the sacrifice.
This earth, verily, is the *upāṃśu*;
for the *upāṃśu* is breath, and it is indeed this [earth].

Breathing out, he breathes forth; that very Antaryāma cup is the out-breath (*udāna*), for the Antaryāma is the out-breath, since by breathing upward toward yonder world, he breathes forth. The Upāṃśusavana stone is the intermediate region itself; it is the through-breath (*vyāna*), for the Upāṃśusavana is the through-breath.
For it is the intermediate space indeed that breathes forth and breathes upon. 4.1.3.
[1] Speech, verily, is his [portion] for Indra and Vāyu; this is the internal [correspondence]: when Indra, indeed, hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra...
Being weaker, he carried it off, thinking, "I am not thirsty," and fearing it, he hid it; even the gods hid themselves there.
Then those gods said:
"Indeed, we do not know whether Vṛtra has been slain or whether he lives. Come, let one of us find out whether Vṛtra is dead or alive. 4.1.3 [3] They spoke to Vāyu.

"This indeed is Vāyu who blows here. O Vāyu, find out this: whether Vṛtra is slain or whether he lives. You are indeed the swiftest among us; if he shall live, you alone will return quickly. 4.1.3 [4]

He said: "What would be mine from that?"—"The very first *vaṣaṭ*-call of King Soma shall be yours."—"So be it," he replied. Vāyu went; he found Vṛtra slain. He (Vṛtra) said: "Vṛtra is slain; do with him what one would do with one who is slain. 4.1.3. [5] Those gods rushed forward.
Just as one who is about to obtain wealth [seizes it], so he seized [the Soma];
that which he obtained alone became dedicated to a single deity; that which two obtained became dedicated to two deities; that which many obtained became dedicated to many deities.
Because they seized him with vessels (*pātra*), therefore they are called *grahas* (libations). 4.1.3. [6]
It became putrid for them;
being thus fetid and stinking, it blew upon them. It was no longer fit for an oblation, nor fit for consumption.
Those gods said to Vāyu:
"O Vāyu, blow upon this for us; make this savory for us. He said, "What shall be mine from that?
[The others replied,] "They shall call these vessels by your name alone. He said, "So be it; but you must blow upon my secret parts as well. 4.1.3. [8]

The gods struck away as much of its fragrance as they could; they placed that [fragrance] among the animals. This is that very stench of a corpse found among animals; therefore, one should not inhale the smell of a corpse, for it belongs to King Soma.
[Regarding] the odor (gandha): 4.1.3.
[9] One should certainly not spit.
Therefore, even if one feels as if one is stuck, one should go around with the wind blowing toward oneself; for Soma is indeed *śrī*.
Evil, consumption—it is just as when a worse person descends before someone better who is approaching; even so, consumption descends away from him. Then the other wind blew through it. 4.1.3. [10]
He tasted it; therefore, there is no need for an oblation, nor for food from this [Soma].
Consequently, these [cups] belong to various deities, yet they are called "Vāyavyas" (belonging to Vāyu). This is the first *vaṣaṭ*-call of King Soma, and they call these his vessels. 4.1.3. [11]
Indra indeed reflected:
"Vāyu has received the largest portion of this sacrifice of ours, as well as the first *vaṣaṭ*-call of King Soma; these are the vessels that they designate for him."

"Come, let there be a share for you in this [cup] as well," he said. He replied, "Vāyu, grant me a share in this cup. "What would result from that? [Vāyu asked. "Speech would indeed speak with articulated form (nirukta)," [Yajña said.
"If speech speaks with articulated form, then I shall grant you a share. Thereupon, this cup for Indra and Vāyu (aindravāyava) became one belonging to Vāyu.
Long ago, before that, Indra said, "Let half of this cup be mine. Vāyu replied, "Only a fourth shall be yours; half shall be mine."
"Thus Indra [received] only a fourth part," said Vāyu.
4.1.3.[14] Those two went to Prajāpati with their question.
That Prajāpati divided the draught into two parts; he said: "This..."

Then he divided the portion for Vāyu again into two halves. He said, "This is for Vāyu; this is yours. He assigned the fourth part to Indra alone. Since it was the fourth, it was called *turīya* (the fourth); from that, this cup became known as the Aindraturīya.
Of this very cup (graha), there are two purorucs: the first is addressed to Vāyu, and the second to Indra and Vāyu;
there are two invitatory verses (anuvākyās): the first is addressed to Vāyu, and the second to Indra and Vāyu; there are two directions for the assistants (praiṣas): the first is addressed to Vāyu.

The Aindravāyava cup was the later one; there were two *yājyā* verses, the first addressed to Vāyu alone and the second to Indra and Vāyu. In this way, he caused him to share in a fourth part after a fourth part.
He said: "Since they have shared me out by a fourth part after a fourth part, then speech itself shall be articulated only by a fourth part."

"It will speak"—this is the fourth, expressed part of speech, which humans speak; then this is the fourth, unexpressed part of speech, which animals speak; then this is the fourth, unexpressed part of speech, which birds speak;
then this is the fourth, unexpressed part of speech, which this small crawling vermin speaks. 4.1.3 [17]

Therefore, this has been declared by the seers: "Speech is measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak. 4.1.3 [18]
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:

"O Vāyu, drinker of the pure, come to us; a thousand are your teams, O possessor of all boons. To you I offer the intoxicating juice, of which, O God, you have the first draught. For Vāyu, thee! 4.1.3. [19]
Then, having set it aside, he brings it back:
"O Indra and Vāyu, these [somas] are pressed; come hither with refreshments, for the drops of soma long for you both.
You are taken with a support; for Vāyu, for Indra and Vāyu, you! This is your womb: for the two who are in harmony."
With "Thee for [Vāyu]," he sets it down. As to why he says, "Thee for the two who are well-pleased": Vāyu is indeed Indra, and Indra is Vāyu;
therefore he says, "This is thy womb; thee for the two who are well-pleased.
Kratu and Dakṣa are indeed his Mitra and Varuṇa.

This is with reference to the self. Whatever one desires in the mind—thinking, "May this be mine; may I do this"—that is *kratu* (will/intention). And when that is accomplished for him, that is *dakṣa* (skill/efficacy). Mitra is indeed *kratu*, and Varuṇa is *dakṣa*. Brahman is indeed Mitra, and Kṣatra is Varuṇa. [He is] truly the one who attains his goal.

The Brahmin is the creator and the Kṣatriya is the ruler. 4.1.4.[2] In the beginning, these two—the Brahman and the Kṣatra—dwelt apart. Then the Brahman was indeed able [to prevail], without the Mitra [the Kṣatriya].
Regarding the statement "to stand firm against the *kṣatra* [power] of Varuṇa":
Varuṇa is not the *kṣatra* without the *brahman*. Whatever ritual act (*karman*) Varuṇa performed, it was [only] through Mitrā and the *brahman*.
That which was produced by Brahmā and Mitra did not indeed succeed for him.
Varuṇa became the Kṣatra;
he addressed the Brahman, Mitra, saying, "Turn toward me."
"Let us two unite; I shall place you in front, and impelled by you, I shall perform the ritual act. "So be it," they replied, and the two united.
From that, this Maitrāvaruṇa cup arose.
That indeed is the office of the domestic priest (*purodhā*).

Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not desire the office of domestic priest for every Kṣatriya, for these two together produce both good and evil deeds; nor indeed should a Kṣatriya appoint every Brāhmaṇa as his domestic priest, for these two together produce both ill-done and evil deeds. Such was the ritual act of Varuṇa from that point.
It was produced by Brahmā through Mitra; indeed, it then prospered for him.
That [offering] is appropriate in each case:
if a Brāhmaṇa were not a Kṣatriya, or if he should obtain a Kṣatriya [as patron], it would be successful.
Now, this is indeed improper: that a Kṣatriya who is not a Brāhmaṇa performs any action whatsoever;

even though it is impelled by the Brāhmaṇa as his friend, it does not succeed for him. Therefore, a Kṣatriya who is about to perform an action must certainly approach a Brāhmaṇa; for then that action, impelled by the Brāhmaṇa, succeeds for him.
The ritual action is performed. 4.1.4.[7] Now, therefore, he indeed draws [the cup]:
"O Mitra and Varuṇa, this Soma has been pressed for you; O you who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*), hear me here."
"Thou art taken with a support; for Mitra and Varuṇa, thee! With these words he takes it.
He mixes it with milk.
As to why he mixes it with milk: Soma was indeed Vṛtra; when the gods slew him...

They said to Mitra, "You too must become a *haṃsa*. He did not desire it, saying, "I am the friend of all; being a friend, I shall not become a non-friend. They said to him, "We shall exclude you from the sacrifice. He replied, "I too shall slay [the sacrifice].
Thereupon the cattle departed from him, saying, "Being a friend, he has become a non-friend. Thus he was deprived of his cattle.
The gods strengthened him with cattle when they mixed him with milk; in the same way, this sacrificer now strengthens him with cattle when he mixes him with milk.
Regarding this, they say: "He truly never desired to kill. Therefore, that which is the milk here is the Soma of Mitra.

Thus [it belongs] to Varuṇa; therefore he mixes it with milk. He mixes it [with the verse]: "May we, having won through wealth, rejoice; may the gods [rejoice] through the oblation, and the cows through pasture.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, do you two grant us that cow every day, never failing. "This is your womb; for Ṛta and Ayu, thee! [he says].
He deposits [the cup], saying: "Thee for Ṛta and Āyus. Brahman indeed is Ṛta, for Mitra is Brahman and Ṛta is Brahman;
Varuṇa is indeed Āyus, for Varuṇa is the year and the year is Āyus. Therefore he says: "This is thy womb; thee for Ṛta and Āyus! 4.1.5.1.
The ear, indeed, belongs to the Aśvins;
therefore, he consumes [the draught] while turning all around, for with this ear one hears from every direction. When the Bhṛgus or the Aṅgirases attained the heavenly world, Cyavana—
Whether he was Bhārgava Cyavana or Āṅgirasa, he abandoned that very [body], having become decrepit and taking on the form of a *kṛtyā*.
Śaryāta Mānava, it is said, was wandering here with his village; he settled down as a neighbor in that very place. Of him—
The boys, playing, thinking this old man—who had the appearance of a sorcerer—to be worthless, pounded him with clods of earth.
He became enraged at the Śāryātas; he cast a spell upon them, and even a father fought with his son and a brother with his brother.
[Regarding the rule] *bhrātrā* 4.1.5.[4]:
Śaryāta indeed reflected, "Because of whatever I have done, I have fallen into this calamity. He...
He called together the cowherds and the shepherds and said (4.1.5):
"Who among you saw anything this very day? They replied, "There lies this old man, a mere phantom;
thinking him of no account, the boys pelted him with clods of earth. He understood. Indeed, he was [Yama].
"Regarding Cyavana" (4.1.5):
Having yoked his chariot and placed Śāryātī Sukanyā upon it, he set out and arrived at the place where the seer was.
Regarding that [4.1.5.7]:

He said, "O Seer, homage to you! Because I did not know [you], I have harmed you. Here is Sukanyā; with her I make amends to you. May my community reach an agreement. From that very moment his community reached an agreement, and from that very moment Śaryāta [recovered].
The Mānava yoked [the horse], thinking, "Lest I should harm another. 4.1.5. [8] Now, the Aśvins were indeed wandering about here practicing medicine;
they approached Sukanyā, and with her—
They two approached as a couple, but he did not perceive it.
They both said, "Sukanyā, why do you lie beside this decrepit wretch, this creature of ill omen? Come after us! She replied:
"Since my father gave me to him, I shall not leave him while he is alive"—this the seer understood.
He said, "O Sukanyā, what did they say to you? She explained it to him.
Having been informed, he said, "If they say this to you again, you must say to them: 'Truly, you two are not at all well-favored,' nor..."

"Or else you two blame my husband as if he were utterly prosperous," they said. If they should say to you, "In what way are we both deficient? In what way are we unsuccessful?", then you should say, "Make my husband young again, and then I will tell you. They approached her again and said this very thing to her. 4.1.5. [11]

She said, "Indeed, you two are neither entirely whole nor fully prosperous, yet you both reproach my husband. They both asked, "In what way are we not whole? In what way are we not prosperous? She said, "Make my husband young again, and then I will tell you. 4.1.5 [12]
The two of them said, "Enter this lake; he will emerge with whatever age he desires.
He entered that lake, and he emerged with the age he desired. 4.1.5 [13]

The two of them said, "Sukanyā, why are we incomplete? Why are we unsuccessful? Harṣi replied to them, "In Kurukṣetra, these gods are performing a sacrifice; they exclude you two from the sacrifice, and for that reason you are incomplete."

"Since we have not succeeded while staying here," those two, the Aśvins, departed from that very place. They arrived at the gods who were performing the sacrifice when the *bahiṣpavamāna* had been chanted. They said: "4.1.5 [14]" "They said:"

"Perform the sacrifice with one that is indeed headless! they said. "How, with a headless one? he asked.

"Invite us, and then we shall tell you," they replied. "So be it," he said, and they invited them. For those two, they drew this cup for the Aśvins; those two became the Adhvaryu priests of the sacrifice, and they restored this head of the sacrifice.

Therefore, this [matter] regarding the *divākīrtyas* is explained in the Brāhmaṇa: "Just as they restored the head of the sacrifice, therefore this cup is drawn when the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted; for it was when the *bahiṣpavamāna* had been chanted that they arrived. 4.1.5. [16]

The two of them said, "We two are indeed the primary ones of the sacrifice, we who are the Adhvaryus; let him bring this cup for us here before the cups for the dual deities. For those two, he brought this cup before [the others].

They brought [the portions] together toward those belonging to two deities; therefore this tenth cup is drawn, and the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered for it at the third [pressing]. Now, as for "the Aśvins," these two, heaven and earth, are indeed manifestly the Aśvins, for they have pervaded (*āśnuvātām*) all this.
As for "the lotus-garlanded ones" (*puṣkarasrajau*), fire is the lotus of this [earth], and the sun is that of yonder [heaven].
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"O Aśvins, with that whip of yours which is honeyed and full of truth, sprinkle the sacrifice.
"You are taken with a support; for the two Aśvins, you!"—with these words he deposits it, saying, "This is your womb; for the two honeyed ones, you!"
He draws it with a verse containing the word "honey" (*madhumatī*), and he deposits it with the words, "Thee for the two honey-loving ones" (*mādhvībhyām*).
As to why he draws it with a verse containing the word "honey" and deposits it with the words "Thee for the two honey-loving ones":
Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed [knew this] regarding these two.

He said to the Brāhmaṇa named Madhu: "That is their beloved abode; by this very means he approaches that for them. Therefore, he takes [the cup] with a verse containing the word *madhu*, and he deposits it with the formula, "Thee for the two Mādhvīs!
Now, these vessels are smooth. The Aindravāyava vessel has a rim;
that is its second form, and by that it belongs to two deities. The Maitrāvaruṇa vessel has a goat’s beard; that is its second form.
Form is his first form; therefore that cup for the Aśvins is for two deities and is made of wood from the *auṣṭha* tree, for that is its second form;
therefore it is for two deities. Now, as for the phrase "the two Aśvins," the Aśvins are indeed the two chief [deities], and this mouth is, as it were, like the *auṣṭha*;
therefore the cup for the Aśvins is made of *auṣṭha* wood. 4.2.1. [1]
The two eyes, indeed, are his Śukra and Manthin offerings.
That which shines yonder is the Śukra; because it shines (tapati) there, it is the Śukra.
The Moon, indeed, is the Manthin. 4.2.1.[2]
He mixes it with groats;
he thus makes it into a stirred drink (*mantha*). Therefore, this [sun] is called *manthya*.
These two, indeed, are the eyes of these creatures; for if these two did not rise, people here would not even be able to distinguish their own hands. 4.2.1. [3]
Of these two, one is the eater;
the first of the two is the eater, the *śukra* cup, while the first of the other is the food, the *manthin* cup.
Of these two, the eater follows the other.
The first [cup] follows one [of the two], and the second follows the other; the *śukra* follows the former, and the *manthin* follows the latter.
Indeed, these two are drawn for one [set of deities] but offered to another. They are drawn for Śaṇḍa and Marka—the Asuras and Rakṣases—but offered to the deities. This is why it is so. 4.2.1. [5]
Wherever the gods struck down the Asuras and Rakṣases, they were unable to strike down these two; for whatever rite the gods performed, those two would surely bewilder them and vanish instantly.
Furthermore, regarding the absence of misfortune: 4.2.1.[6] Those gods said, "Devise a way by which we may drive these two away. They said, "Let us seize them with the very *grahas* (libations)."
"Let us take them; when they have descended, we shall seize them and strike them down. With these words, they took the two cups.
When those two had descended, they seized them and struck them down. Therefore, they are taken with the formula "for Caṇḍa and Marka," and they are offered to the deities. 4.2.1 [7]
Moreover, Yājñavalkya said:
"Should I not rather draw [the cups] for the deities alone? For this [world] is, as it were, of the nature of conquest.
Thus he indeed reflected upon that, but he did not do it. 4.2.1. [8]

Some indeed make this the *puroruc* for the *śukra* cup: "This Vena impels those born of the speckled womb, the light-enveloped, the measurer of the region. This is the form of him who shines there, when he says: "We make this its form."
"Jyotirjarāyu... (4.2.1.9).
One should, however, use this very *puroruc* for the *śukra* cup:
"Him [we invoke] as of old, as of former times, as of all times, as of these times..."

"O foremost one, seated upon the sacrificial grass, finder of light! For he is indeed the eater, and the eater follows him; and since he is the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*), therefore he says, "O foremost one, seated upon the sacrificial grass, finder of light.
"The facing enclosure, the roaring, swift one, whom thou dost conquer, along whom thou growest"—"Thou art taken with a support; for Śaṇḍa thee! This is thy womb; protect manliness! Thus he says.
For the Eater indeed swallows this [Soma], for the Hero follows after the Eater; therefore he says, "This is thy womb; protect heroism!
He places it on the southern half, for he moves along that direction. 4.2.1.
Then he draws the Manthin cup.
This Vena impels the ones born of the speckled [cow], those whose womb is light, in the measuring of the mid-region;
at the meeting of the waters and the sun, the sages lick him with their hymns as if he were an infant. You are taken with a base;
for Marka, you! 4.2.1. [11]
He mixes it with groats.
As to why he mixes it with groats: Varuna, indeed, once crushed the eye of King Soma;
it swelled, and from that the horse (aśva) came into being. Because it came into being from swelling (aśvayat), therefore it is called a horse (aśva).
A tear fell from her, and from that the barley (*yava*) came into being; therefore they say, "Barley belongs to Varuṇa.
Whatever of his eye was lost there, by that very means he now restores it and makes it whole.
Therefore, he mixes [the oblation] with flour-meal (*saktu*). 4.2.1. [12]

He mixes [the libation]. "In whose invocations you two, like minds, with power, accept the sharp inspired songs while rushing forward—he, the one of many manly deeds, who with his arrows has mixed the direction in his hand"—this is your womb; "protect the offspring," he says, and seats [the cup], for these people, the clans, are to be eaten by him; therefore he says, "This is your womb; protect the offspring. 4.2.1. [13]
There are two sprinkled splinters of the sacrificial post and two unsprinkled ones.
The Adhvaryu takes one sprinkled and one unsprinkled, and in the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes one sprinkled and one unsprinkled.
The Adhvaryu takes up the *śukra* cup which has been sprinkled with water, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the *manthin* cup.
That Adhvaryu wipes [the cup] with an unsprinkled splinter of the sacrificial post, saying: "Śaṇḍa is wiped away. In this very same manner [the other is wiped].

"The *marka* has been wiped away," says the *pratiprasthātṛ*. As they take up [the vessels], the *adhvaryu* goes out with the formula, "The gods who drink the *śukra* lead you forth; we have struck down the Asuras and Rakṣases. The *pratiprasthātṛ* [goes out] with, "The gods who drink the *manthin* lead you forth.
Thus, these two lead them forth for the sake of the deities. 4.2.1. [15]
With their elbows behind the Āhavanīya fire, they join their palms together;
they place them on the Uttaravedi—
the Adhvaryu on the southern hip and the Pratiprasthātṛ on the northern— without letting go, saying, "Thou art unassailable."
By means of those very *rakṣases*, the two of them make this high altar unassailable while intending to pass by it; for they are about to pass beyond Agni.
Thus, they conceal it from him, and so Agni does not harm them as they pass by.
Then the Adhvaryu goes around.
"May he go around, a good hero, engendering heroes," he says; for he is indeed an eater, and the hero follows the eater.

Therefore he says, "May he go around, a good hero, engendering heroes. "With abundance of wealth, [he goes] toward the sacrificer"—by saying this, he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer when he says, "With abundance of wealth, toward the sacrificer. 4.2.1. [17]

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ goes around [the fire], saying, "May he go around, procreating offspring rich in progeny. For these subjects are indeed eaters; therefore he says, "May he go around, procreating offspring rich in progeny," [and] "with abundance of wealth."
"May the sacrificer [prosper]"—by saying this, he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer when he says, "May the sacrificer [prosper] with abundance of wealth.
Having covered those two [the fire-pan and the cake], they go out;
they thus keep them concealed, and therefore these two, the sun and the moon, are hidden.

No one sees them as they go forward; having gone around in front, they uncover [the fire], and standing in front, they offer. Thus they make these two manifest. Therefore, everyone sees these two, the sun and the moon, as they go backward.
Therefore, no one sees the semen as it is being poured out; but that which is being born is seen from behind.
Everyone indeed looks on.
4.2.1.[19] Those two join their forearms behind the sacrificial post;
provided that fire does not obstruct them, and if...

The two should push the fire forward along the front of the sacrificial post and join their arms at the height of the aratni. The Adhvaryu should say, "Uniting with heaven and earth, the bright one with the bright luster," and the Pratiprasthātṛ should say, "Uniting with heaven and earth, the stirred one with the stirred luster.
Thus they provide a resting place for the eyes; it is the eyes themselves that they thus join together. Therefore, these two...
The two bones on both sides are joined to the eyes.
4.2.1.[20] That Adhvaryu throws away an unbesprinkled chip of the sacrificial post, saying: "Śaṇḍa is cast out," in this very manner.

The Pratiprasthātṛ says, "The Marka is driven away," whereby he strikes away the Asuras and Rakṣasas before the oblations. Then the Adhvaryu throws a sprinkled chip of the sacrificial post into the Āhavanīya fire.
"Thou art the support of the *śukra*," [says the Adhvaryu]; likewise, "Thou art the support of the *manthin*," [says] the Pratiprasthātṛ.
These two are indeed fuel-sticks for the eyes; he thus kindles the two eyes. Therefore, these two eyes are kindled. 4.2.1. [22] There he mutters:
"O divine Soma, may we be givers of that unpracticed, heroic wealth and abundance"—this is indeed the blessing of this ritual; he thus invokes this very blessing.
Then, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says:

"Prompt the [Hotṛ] for the Soma-pressings offered every morning, bright, dripping with honey, intended for Indra!"—at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu makes the offering; following him, the Pratiprasthātṛ;
and following him, the Camasādhvaryus. 4.2.1. [24]
Standing in front, those two indeed offer the oblations. These two are the eyes; thus they place the eyes in front.
Therefore, these eyes are in the front. 4.2.1 [25]
Standing on both sides of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they offer oblations.
For the sacrificial post is indeed like the nose; therefore, these two eyes are on both sides of the nose. 4.2.1.[26]
When these two have been consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call, they are offered with a mantra;

by this indeed do these two partake of that which is offered throughout the entire pressing for them. And because these two are offered throughout the entire pressing, they indeed belong to Prajāpati.

For these two eyes are most directly perceptive; truth indeed is the eye, and truth is Prajāpati; therefore, everything is offered after these two at every pressing. 4.2.1. [27] He offers: "He is the first consecration, the possessor of all boons; he is the first Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni. He...
"Bṛhaspati is the first, the wise one; offer this pressed [soma] to that Indra, Svāhā! 4.2.1.[28] As for the fact that he offers:
"He is the first, he is the first"—for indeed, of the emitted seed, it is the two eyes alone [that are first].
"Because it is possible in the first [offering], he offers that which is the first. 4.2.1. [29] Then he issues the direction:
"Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forward; let the cup of the Brahman go forward; let the cups of the Udgātṛs go forward."

"Let [the portions] go to the sacrificer; O Camasādhvaryus of the Sadasyas and the Hotṛs, come forward and draw up the *śukra*!"—this is the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*). Having gone around, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue from the Adhvaryu’s cup into his own;
thus he causes this first offering to be brought here. The Adhvaryu [pours it] into the Hotṛ’s cup.
He brings [the cup] for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer to consume, for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is indeed the breath.
That breath, as he utters the *vaṣaṭ*, has turned away from him; since the consumption is the breath, he thereby places that breath back into himself.
Now, as to why they do not carry these two cups back [to the sacrificer].
They take away other cups, for these two [the eyes] are indeed the *saṃsrava*; he pours it into the *hotṛcamasa*. Then they fill up the cups of the *hotrakas*.

These remnants of the oblations are indeed the remains of what has been offered; they are not sufficient for a further offering. It is these very remnants that they cause to swell again, so that they become sufficient for an offering.
Therefore, they pour more into the goblets of the Hotṛs. 4.2.1. [32]
Then they cause the Hotṛ-priests to perform the *saṃyājana* offerings.
For it is the Hotṛ-priests who, when harnessed, carry the sacrifice to the gods;
it is them that they thus satisfy, thinking, "May they, being satisfied and gratified, carry the sacrifice to the gods. Therefore, [they offer] to the Hotṛ-priests.
They perform the *saṃyājana* offerings (4.2.1).
He recites the consecratory formula (*anumantrayate*) either after the first *hotrā* offering has been performed, or after the last one: "May the *hotrās* be satisfied."

Those offerings of honey which are well-sacrificed, well-pleased, and well-poured with the cry of "svāhā"—this is indeed the satisfaction of the Hotṛ-offices. Then, having gone back, he sits down facing westward, saying, "The Agnīdh has sacrificed. For here the Agnīdh sacrifices as the last of those who sacrifice;
therefore he says, "The Agnīdh has sacrificed. 4.2.2. [1]
The Āgrayaṇa is indeed his self;

it belongs to him entirely, for this self is everything. Therefore, he draws it with this [earth]; for this [earth] is a vessel (sthālī), and he draws it with a vessel. This [earth] is everything, and this [Āgrayaṇa] is everything.
Therefore, one takes it with this [formula].
4.2.2.[2] One takes it full. The full is indeed everything; this cup is everything; therefore, one takes it full. 4.2.2.[3]
He draws [the cup] for the Viśve Devās.
The Viśve Devās are indeed everything; this cup is everything.
Therefore, he draws it for the Viśve Devās. 4.2.2. [4]
He draws [the cup] at all the pressings. All indeed are the pressings; this cup is everything; therefore he draws it at all the pressings. 4.2.2. [5]

If it should fail for the king, they should extend it from that very point and propagate it from there; for the Āgrayaṇa is the self, and from the self all these limbs proceed. Therefore, at the end, he draws the Hāriyojana cup.
In the end, the sacrifice is established in this very foundation, which is the Self itself. 4.2.2.
[6] Now, as to why it is called Āgrayaṇa:
when one takes up that pressing-stone (grāvan), one restrains speech; it is at this point—indeed.
Because she spoke first (*agre*) among them, therefore it is called the *Āgrayaṇa*.
Out of fear of the Rākṣasas, they uttered that speech.
From here, he draws six cups toward the east; then this [cup follows].
The year consists of either seven or six seasons; indeed, the year is everything. 4.2.2.

[8] When all had been conquered, when it was free from fear and free from harm, the gods first spoke this speech here. In the same way, he now speaks this speech here, when all has been conquered, when it is free from fear and free from harm. 4.2.2. [9]
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"O gods who are eleven in heaven, who are eleven upon the earth, who dwell in the waters—ye eleven by your greatness—O gods, enjoy this sacrifice! You are taken with a support; you are the Āgrayaṇa."

"Thou art the *svāgrayaṇa*," he says; thereby he makes speech itself free from weariness. Therefore, although it is the same [speech], one speaks with it in a reversed manner to avoid monotony; for he would commit a repetition if he were to draw [the cup] saying, "Thou art the *āgrayaṇa*, thou art the *āgrayaṇa*.
Therefore he says, "Thou art the *āgrayaṇa*, thou art the *svāgrayaṇa*. 4.2.2. [10]
"Protect the sacrifice, protect the lord of the sacrifice"—this he says to the speech that has been released: "Guard the sacrifice.
"Protect the lord of the sacrifice"—this he says to the speech that has been released: "Guard the sacrificer," for the sacrificer is indeed the lord of the sacrifice.

"May Viṣṇu, the lord of sacrifice, protect you with his power; protect you, O Viṣṇu!"—this he says regarding speech that has been released. "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; may the sacrifice protect you with its vigor. "Protect you, O Viṣṇu!"—this he says regarding speech that has been released, meaning "protect the sacrifice. "Protect [us] throughout the pressings"—this refers to him.
The Grāvastut says: "For he [the Sun] extends across all the pressings" (4.2.2.11).
Then, having taken hold of the *daśāpavitra* filter, he utters the sound *hiṅ*. That very Speech, when it was not being uttered, became exhausted; therein the gods—
When speech was exhausted, they restored breath by means of the *hiṅkāra* alone; for the *hiṅkāra* is indeed breath, and breath is indeed the *hiṅkāra*.
Therefore, one who has closed his nostrils is unable to utter the *hiṅkāra*. By means of that breath, he recovered;
for when one who is exhausted regains breath, then he recovers. In the same way, this [sacrificer], when his speech is exhausted, [recovers] by means of the *hiṅkāra* alone.

He bestows vital breath; by means of that very breath he unites himself. He utters the *hiṅ* sound three times, for the sacrifice is threefold. Then he says, "Soma purifies itself. That [he does] out of fear of those same *asuras* and *rakṣases*.
They proclaimed that very [Soma]; now, when everything has been conquered, made free from fear and free from harm, he proclaims it here; he makes it manifest.
Therefore he says, "Soma flows.
"For this priesthood, for this nobility."
"Therefore, [he says], 'It flows for the sake of this Brahman and Kṣatra, for this sacrificer who presses the Soma'; thus he speaks for the sake of the sacrificer.
Regarding this, they say: "One should set it down after saying only this much; for all this that exists is as much as the Brahman and the Kṣatra."
"Indra and Agni are indeed this entire universe; therefore, one should set [the cup] down after saying only this much.
But one should rather say more:
"For sap, for strength, he purifies. By saying "for sap," he speaks of rain; by saying "for strength," he speaks of that which is...
From rain, the essence of food is produced; therefore he says, "He purifies himself from the waters and the plants.

Thus he speaks of both the waters and the plants. "He purifies himself for heaven and earth"—thus he speaks of these two, heaven and earth, upon which all this rests. "He purifies himself for well-being"—that is, for what is good. "He purifies himself."

Thus he says this very thing. 4.2.2.[16] Now, some indeed say: "It purifies for the sake of spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa). But one should not speak thus; rather, as for what he says, "to him... [the rest follows].

"For Brahman"—by this he speaks for the sake of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). "For all the gods; this is your womb; for all the gods, you"—with these words he sets it down, for he draws it for all the gods.
He sets it down in the middle, for this is its self (*ātman*); indeed, this self is as if in the middle. To the south is the *ukthya* vessel.
The *uttarā* [vessel] belongs to Āditya (4.2.3.1).
Indeed, this Ukthya is his undefined self;
it is truly his very self.
This breath is undefined; it is his very life-force (*āyus*). Therefore, he draws [the cup] with this [verse].

For this [earth] is a vessel (*sthālī*), and he draws it with a vessel; for this [earth] is undecaying, and the life-force is undecaying and immortal; therefore, he draws it with this [verse]. 4.2.3. [2]
He draws it full;
for that which is full is everything, and that which is life is everything; therefore he draws it full. 4.2.3 [3]
His very life-span is that *dhruva* cup; by it his self is joined together and his joints are made continuous. Therefore, for this *acāvāka*, the final cup remains unextracted. 4.2.3. [4]
Then he brings down the King Soma;

he pours out a third of the *vasatīvarī* waters, and thus that joint is reached. He performs the first part of the subsequent pressing as the final part of the preceding one; for what belongs to the subsequent pressing—

He performs that first [rite] which belongs to the preceding [savana]; that is the best. He interlinks them; therefore these joints (parvāṇi) are interlinked—this one thus, and this one thus. It is exactly the same at the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana).
Even while it remains unextracted from this Āgnīdhra, the last cup becomes [ready] for the Acāvāka;

then he pours out the third portion of the *vasatīvarī* waters. That constitutes the joint [of the ritual]. He makes the first part of the subsequent pressing the last part of the preceding one; what belongs to the subsequent pressing he makes first, and what belongs to the preceding pressing he makes last.
He interweaves it; therefore these joints are interwoven—this one thus, this one thus.
Because his self is joined by this [sacrifice], therefore this is his life-span.
This very [cow] is the wish-fulfilling cow, the special portion for Indra.

He draws it out for him from exactly three *ukthas* at the morning pressing and from three at the midday pressing; that makes six times. There are six seasons, and the seasons indeed ripen all these desires. By this means, it is truly Indra’s own share, a cow of plenty. 4.2.3 [7]
He draws that cup without a *puroruc* formula;
for the *uktha* is a *puroruc*, and the *ṛc* is a *puroruc*, while the *sāman* is the cup-draught.
Now, whatever else he mutters, that is the *yajus*. These [three] were originally on one side of the *ṛcs*; they were on the other side.
"More than half [of it] belongs to the Yajus, and more than half to the Sāmans.
(4.2.3.8) Those gods said, "Come, let us place these [Sāmans] within the Yajus; thus this knowledge will become even more abundant.
They placed them within the Yajus, and from that time on, this knowledge became even more abundant. (4.2.3.9)
As for the fact that he draws it without a *puroruk*:
the *uktha* is indeed the *puroruk*, for the *ṛc* is the *puroruk*, and the *ṛc* is the *uktha*.
Since he draws it apart from the *ukthas*, by that very act this [cup] of his comes to possess a *puroruk*.
Therefore, he draws [the cup] without a puroruk-formula. 4.2.3.
Now, therefore, he indeed draws it:
"Thou art taken with a support; for Indra, the mighty, the vigorous, thee! For Indra is indeed...

The deity of the sacrifice is therefore; thus he says, "To Indra thee! When he says, "To the mighty, to the vigorous," he thereby means "to the powerful. When he says, "I take the Ukthavya," he indeed takes it for the sake of the Ukthas. When he says, "O Indra, that which is thy great vigor," he thereby means "that which is thy power, O Indra. [He says] "To him thee! To Viṣṇu thee!"—this is for the sake of the sacrifice.
He draws it for the sake of long life; therefore he says, "For thee, for Viṣṇu. "This is thy womb; for the hymns (ukthas) thee!"—thus he deposits it, for he draws it for the hymns.
He divides it.
"I take thee, the one who favors the gods, for the gods, for the life of the sacrifice"—thus he should perform the instruction;
yet he should divide [the portions] according to the respective deities:
"For Mitra and Varuṇa, thee! 4.2.3. [12]
"I take thee for the gods' favor, for the life of the sacrifice"—thus [he takes it] for the Maitrāvaruṇa;

for they chant praises for him in verses addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa, he recites the *anuśaṃsa* in verses addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa, and he offers the oblation with a verse addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa. 4.2.3.
"For Indra thee!"

"I take thee for the gods' favor, for the life of the sacrifice," he says; [this is] for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, for they praise him with verses addressed to Indra, he recites the *anuśaṃsa* with verses addressed to Indra, and he sacrifices with a verse addressed to Indra. 4.2.3. "Thee for Indra and Agni!"

"I take [the draught] for the gods' favor, for the life of the sacrifice"—thus [he says] for the Acchāvāka; for they praise him with verses addressed to Indra and Agni, he recites the *anuśaṃsana* for Indra and Agni, and he offers the oblation with a verse addressed to Indra and Agni. "For thee, O Indra!"—thus at the midday pressing;
for the midday pressing belongs to Indra. 4.2.3. [15]
Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus draw it out separately:
"Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, the one who wins the gods, for the gods; the one who wins the hymns, for the hymns; acceptable to Mitra and Varuna; this is thine."
He deposits it with the formula, "The womb for Mitra and Varuṇa, thee! He touches the vessel with, "Thou art a renewed oblation. [4.2.3.16] "Thou art taken with a support;
for the gods thee, the god-pleasing; for the hymns thee, the hymn-pleasing; acceptable to Indra."

"I take this; this is your womb; for Indra you!"—with these words he deposits it. "Thou art a renewed oblation," with these words he touches the vessel. "Thou art taken with a support; for the gods thee, the god-pleasing; for the hymns thee, the hymn-pleasing; for Indra and Agni."

"I take what is favored; this is your womb; for Indra and Agni, you!"—with these words he deposits it. Here he does not touch the vessel with "Thou art the re-offering. At the midday pressing, he touches the vessel with "For Indra, thee! For Indra, thee! for the midday pressing belongs to Indra.
Twice he touches the vessel with "Thou art the re-offering," and silently a third time.
He sets it down. 4.2.3.[18] One should not indeed take it with the *upayāma* formula;
one should not place it in the womb [of the altar], for it has already been taken with the *upayāma* formula at the very beginning.
It is placed first upon the womb for the sake of kinship; he would indeed commit a violation of kinship if he were to take it here with a libation-vessel (*upayāma*).

If he were to set it down upon the womb, then, since he is about to take another draught from this vessel, he should not heed that [formula "thou art a sacrificial oblation"] but should simply set it down silently. 4.2.4. [1]
This indeed is his vital breath (*prāṇa*):
that which is in front is Vaiśvānara, and that which is behind is Dhruva. Formerly, they used to draw these two cups first, namely the Dhruva and the Vaiśvānara.

Of these two, even now only one is taken; that [cup] is indeed fixed. If he should recite it for the Carakas or from whatever source, he should pour it into the cup of the sacrificer; then this very one [is poured] into the Hotṛ's cup.
Or rather, that which is below his navel.
This is that very self of his; this is his life itself. Therefore, he takes [the Soma] with this [ladle].
For this [ladle] is a vessel (sthālī), and he takes it with a vessel. This [ladle] is ageless and immortal; for life is ageless and immortal. Therefore, he takes it with this. 4.2.4. [3]
He draws it full;
for that which is full is everything, and that which is life is everything; therefore he draws it full. 4.2.4 [4]
He draws [the cup] for Vaiśvānara.
Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; the year is life. Therefore, he draws [the cup] for Vaiśvānara. 4.2.4.[5]
It is drawn at the morning pressing;
it remains lying there until this time, and thus he carries it through all the pressings.
One should not pour it out while the Stotra is being chanted.
If he were to pour it out while the stotra is being chanted, the sacrificer would surely not live beyond a year; therefore,
he pours it out while the śastra is being recited.

Thus he leads this twelfth *stotra* across; in this way he attains a life-span that passes from one stage to the next, and so the sacrificer lives long. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should sit through the *agniṣṭoma*;
he should not move away from this oblation, nor should he urinate; in this way he attains a full life-span, for this [oblation] is indeed his life-span. Thus it is.
He attains a full lifespan. 4.2.4.[8] Whatever part of him is below the navel, that is his very self (*ātman*); if he were to move away before this oblation is offered, or if he should die...
Or he might cause [the Soma] to flow out; he would surely urinate, thinking, "Lest I urinate while the *dhruva* cup is present.
Therefore, the *agniṣṭoma* indeed remains seated. That is truly so; for this belongs to the sacrificer himself, as it is his own self.
He, indeed, remains seated at the *agniṣṭoma*.

Soma is indeed glory; therefore, both he who obtains [something] at the Soma sacrifice and he who does not both come [to the feast]. They come for the very purpose of beholding this glory. Now, when the Brahmins, having spread out together, consume [the remains], they place that glory within themselves. He who knows thus becomes glory itself.
The learned man eats [the remains]. 4.2.4.[10] Now, these [priests], while crawling along, crawl having placed this glory (yaśas) within the Agniṣṭoma-sitting; they thus turn away from that glory.
Therefore, having grasped it, he places that glory back into himself; indeed, among them, he alone is the most glorious.
Having become thus, he goes forth— he who, knowing this, becomes a performer of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
4.2.4.[11] Now, both the gods and the Asuras,
both being the offspring of Prajāpati, contended for this sacrifice, their father Prajāpati.
"In this year it shall be ours; in this [year] it shall be ours.
Then the gods, praising and toiling, moved forward; they saw this Agniṣṭomasadya sacrifice.
By means of this Agniṣṭomasadya, they appropriated the entire sacrifice and excluded the Asuras from the sacrifice. And so it is likewise for us.
Thus, by means of this Agniṣṭomasad cup, he encompasses the entire sacrifice; he excludes his rivals from the sacrifice. Therefore, it is indeed called the Agniṣṭomasad.
Having drawn it, he places it in the northern Havirdhāna cart, thinking, "The cups are the vital breaths; let me not confuse the vital breaths," on the scattered [grain].
Or he deposits the other cups; then, having shifted this one aside, he places it without even a blade of grass intervening.
For that part of his [body] which is above the navel—that is, what is above—is, as it were, the upper part of his self.

That which is strewn above the navel is indeed this [body]; therefore, he places [the offering] on what is strewn. Then, having spread this [grass] out, he places it without even a blade of grass being interposed—whatever part of him is below the navel.

Now, that which is below the navel is, as it were, the lower part of this self; and this [earth], being below, is as it were the lower part. Therefore, having pushed it aside, he sets it down without even a blade of grass intervening. 4.2.4 [16]
This indeed is Prajāpati,

who is this sacrifice being performed, from whom these creatures were born, and even now they are born after him. Because he sets them down upon what has been strewn, therefore the creatures follow after them.

Those [beings] that are born from something other than their own self find support on this earth; indeed, those that stand by means of hooves find support on this earth through something other than their own self. Now, when he has spread this [earth] out and places [the fire-pan] upon it without interposing even a blade of grass, therefore those offspring which are born after him find support on this earth through their own selves.

And humans and beasts of prey. This, indeed, he makes another layer over this very one when he strews [the grass]; and because he places those [bricks] on what has been strewn, therefore those offspring which are born after them establish themselves upon this earth by means of their own hooves.
This, indeed, is that: they offer into the Āhavanīya fire the cake, the parched grains, the groats, the curds, and the clotted curds.

It is just as if one were to pour [food] into the mouth; so it is with that. Yet this [breath] remains uniform, like water. Therefore, whatever food of various forms he eats with this mouth, he causes it to flow out as something of a single form through this breath—namely, water.
Now, as for why it is called *dhruva*: Once,
while the gods were performing a sacrifice, they were afraid of an attack by the Asuras and Rakṣasas.

The Asuras and Rakṣases placed themselves to their right; they repelled those [enemies] and struck down these southern cups (grahas), and they even struck down this southern oblation-holder (havirdhāna). But they were unable to strike down this very one—that northern oblation-holder.
He made the southern *havirdhāna* firm. Because they were unable to lift it up, it is therefore called *dhruva*.
They guard it;
for this is the head of that *gāyatrī*, and the sacrifice is indeed the *gāyatrī*. There are twelve *stotras*.

There are twelve sacrificial formulas; that makes twenty-four. The Gāyatrī indeed consists of twenty-four syllables; this [Sāman] is its head. Prosperity (*śrī*) is indeed the head, for prosperity is the head. Therefore, when someone is the most excellent in a region, they say of him, "He is the head of that region. If he were to suffer distress, the most excellent one would suffer distress; but the most excellent one is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), so that the sacrificer may not suffer distress.
"Because they are distressed, therefore they protect [it]. This [sacrifice] is indeed a calf; the Gāyatrī is this [cow], for the sacrifice is the Gāyatrī. There are twelve stotras and twelve śastras.

That [altar] consists of twenty-four [bricks]; the Gāyatrī indeed has twenty-four syllables; this [altar] is its calf. When they guard it, they guard these calves for the sake of milking; just as one milks this milk for the sake of the calves, so does this Gāyatrī milk all desires for the sacrificer. Therefore, they guard it. 4.2.4. [22]
Now, as for the fact that the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ both step out and step forward:
just as one would attend to a cow with its calf tied, so do they attend to this cup; he pours it out.
He thereby causes this Gāyatrī to flow forth, thinking, "May this Gāyatrī, being offered, milk all desires for the sacrificer.
Therefore, he pours it out.
He pours it out as follows.
"Steadfastly with a steadfast mind, I pour down Soma," he says, or "I take it.

"So that Indra may make our people free from enemies and of one mind"—by this he means: "So that Indra may make these subjects, these people, free from enemies and of one mind for the sake of prosperity, glory, and the eating of food. 4.2.4 [24]
Now, therefore, he indeed draws [the cup]:
"The head of heaven, the messenger of earth, Vaiśvānara born in the cosmic order (ṛta), Agni— the sage, the sovereign,
the guest of men— the gods generated as a vessel for their mouths."
"You are taken with a support;
you are the firm one, the firm abode, the firmest of the firm, the most immovable of the immovable. This is your womb:
for Vaiśvānara, for you! Having thus set it down, having spread it out without placing even a blade of grass in between—for he [is offered] to Vaiśvānara.
He takes [the cups]. Having taken the cups and having gone out, he performs the oblation of the droplets; as for that which is the oblation of the droplets—
He offers [the drops]. Whatever drops of his spill here, those he thereby makes well-disposed (*svagākṛ*) in the Āhavanīya fire;
for the Āhavanīya is the foundation of oblations. Therefore, he performs the offering of the drops.
4.2.5. He offers, saying: "Thy drop that spills, thy stalk that spills"—for whatever small portion (*stoka*) spills, that is it.
"The drop has told that which is yours," he says; by this he means the stalk. "The stalk shaken by the pressing-stones from the lap of the two bowls," he says;
for it is indeed shaken by the pressing-stone and spills from the two filtering-sieves.
Or, "from the Adhvaryu or from the filter," he says; for it spills either from the hands of the Adhvaryu or from the filter. "That [drop] of yours I offer with my mind."

"Vaṣaṭ! Svāhā!"—just as an oblation is offered when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, so does this become for him. 4.2.5 [3] Then, from the strewn sacrificial altar (*vedi*), the Adhvaryu takes two blades of grass; these two Adhvaryus are the first to proceed.

Now, the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the up-breath (*udāna*) are the *prastotṛ* of the sacrifice; speech itself is the *udgātṛ* of the sacrifice; the self (*ātman*) is Prajāpati, the *yajamāna* of the sacrifice;
and the healer, or the diffused breath (*vyāna*), is the *pratihartṛ*.
These five officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) the sacrificer takes hold of; for as great as all this sacrifice is, so great are these.
There are five officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), for the sacrifice is fivefold; thus the sacrificer thereby takes hold of the sacrifice itself.
Then he throws away one blade of grass toward the *cātvāla* pit with the formula, "Thou art the stepping-off place of the gods," for where indeed the gods...
By means of the sacrifice, they attained the heavenly world; from this *cātvāla* pit, they ascended upwards toward the heavenly world.
Thus, he causes the sacrificer himself to follow along that path leading to heaven.
Then, [he takes] another blade of grass.
He throws it down silently in front of the Udgātṛs. The Udgātṛs are indeed this Stoma, which is Prajāpati; he joins together all this, and in him all this comes into being.
For him, he thus places this blade of grass as a cover. Thus, indeed, he does not join with the Adhvaryu, nor does he come into being with him. Now, when...
"For here the *udgātṛ*s chant, they indeed chant. 4.2.5.
[7] Then he introduces the *stotra* with the words, "Soma purifies himself. He indeed introduces the *stotra* while facing away, and [the chant proceeds] away from him.

These *pavamāna* chants are indeed praises that have turned back toward the gods; for by means of these, the gods attained the heavenly world moving forward. Therefore, he introduces the chant while moving forward, and they chant while moving forward. Other chants, however, are [introduced with the words], "Turn back! (4.2.5).
They chant the Dhurya verses with a turning back; for these creatures have turned back toward these chants. Therefore, these creatures are born again, turning back toward [the world].
Now, as to why they chant the Bahiṣpavamāna here.
In this place, indeed, yonder sun was at first;
the seasons, having encompassed it, ascended from here upwards toward the heavenly world. That very sun shines, established in the seasons.
In the same way, the officiating priests, having encompassed the sacrificer, ascend from here upwards toward the heavenly world.
Therefore, they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* here. Indeed, this *bahiṣpavamāna* is a ship that leads to heaven; the officiating priests are its oars and rudders.

He who is censurable is the only one who can cause one to sink in the crossing over to the heavenly world. Just as one might board a full boat and cause it to sink, so does he cause this [sacrifice] to sink. Indeed, the entire sacrifice is a boat for reaching heaven;
therefore, one should strive to avoid anyone censurable from every sacrifice. 4.2.5. [11]
Then, having been praised, he utters this speech:
"O Agnīdh, distribute the fires; strew the sacrificial grass (barhis);
prepare the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas); bring the animal victim! Thus the Agnīdh distributes the fires; he kindles them; and on the strewn sacrificial grass, he strews it.
"He kindles [the fire], thinking, 'I shall offer to the gods'; thus he prepares the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), for he is about to proceed with the cakes.
"Come, O animal!"—thus he approaches the animal, for he is about to dedicate it. 4.2.5.
[12] Then, having entered again...

He draws the Āśvina cup; having drawn the Āśvina cup and gone out, he encircles the sacrificial post; having encircled the post, he dedicates the animal victim. He thereby places essence into it. At the morning pressing, it is sacrificed.
Remaining unpressed until the third pressing, it lies there; thus he places essence into this entire sacrifice and permeates the whole sacrifice with essence.
Therefore, at the Agniṣṭoma, one sacrifices an animal dedicated to Agni.
For that is consistent with the hair [of the sacrifice]: if it be an Agniṣṭoma, he should immolate an animal for Agni;
if it be an Ukthya, he should immolate a second one for Indra and Agni, for the Ukthas belong to Indra and Agni;
if it be a Ṣoḍaśin, he should immolate a third one for Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin belongs to Indra; if it be an Atirātra, [he should immolate] one for Sarasvatī.

One should offer a fourth [victim]; for Sarasvatī is speech, and speech is female, and the night is female; thus he distinguishes the sacrificial rites according to their proper order. Then he proceeds with the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes.
"Soma is indeed a god, for Soma is in heaven. Soma was indeed Vṛtra;
that which is the mountains and the rocks is his body, and from that this herb called *uśanā* is born," so said Śvetaketu Auddālaki. "Having brought that [herb] here, they press it. 4.2.5. [16]

When he immolates the victim, he thereby bestows essence upon it; then, when he proceeds with the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) belonging to the pressings, he thereby bestows the vital sap (medha) upon it. Thus, this [victim] of his becomes truly Soma itself. 4.2.5. [17]
All [the offerings] belong to Indra.
Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore, all belong to Indra.
Now, as for the fact that there are the cake, the parched grains, the groats, the curds, and the clotted curd—it is those deities of the sacrifice who are present.
"They were well-pleased," [so it is said].
4.2.5.[19] Indeed, having eaten this cake, one desires: "May I eat parched grains; may I eat gruel."
"I would eat curd; I would eat *āmikṣā*. These are all his desires: "May those who are the deities of the sacrifice be well-pleased.
Now, as for the fact that this *maitrāvaruṇī payasyā* is prescribed only at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) and not for the other two pressings. 4.2.5. [20]
The Gāyatrī indeed carries the morning pressing;
the Triṣṭubh carries the midday pressing, and the Jagatī carries the third pressing. Now, the Triṣṭubh carries the midday pressing not alone, but together with the Gāyatrī.
The *jagatī* is not alone, accompanied by the *bṛhatī*; the third pressing is [accompanied] by the *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, and *kakubh*, and by the *anuṣṭubh*. 4.2.5.
[21] The *gāyatrī* alone carries the morning pressing;
it does so together with these two *paṅkti*s and the *stotrapaṅkti*.

With the *haviṣpaṅkti* there are four butter-offerings; the *bahiṣpavamāna* is the fifth. This five-part *paṅkti*—together with this sequence of stotras—the *gāyatrī* alone carries the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) belongs to Indra.

The parched grains are for the two Aśvins, the groats for Pūṣan, the curdled milk for Sarasvatī, and the whey for Mitra and Varuṇa; this is the five-footed *paṅkti*. By means of this *haviṣpaṅkti*, the *gāyatrī*—though not alone—carries the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). It is for the sake of the perfection of this very *paṅkti* that she [the *gāyatrī*] is present at the morning pressing itself.
The curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa is prescribed; it does not belong to the other two pressings.
Having consumed [the portion], and having said, "We have been invited together," he rises, taking a piece of the sacrificial cake.

Now, when the Acāvāka, having sat down near him, recites, then [the sacrificer], placing a piece of the sacrificial cake in his hand, says to him: "O Acāvāka, speak what you have to say. For the Acāvāka had indeed been left behind; Indra and Agni then restored him to wholeness.

For the procreation of offspring, the Acāvāka belongs to Indra and Agni; he attains success through this oblation, by placing this fragment of the sacrificial cake in his hand, and by that ancestral lineage which he recites when he speaks after it. 4.3.1. [3]
When the Acāvāka has sat down, he proceeds with the seasonal cups (ṛtugraha). Now, as to why he proceeds with the seasonal cups once the Acāvāka has sat down:
the Acāvāka is indeed a pair; for the Acāvāka belongs to Indra and Agni, and Indra and Agni are two—a pair, for a pair is productive.
From this pair, from this source of generation, he generates the seasons and the year.
Furthermore, as to why he proceeds with the seasonal cups (ṛtugraha) when the Acāvāka is seated: the seasons indeed constitute the entire year.

He produces all this; therefore, when the *graha* has been set down, the *acāvāka* proceeds with the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*). One should indeed draw twelve of them, for there are twelve months in a year; therefore, there are twelve.
One may take thirteen, or one may even take thirteen, thinking, "There is a thirteenth month"; however, one should take only twelve, for this is the perfect correspondence.
He takes from the *droṇakalaśa*.
The Droṇakalaśa is indeed Prajāpati; from this Prajāpati he brings forth the seasons and the year.
He draws [the Soma] with two vessels that have openings on both sides.
Whence could there be ends for those two which face in both directions?
Therefore, this year revolves as something without end; having taken it up, he does not set it down; therefore, this year is unestablished.
He does not recite an invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), for he indeed summons [the season] with the invitatory verse; whether it be by day or by night, this season has already arrived.
He does not perform the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvaṣaṭkāra*) lest he should exclude the seasons. They both take up the first two cups together.
This entire [universe] is indeed encompassed by the year; thus this whole world is encompassed by the year. One of the two departs from it. 4.3.1.
[9] One of the two departs from it.
One steps out first, and the other enters; therefore these months proceed in succession.
