For if both were to step out together, or if both were to enter together, these months would surely go separately.
Therefore, one indeed steps out and the other enters. 4.3.1 [10]
With "With the season," those two perform six [pressings]; with that they created the day. With "With the seasons," they performed four; with that they created the night.
If it had been only this much, there would have been only night, and it would not have expanded. 4.3.1. [11]
These two indeed move twice over from above with the words "by the season. The gods placed the day in front; therefore, this is today the day, then the night, then tomorrow the day will be.
Thus, by the word "season," the gods [established the order].

With the words, "He created men by means of the seasons," he created cattle. Because they created cattle in the middle [of the sequence], therefore these cattle are seized on both sides and have come under the control of human beings.
Having performed six [steps] with the formula, "Those two [worlds] by means of the seasons," [he proceeds].
Otherwise the two vessels are inverted; having performed four [pressings] with the seasons, the two vessels are inverted. On one side the gods created the day, on the other side the night;
on one side the gods created human beings, on the other side the cattle. 4.3.1. [14]
Now, therefore, he indeed draws [the cups].
"Thou art taken with a support; for Madhu thee!"—thus the Adhvaryu draws; "Thou art taken with a support; for Mādhava thee!"—thus the Pratiprasthātṛ draws. These two [form] the pair.
These two belong to spring; because in spring the plants are born and the trees bear fruit, therefore these two are Madhu and Mādhava.
You are taken with a support.
With "For Śukra thee," the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]; with "Thou art taken with a support; for Śuci thee," the Pratiprasthātṛ [draws].
These two indeed are the cups of the summer season. Because it burns most intensely during these two [months], therefore they are called Śukra and Śuci.

"Thou art taken with a support; for Nabhas thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu takes [the draught]; "Thou art taken with a support; for Nabhasya thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [takes his]. These two indeed belong to the rainy season (*vārṣika*); from yonder sky it rains; therefore these two are called Nabhas and Nabhasya. 4.3.1. [17]
"You are taken with a support;

for sap, you!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]. "You are taken with a support; for strength, you!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [draws]. These two [cups] belong to the autumn. Because in autumn the sap and the plants ripen, therefore it is so.

"Haitāviṣa and Ūrja. 4.3.1.[18] "Thou art taken with a support; for Sahas [I take thee]," with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]; "Thou art taken with a support; for Sahasya [I take thee]," with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [draws].
These two are the winter cups. For when it is winter, these creatures, as it were, submit to their own [power].

He brings them under his control; therefore, these two are called Saha and Sahasya. "Thou art taken with a support; for Tapas thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]; "Thou art taken with a support; for Tapasya thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ draws [the cup].
These two are indeed the two Śaiśiras (months of winter). Because it freezes most intensely during these two, therefore these two are called Tapas and Tapasya.
And regarding the *tapasya* cup:
"Thou art taken with a support;
for Aṃhasaspati thee!"—with these words he draws the thirteenth cup, if there is a thirteenth.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ takes [the cup]; the Adhvaryu pours the residue into the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup, or the Adhvaryu pours the residue into the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup;
he brings the portion for consumption. 4.3.1. [21] Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, with the cup that has not been consumed...
He draws the draught for Indra and Agni.
As to why he draws the draught for Indra and Agni with a cup that has not been consumed:
one does not pronounce the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call for the seasonal draughts; it is for these [seasonal draughts] that he intends to draw the draught for Indra and Agni.
Therefore, these [libations] for him are accompanied by the *anuvaṣaṭ* call with the Aindrāgna [verse].
Furthermore, as to why he draws the Aindrāgna cup:
he has indeed brought forth all this [universe], since he drew the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*). 4.3.1. [22]

He brings forth all this; he establishes all this very thing in out-breathing (prāṇa) and up-breathing (udāna). Thus, all this is established in out-breathing and up-breathing, for Indra and Agni are out-breathing and up-breathing; these two, heaven and earth, are out-breathing and up-breathing, for upon them all this is established. 4.3.1. [23]
Furthermore, as to why he draws the draught for Indra and Agni:
he has indeed procreated all this when he drew the seasonal draughts;
having procreated all this, he now places the out-breathing and the in-breathing within this very universe.
These two, prāṇa and udāna, are placed within this entire [body]. 4.3.1.[24] Now, therefore, he takes up [the draught]:
"O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed juice; [come] with songs to the desirable cloud. Drink of this!"
"Sent forth for wisdom! You are taken with a support; O Indra and Agni, you are he whom I take. This is your womb;
for Indra and Agni, you!"—with these words he deposits it, for it is indeed for Indra and Agni that he draws it.
Then he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup.

He generated all this; for he drew the seasonal cups (ṛtugraha). If it had been only as much as that, then there would have been only as many creatures as were created in the beginning, and they would not have multiplied.
Now, as for the fact that he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup:
it is this very universe, these creatures, that he thereby causes to be released according to their respective natures;
therefore these creatures are born again and again. He draws it with the Śukra vessel; this—
Verily, that which shines yonder is Śukra; its rays are the Viśve Devās. Therefore, he draws [the cup] with the Śukra vessel.
4.3.1.[27] Now, therefore, he indeed draws it:
"O protectors, supporters of men, Viśve Devās, come hither! O bounteous ones, [come] to the pressed juice of the donor."
"You are taken with a support; for all the gods you, this is your womb;
for all the gods you"—with these words he sets it down, for he draws it for all the gods.
Indeed, the Hotṛ praises when he recites.
Therefore, the Adhvaryu responds to him who thus recites; hence it is called the *pratigara* (response).
He calls out to him while he is seated facing east.
Or else, all others perform the priestly office for the Udgātṛ facing eastward; thus, indeed, his priestly office is performed even beforehand. Prajāpati, verily, is the Udgātṛ.

The Hotṛ is the male, and this Prajāpati is the Udgātṛ; he pours seed into the female, the Ṛc, which is the Hotṛ. When it has been praised, the Hotṛ brings that seed forth by means of the Śastra; he sharpens it, just as this person is sharpened.
Because he sharpens it (śyati), therefore it is called Śastra. 4.3.2 [4]
Having supported it, he responds;
he thus causes this emitted seed to be pressed down.
Now, if he were to respond while standing with his face turned away, that emitted seed would indeed perish and no offspring would be produced; but they [respond] facing each other.
And having become this, they cause this emitted semen to procreate. 4.3.2.
[5] The meters (candāṃsi) indeed have their power exhausted by the gods;
for by means of the meters, the gods attained the heavenly world. Therefore, one must not be intoxicated.
The response (*pratigara*) is indeed intoxication; that which is the exhilaration in the *ṛc* is the essence (*rasa*) in the *sāman*.
He thus places this essence into the meters themselves and makes them free from weariness. With those [meters] that are free from weariness, they extend the sacrifice.
Therefore, if he should recite by half-verses...

He should respond at every half-verse if he recites by the half-verses; he should respond at every foot if he recites by the feet. For when one who is reciting draws breath, the Asuras and Rakṣases descend upon the sacrifice; he joins [the recitation] together with the response so that the destructive Rakṣases do not descend upon it.
And thus he cuts off for the sacrificer the world of his rival.
4.3.2. [7] In the beginning, indeed, the meters consisted of four syllables each. Then the Jagatī flew toward Soma; she [lost] three syllables.
Having abandoned it, Triṣṭubh then went away; she pursued Soma, but having abandoned one syllable, she went away. Then Gāyatrī pursued Soma;
she came back, taking those syllables and bringing Soma with them. Thereupon Gāyatrī became eight-syllabled;
therefore they say, "Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables. 4.3.2. [8]
With her they performed the morning pressing;
therefore the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī. With that same [metre] they performed the midday pressing; then the Triṣṭubh said to her, "I will come to you with three syllables; come to me."

"Call me; do not exclude me from the sacrifice," she said. "So be it," he replied, and he called her. Thereupon the *triṣṭubh* became eleven-syllabled; therefore they say, "The midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*.
With that very [metre], they performed the third pressing.
The Jagatī said to her: "I will come to you with one syllable; invite me, lest I go out from the sacrifice. "So be it," she replied, and she invited her. Thereupon the Jagatī became twelve-syllabled;
therefore they say, "The third pressing belongs to the Jagatī. 4.3.2. [10]
Regarding this they say: "All the pressings are indeed Gāyatrī, for it is the Gāyatrī that approaches here.

Therefore, one should respond at the morning pressing when it is fully established, for the Gāyatrī has arrived when it is fully established. At the midday pressing, [the response] should contain the word "mada" (intoxication) once, for there is only one syllable [in excess].
By departing from it and returning to it, he thus causes this [sacrifice] to prosper; he makes it complete.
4.3.2. [11] Where the *triṣṭubh* verses are recited, there is the "threefold" at the third pressing, for there are three syllables.
Having left them behind, he comes; by means of these very [verses], he thus causes her to prosper and makes her complete.
Where the *dyāvāpṛthivya* hymn is recited—these two, heaven and earth, are indeed what these creatures subsist upon.

Thus he places the essence into these very two, heaven and earth; these creatures subsist upon these two, which are full of essence and worthy of being lived upon. He should respond with "Om" alone, for that is the Truth, and the gods know that. 4.3.2. [13] Now, some respond with "Othāmo daivā vāk," saying, "The response is speech; thus we attain speech."

Regarding this, they say one should not do so; for when one responds with speech, his speech becomes merely acquired, since he responds with speech. Therefore, one should respond only with "Om," for that is the Truth, and the gods know that. 4.3.3.
[1] He presses [the Soma], saying, "iha! iha! (here! here!).
By saying "the great, the great," he thus causes Indra to come hither; by saying "the great, the great," he thus causes Indra to come hither.
He draws the Śukra and Manthin cups first, for this pressing is characterized by the Śukra; then the Āgrayaṇa.
For this [cup] is drawn at all the pressings; then the Marutvatīya, and then the Ukthya, for the *ukthas* (recitations) occur here as well.
Regarding this, some indeed, having drawn the Ukthya, then draw the Marutvatīya; but that is not so.
Having drawn the Marutvatīya cup, he should then draw the Ukthya.
Indeed, these five cups he draws: this midday Pavamāna is indeed the thunderbolt;
therefore it consists of fifteen [verses] and has five Sāmans, for the thunderbolt is fifteenfold. He [the sacrificer] [proceeds] with these...
With five grasps he strikes these five fingers; indeed, with the fingers one strikes. 4.3.3.[5] Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra.
Having struck down Vṛtra, who is evil, he [remained] in the conquered, fearless, and secure realm.

He led the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) southward; therefore even now, whenever they chant with this Mādhyandina Pavamāna, then the sacrificial fees are led southward in a conquered, fearless, and secure place. In the same way, he hurls the thunderbolt at evil and at his hateful rival by means of these five cups; having slain Vṛtra, that is, evil, he [stands] in a conquered place.
"In fear and in danger, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) leads one away; therefore, for this reason, he draws these five cups.
Now, as to why he draws the Marutvatīya cups:
that which is the midday pressing is indeed Indra’s exclusive libation (niṣkevalya)."
With that [soma], he sought to slay Vṛtra; with that, he sought to conquer. The Maruts, however, having departed, stood by the *aśvattha* tree.
Indra is the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the Maruts are the common people (*viś*). Indeed, through the common people, a nobleman becomes powerful.
Therefore, the two *ṛtupātra* vessels should be made of *aśvattha* wood; yet they are indeed made of *kārṣmarya* wood. 4.3.3. [7]
Indra addressed them, saying, "Turn toward me; with your strength I shall slay Vṛtra. They said, "What will be ours from that? For them he drew these two Marutvatīya cups. 4.3.3. [8]
They said, "Let us approach him with our vigor after having hidden it away. Having hidden it away, they indeed approached him with their vigor.
Indra perceived this, thinking, "They have approached me with their vigor after having hidden it away.
He said, "Approach me together with your vigor! "Then, for us, take a third draught," they replied.

From them he drew this third cup, saying, "Thou art taken with a support; thee for the Maruts' vigor! They returned to him together with their vigor; with them he conquered, and with them he slew Vṛtra. Indra is the nobility (kṣatra) and the Maruts are the common people (viś); indeed, by means of the common people, a kṣatriya becomes powerful. Thus, he places that power within the nobility itself.
Therefore, he draws the cups for Indra accompanied by the Maruts (marutvatīya).
He should indeed draw [the cup] for Indra alone accompanied by the Maruts;
he should not draw it for the Maruts either. Even if he were to draw it for the Maruts...

If he were to draw [the cup] for the Maruts, he would indeed make the people (viś) rise up against the nobility (kṣatra). But by this [offering], he causes the Maruts to follow Indra; thus he makes the people submissive to the nobility, acting in accordance with it and following its path. Therefore, one should draw [the cup] for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and not for the Maruts alone. 4.3.3. [11]
He was indeed afraid they might depart from him, thinking, "Lest these should depart from me, lest another [deity] should be supported instead. He thus made them non-departing;
therefore, one should draw [the cup] for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, but not for the Maruts alone. 4.3.3. [12]
He draws [the cups] with two seasonal vessels (*ṛtupātra*).

The seasons are indeed the year, and the sacrifice is that [year]. Those [seasons] are directly manifested at this morning pressing when he draws the seasonal cups; but here at the midday pressing, they are manifested indirectly.
They provide for the pressing when he draws the Marutvatīya cups with the two Ṛtu vessels. The Maruts are indeed the subjects (viś), and the subjects are food;
the seasons cook all this food here. Therefore, he draws the Marutvatīya cups with the two Ṛtu vessels. 4.3.3. [13]
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma here, just as you drank of the pressed juice at Śāryāta’s sacrifice.
Under your guidance and in your protection, O Hero, the sages who perform excellent sacrifices desire to win [favor]."
"You are taken with a support; for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, you! This is your birthplace; for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, you! [4.3.3.14] "The bull accompanied by the Maruts..."
We invoke here for new protection that Indra, who has grown great, the foeless warrior, the divine ruler, the all-conquering, the fierce bestower of victory.
You are taken with a support; I take you for Indra accompanied by the Maruts. This [is the draught].

"Thou art their source; for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, thee! Thou art taken with a support; for the strength of the Maruts, thee!"—with these words he draws the third cup. Then he draws the cup for Mahendra.

Indra was indeed mixed with evil when he was together with the Viś and the Maruts; just as one might eat from a common vessel with the Viś for the sake of victory, so it was when they drew this cup for him in common with the Maruts. 4.3.3. [16]

The gods, when all had been conquered and was free from fear and destruction, drew him out from everything evil—just as one would pull a reed from its sheath—by taking up the draught for Mahendra. In the same way, this sacrificer now is freed from everything evil by taking up the draught for Mahendra; he becomes like a reed stripped of its sheath.
He draws the cup.
4.3.3.[17] And as to why he draws the Māhendra cup:
before the slaying of Vṛtra, this one was indeed Indra; but after the slaying of Vṛtra...
Just as a great king becomes [known] as "the Conqueror" after having conquered, so did Mahendra become; therefore, he draws the Māhendra cup.

He indeed makes him great for the slaying of Vṛtra; for that very reason, he draws the Māhendra cup. He draws it with the Śukra vessel; for he who shines yonder is indeed the Śukra, and he is truly this very one.
Therefore, he takes [the draught] with the *cukra* vessel.
Now, therefore, he indeed takes it:
"Great is Indra, man-like, filling the people; moreover, doubly powerful, undiminished in his strengths."
"He has indeed grown strong for us through heroic deeds; vast and wide, he has been made well-fashioned by the makers.
"Thou art taken with a support; for Mahendra thee! With these words he deposits it, saying, "This is thy womb; for Mahendra thee," for he draws it for Mahendra.
Then, having introduced the animal, he utters this speech.

"Pressers, press! Unload the mortars! Agnīdh, bring the *āśira* mixture! Be mindful of the Soma!"—thus indeed they press for the third pressing, they unload the mortars for the third pressing, and the Agnīdh brings the *āśira* mixture for the third pressing. For the third pressing.
He cooks a mild *caru* offering. These two pressings—the morning pressing and the midday pressing—are indeed bright and full of essence;
but this third pressing has its brightness drained away. He thus reproduces that very [third pressing] from this midday pressing. And so...
This third pressing has a flavor like sour gruel; therefore, he utters this speech here.
Indeed, they strike down this sacrifice when they perform it;
for when they press the King (Soma), they strike him.
When they kill the sacrificial animal, when they quiet it, and when they dissect it—that is how they kill it;
with the mortar and pestle and the lower and upper grinding stones, they kill the *havis*-sacrifice.
This very sacrifice, being thus killed, was no longer capable of bestowing its fruit.

The gods invigorated him with sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās); because they invigorated him with sacrificial gifts, therefore they are called *dakṣiṇās*. Whatever part of this sacrifice, once it has been slain, falters, that very part he now invigorates for him with sacrificial gifts; thus the sacrifice becomes successful. Therefore, they are called *dakṣiṇās*.
He gives. Regarding this, they give six or twelve [cows] at a Havis-sacrifice;
however, a Soma-sacrifice with less than a hundred as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is not truly so.

This Soma-sacrifice is indeed the manifest sacrifice, for Prajāpati is the sacrifice; and man is nearest to Prajāpati. He [the sacrificer] has a hundred years of life, a hundredfold luster, and a hundredfold vigor; he thus endows him with a hundredfold [gifts], not with less than a hundred. Therefore, this Soma-sacrifice should not have fewer than a hundred as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); it should not indeed be performed with a fee of less than a hundred.

"The officiating priests shall be for the sacrificer; may I not become an object of their eyes, thinking, 'Whom these will surely kill, they will not cause to prosper. 4.3.4. [4] "Truly, there are two kinds of gods."
Now, the gods are indeed [the gods], and those Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in sacred tradition are the human gods.

For them, the sacrifice is divided into two parts: oblations belong to the gods, while sacrificial gifts belong to the human gods—the Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in sacred tradition. By means of oblations alone, one gratifies the gods.

Through sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he gratifies the human gods—the Brahmins who have heard the tradition and are learned in the Vedas—and both these classes of gods, being pleased, carry him to the heavenly world. These sacrificial fees belong indeed to the officiating priests; for they prepare another [body] as his own self.
The sacrifice consists of the Ṛg, the Yajus, the Sāman, and the oblation; that becomes his self in yonder world.

Therefore, regarding those who have brought him forth, he should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) only to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and not to those who are not officiating priests. Then, having returned to the Gārhapatya fire—

He offers the Dakṣiṇā oblations; having tied gold in a fringed cloth and placed it [in the ladle], he offers. "May there be a place for me in the world of the gods"—with this thought indeed one sacrifices who sacrifices.
This sacrifice of his goes forth toward the world of the gods, and the Dakṣiṇā which he gives follows after it. Having taken hold of the Dakṣiṇā, he proceeds.
The Sacrificer (4.3.4).
There are indeed four sacrificial gifts: gold, a cow, a garment, and a horse. That which pertains to the horse is not appropriate [for all].

Or rather, a cow might place a foot [of gold] upon it; therefore, having tied gold to a cloth used for the ten-day sacrifice and placed it [upon the fire], he offers the oblation with two verses addressed to Sūrya. 4.3.4. [8] He offers with two ṛg-verses dedicated to Sūrya.
That world is indeed hidden by darkness; he, having dispelled the darkness by means of this light, ascends to the heavenly world.
Therefore, he offers oblations with two verses addressed to Sūrya.
He offers: "The rays bear aloft that god Jātavedas..."
"Swāhā to Sūrya for all to see!"—with this Gāyatrī verse he offers. This earth is indeed the Gāyatrī; she is the foundation.
Thus, he establishes himself upon this very foundation. 4.3.4 [10]
Then he offers the second oblation with this *triṣṭubh* verse: "The brilliant face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni;
Sūrya has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-region—the soul of all that moves and stands—*svāhā*!"
By this [offering], he approaches the world itself. 4.3.4.
[11] Then, at the Āgnīdhra fire-altar, he offers either two or one oblation. As for that which [he offers] in the fire at the Āgnīdhra—whether two or one—
He offers the oblation. Agni indeed rules over cattle; they settle around him on every side. He gratifies him with this offering;
he, being gratified, gives his consent. With his consent, one bestows [the gift]. 4.3.4. [12] He offers: "O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knowest all ways."
"Drive away from us crooked sin; we shall offer you the most abundant word of homage, Svāhā!
Then, if he intends to give a horse—whether already harnessed or unharnessed—he should offer a second oblation; but if he does not care for it, he need not do so.
He offers: "May this Agni make room for us; may he go before us, shattering our adversaries. This...
"May he win prizes in the contest for prizes; may he, exulting, conquer his enemies—svāhā! For the horse is indeed a winner of prizes. 4.3.4. [14] Then, taking gold, he approaches the hall.
To the south of the altar, the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) stand; he [approaches] along the front.

Standing at the hall, he consecrates it with the mantra: "By means of your form, I have approached your form. For in the beginning, the cattle were not willing to be given away; they stood there having set aside their own forms, presenting themselves only with their physical bodies. Then the gods approached them from the midst of the sacrifice by means of their own forms. Recognizing their own forms, the cattle came toward them with gratified minds.
"Thus they were indeed capable of giving; even so, he now approaches them from the middle of the sacrifice with their own forms.
Recognizing their own forms, they descend [to meet him]; being gratified in mind, they become capable of giving.
"In the same way, may Viśvavedas distribute [the portions] for you. 4.3.4.[15]

Tutha is indeed the Brahman; thus he distributes them by means of the Brahman. The Brahman indeed knows who is worthy of the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇīya*) and who is not; in this way, these gifts of his are given only to one who is worthy of the gift, and not to one who is not. 4.3.4 [16]
"Go by the path of *ṛta*," he says. For whoever goes by the path of the gods, he goes by the path of *ṛta*. "With the moon as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," he says;
thus they go with this light. 4.3.4. [17]
Then he approaches the Sadas, saying:
"Behold the sky, behold the atmosphere! By this he means: "May I discern the world through you, the sacrificial gift. 4.3.4.[18]
Then he looks toward the *sadas*, saying, "Exert yourself with the members of the *sadas*"; by this he means, "May the members of the *sadas* not overlook you.
Then, taking the gold, he approaches the *āgnīdhra*.

"May I today find a Brāhmaṇa who has a father and a grandfather"—for he who is well-known and born of a renowned lineage is one who has a father and a grandfather; and when one gives even a small number of sacrificial fees to a person who is well-known, one wins great merit through them; "a Ṛṣi and of Ṛṣi-descent"—for he who is well-known and learned in the Vedas is such a one.
"The seer, of seer-lineage, with Sudhātṛ as his sacrificial fee"—for he indeed had Sudhātṛ as his sacrificial fee. 4.3.4.
[20] Then, having approached in this manner, he gives gold to the *agnīdh* priest, saying: "Given by us, may it go among the gods. For which...

With a gratified mind and free from doubt, he gives the sacrificial gift; through it he gains great wealth and goes to the world of the gods, thinking, "May there be a place for me in the world of the gods.
He who sacrifices sacrifices with this very thought; thus he makes him one who has attained the world of the gods.
"May it enter the giver," he says; by this he means, "May it enter me. And so these [gifts] do not perish, turning away from him.
In that he gives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) first to the Āgnīdhra— since from him indeed all the gods won immortality— therefore he gives the sacrificial fee first to the Āgnīdhra.
Then, having approached in this very same manner...

He gives gold to the descendant of Atri. For where they recite that morning litany (prātaranuvāka), there in former times they used to praise this [gold]: "Atri was indeed the Hotṛ among the seers; then this seat became filled with the darkness of the Asuras. The seers said to Atri, "Come! Drive away this darkness from here. He...

"Drive away this darkness; he indeed is the light who has driven away this darkness. For him, they brought this light, gold, as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for gold is light. By means of that brilliance and power, the seer drove away the darkness;
and now this [sacrificer] likewise drives away the darkness by means of this very light. Therefore, one gives gold to the descendant of Atri. 4.3.4 [22]
Then to the Brahman;
for the Brahman protects the sacrifice from the south. Then to the Udgātṛ, then to the Hotṛ, then to the two Adhvaryus seated at the *havirdhāna*, and then, having returned, to the Prastotṛ.

Then he gives to the Maitrāvaruṇa, then to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, then to the Potṛ, then to the Neṣṭṛ, then to the Acchāvāka, then to the Unnetṛ, then to the Grāvastut, then to the Subrahmaṇyā, and finally to the Pratihartṛ. For this one is indeed the Pratihartṛ; it is to him that he finally offers this. Thus these [cups] do not perish by turning away from him. 4.3.4. [23]
Then he said, "Recite for Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
At that time, when Prajāpati first gave [the oblation], Indra reflected: "He will surely give away all this; nothing at all will remain for us. He [then] took this...
"Recite for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, as he raises his thunderbolt, so that he may give!"—but then he did not give. Even now, this very same thing happens:
when it is said, "Recite for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, as he raises his thunderbolt, so that he may give! then he does not give.
There are indeed four sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). 4.3.4 [24]

Gold: by this he protects the life-span of his self, for gold is the life-span; he gave it to the Āgnīdhra as he was performing his duties for Agni; therefore even now gold is given to the Āgnīdhra. 4.3.4. [25] Then the cow: by this he protects the vital breath of his self, for the cow is the vital breath, and the cow is food, for food is the vital breath.

He gave that breath to Rudra as the Hotṛ-priest. 4.3.4.[26] Then there was the garment. By this he protects the skin of his own self, for the garment is indeed the skin; he gave that to Bṛhaspati as the Udgātṛ-priest. 4.3.4.[27]

Then there is the horse. The horse is indeed a thunderbolt; he thus places the thunderbolt at the front. He who sacrifices sacrifices with the thought, "May there be a place for me in the world of Yama. Thus, he makes him a sharer in that very world of Yama. He gave it to Yama, the Brahman. 4.3.4. [28]
He receives the gold with the formula:
"May Varuṇa give thee to me for Agni; may I attain immortality through this which Varuṇa bestowed upon Agni; be thou a giver of life to the giver, and a source of joy to me, the receiver. 4.3.4. [29]
Then he approaches the cow with the formula:
"May Varuṇa give thee to me for Rudra. For indeed, Varuṇa gave her to Rudra. [He continues: "May I attain immortality; be thou breath to the giver and vigor to me, the receiver. 4.3.4. [30]
Then he receives the garment with the formula:

"May Varuna give thee to me for Bṛhaspati. For Varuna indeed gave this to Bṛhaspati. [He continues: "May I attain immortality; be a skin to the giver, and a source of joy to me, the receiver. 4.3.4. [31]
Then he approaches the horse with the formula:

"May Varuna give you to me for Yama. For Varuna indeed gave this [horse] to Yama. [He says: "May I attain immortality; O horse, be a gift for the giver and a source of vigor for me, the receiver. 4.3.4. [32]

Now, as for what else he gives, he gives that out of desire alone, thinking, "May this also be mine in the next world. He recognizes it thus: "Who gave? To whom was it given? Desire gave; to Desire was it given. Desire is the giver; Desire is the receiver. O Desire, this is yours!"
He extends [the rule] to the deity:

4.3.4.[33] Regarding this they say: "One should not extend [the rule] to the deity; for whichever deity one kindles here, she, being kindled, becomes increasingly excellent day by day. Indeed, whichever fire people place fuel upon here, that very fire, being kindled..."
Day by day one becomes better; indeed, day by day he becomes better who, knowing this, accepts [the gift].
Just as one would offer an oblation when the fire is kindled, so does he offer this [gift] which he studies and gives.
Therefore, while studying, one should not bestow it [on others]. 4.3.5. [1]
There are indeed three classes of gods: the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas. Their Soma-pressings are divided accordingly:
the morning pressing belongs to the Vasus, the midday pressing to the Rudras, and the third pressing to the Ādityas. Now, that...
The morning pressing belongs exclusively to the Vasus, the midday pressing exclusively to the Rudras, and the third pressing is shared among the Ādityas. Then those Ādityas said: [4.3.5.2]

"Just as this morning pressing of the Vasus is unmixed, and the midday pressing of the Rudras is unmixed, so too do not offer this [oblation] for us before the mixture," they said. "So be it," the gods replied; and thus, while the midday pressing was already concluded but before the third pressing, they offered this [oblation]. He...
Even now, this *graha* is offered in exactly the same way; it remains fixed at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) before the third pressing (*tṛtīya-savana*).
Then those Ādityas said:
"Neither shall we be in the other pressing, nor in the one other than that, so that the *rakṣases* may not harm us.
They then spoke to the deities of the two cups (*dvidevatya*).
"We are indeed afraid of the *rakṣas* demons; come, let us enter into you!
[4.3.5(5)] Those [cups] dedicated to the dual deities said, "What would accrue to us from that? [They replied,] "When the *anuvaṣaṭ* call is made, it shall be made for us."
"You shall become [the Adityas]," said the Adityas; "So be it," they replied, and they entered the cups belonging to the dual deities (dvidevatya).
When, at the morning pressing, he proceeds with the offerings to the dual deities, then the Pratiprasthātṛ [proceeds] with the Aditya cup.

He draws [the cup] from the *droṇakalaśa* with the formula "Thou art taken with a support," and the Adhvaryu alone calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*. Following the Adhvaryu's offering, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers his own oblation and pours the residue with "To the Ādityas, thee! He does exactly the same for all [subsequent cups]. 4.3.5. [7]
Now, as for why the Pratiprasthātṛ draws [the portion] back:

the Ādityas said, "You shall enter among those belonging to the two deities; you shall be offered the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call by us. Indeed, that second oblation which one offers belongs to the Sviṣṭakṛt.
He offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation; these [libations] are indeed followed by the *anuvaṣaṭ* call. Thus, for him, these become offered with the *anuvaṣaṭ* call and accompanied by the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
He offers on the northern half [of the fire], for this is the quarter of this god; therefore he offers on the northern half.
Furthermore, as for why the Pratiprasthātṛ draws back [the portions].
They indeed entered into the cups belonging to two deities;

he now fashions them out from those very ones into which they entered. Then he covers them, for they were afraid of the Rakṣases, saying: "O Viṣṇu of wide stride, this is your Soma; guard it, let them not deceive you. The sacrifice, indeed, is Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu entrusts him to that sacrifice for its protection; then, when the midday pressing has been completed but before the third pressing, he says, "Come, O sacrificer! and they enter together. 4.3.5 [9]

The *adhvaryu*, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the *agnīdhra*, the *pratiprasthātṛ*, and the *unnētṛ*—and whoever else is an attendant—close both doors, for they were afraid of the *rakṣases*. Then the *adhvaryu* takes the *āditya* vessel and the *āditya* cup; he [places them] directly above the *pūtabhṛt* [vessel].
"He does not withhold it; let it flow down," [he thinks]. 4.3.5.
[10] Then he draws [the cup]:
"Never art thou barren, O Indra, nor dost thou fail the donor; evermore, O Maghavan, grant us more."
"Now, this gift of the god is mixed [with the water] with the formula: 'For the Ādityas, thee! (4.3.5.11).
One should indeed not take it with the *upayāma* formula;
for this [cup] has already been taken with the *upayāma* formula at the beginning, in order to avoid repetition (*ajāmitā*).
"He would indeed commit a kinship-offense (jāmi) if he were to draw [the cup] here also with the *upayāma* formula. Then, having withdrawn it, he brings it back again:
'Never art thou negligent; thou guardest both births, O fourth Āditya! (4.3.5.12)
"The pressing of thee, O Indra, has attained immortality; for the Ādityas, thee! 4.3.5 [13].
Then he takes the curds.
The third pressing indeed belongs to the Ādityas; it is after the Ādityas that [he acts].

"Animals are [the source]; thus he places this milk back into the animals themselves. This milk is placed within the animals. "One should take it from the middle," they say, "for this milk of the animals is, as it were, in the middle. But rather, one should take it from the hind part, for this milk of the animals is, as it were, at the hind part. 4.3.5. [14]

Moreover, as to why he takes curds: these remnants of the oblations are indeed the remains of what has been offered; they are not sufficient for a further offering. He thus causes them to swell again so that they become sufficient for an offering. Therefore, he takes curds. 4.3.5. [15]

He takes it up with the formula: "The sacrifice goes toward the favor of the gods; O Ādityas, be gracious! May your benevolence turn hitherward, which is the best finder of room even out of distress. For the Ādityas, thee! (4.3.5.16).
He then stirs it with the Upāṃśusavana stone.
This Upāṃśusavana stone is, in its essence, Vivasvat Āditya;
and this Āditya cup is indeed that [stone]. Thus he gratifies him in his own portion.
He does not touch it with the fringes nor with the filter, for these two pressings are indeed bright and full of sap.
The morning pressing and the midday pressing are [the Soma], while this third pressing is the squeezed-out bright juice.

In that he does not touch it with the fringes nor with the filter, by that very fact his third pressing becomes possessed of bright juice and full of essence; therefore, he does not [touch it] with the fringes nor...
He touches [the water] with the strainer. 4.3.5.
[18] He stirs it, saying:
"O Vivasvat Āditya, this is your Soma-draught; rejoice in it! Then [he stirs it] for the Unnetṛ.
He hands over the *upāṃśusavana* stone; then he says, "Release the pressing-stones to the *unnetṛ*," and he releases them either into the *ādhavanīya* vessel or into the cup (4.3.5).
Having drawn the King [Soma].
The third pressing belongs to the Ādityas; since the pressing-stones follow the Ādityas, he thus gratifies them in their own portion. They open the doors, and having covered [the Soma], he goes out.
For they were indeed afraid of the *rakṣases*. Then [the Adhvaryu] says, "Recite for the Ādityas!

At this point, he should look [at the sun], if he so desires; however, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he should indeed look [at the sun], saying: "Prompt for the Ādityas, who are beloved, whose abodes are beloved, whose vows are beloved, the lords of the great year!"

He offers at the *vaṣaṭ*-call with the formula, "To the overseers of the intermediate space, the breast," and he does not perform the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvaṣaṭkāra*), lest he should cast the cattle into the fire.
He hands over the two residues (*saṃsrava*) to the *pratiprasthātṛ*.
Then, having re-entered [the *sadas*].
He takes the Āgrayaṇa vessel; they spread out the filter with its fringes pointing northward;
the Adhvaryu causes [the Soma] to flow down; the Pratiprasthātṛ receives it from the Āgrayaṇa; the Unnetṛ brings the residues, either with a cup or with a ladle. 4.3.5. [22]
He draws the Āgrayaṇa from those four streams.

The third pressing belongs to the Ādityas, and cows indeed follow the Ādityas; therefore, this milk of cows is distributed in four ways, and for that reason the Āgrayaṇa is drawn from the four streams.
He takes [the two residues].
4.3.5.[23] Now, as for the fact that the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the two residues together:
this indeed becomes the Āditya cup, or rather it is not.

He pronounces the *anuvaṣaṭ* for the Āditya cup; for it is from this [cup] that he is about to draw the Sāvitra cup, and thus it becomes for him one over which the *anuvaṣaṭ* has been pronounced by means of the Sāvitra [formula]. Furthermore, as for why the Pratiprasthātṛ collects the two residues together.

In former times, they drew this cup for them from the mixture before the third pressing; for this cup is drawn for the sake of the third pressing. Thus the Ādityas enter into the third pressing, and so they do not remain outside of the sacrifice.
Therefore, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the two residues.
For Savitṛ is indeed his mind;
therefore he draws the cup for Savitṛ. And Savitṛ is indeed his breath.
In that he draws the Upāṃśu cup, he thereby places that very breath in him in front;
in that he draws the Sāvitra cup, he thereby places that very breath in him behind. Thus these two breaths are placed on both sides—both that which is above and that which is below. 4.4.1 [2]

The seasons are indeed the year, which is the sacrifice. Those [seasons] are explicitly provided for at this morning pressing when he draws the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*); but they are provided for implicitly at this midday pressing.
When he draws the Marutvatīya cups with the two Ṛtu vessels, they do not draw any cup here for the Seasons (*ṛtu*), nor is any cup drawn from the two Ṛtu vessels.
This one who shines yonder is indeed Savitṛ.
He indeed is all the seasons; thus the seasons and the year are directly manifested at the third libation. Therefore, he draws the cup for Savitṛ.
He draws it with the Upāṃśu vessel.
Savitṛ is indeed his mind, and the Upāṃśu is his breath;
therefore, he draws [the cup] with the Upāṃśu vessel or with the Antaryāma vessel, for these two are the same, since the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma are the out-breathing and the in-breathing. 4.4.1. [5]
He draws [the cup] from the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
Savitṛ is indeed his mind, and the Āgrayaṇa is his self; thus he places the mind in his very self.
Savitṛ is indeed his breath, and the Āgrayaṇa is his self; thus he places the breath in his very self. 4.4.1. [6]
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"O Savitṛ, grant us what is auspicious today, and what is auspicious tomorrow; day by day, grant us what is auspicious.
For through this prayer, O God, may we be partakers of the auspicious abundance of your dwelling. You are taken with a base."
"Thou art Savitṛ’s; thou art the bestower of joy; thou art the bestower of joy; bestow joy upon me; quicken the sacrifice; quicken the lord of the sacrifice;
[grant] fortune!
Having taken it, he does not set it down.

Mind, indeed, is his Savitṛ; therefore this mind does not cease. Breath, indeed, is his Savitṛ; therefore this breath does not cease, but moves about. Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the god Savitṛ. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt [the offering] for the god Savitṛ. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering; he does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call. Mind...
"May Savitṛ not cast his mind into the fire," he thinks; "may Savitṛ not cast his breath into the fire," he thinks.
Then, with a vessel that has not been consumed:

He draws the Vaiśvadeva cup. Now, as to why he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with a vessel that has not been consumed: one does not utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* for the Sāvitra [cup]; it is precisely for this reason that he is about to draw the Vaiśvadeva cup, and thus for him the *anuvaṣaṭ* is uttered by means of the Vaiśvadeva itself. 4.4.1. [9]
Furthermore, as to why he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup:
Savitṛ is indeed his mind, and the All-gods are all this [universe].
Thus, he makes all this a follower and a track of the mind; therefore, all this is of the mind.
"Following the path of what has been done" (kṛtānukaramanuvartma) 4.4.1.[10].
Furthermore, as to why he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup:
Savitṛ is indeed his breath, and all these Viśve Devās are this entire universe.
In this very whole, he places the out-breath and the up-breath; for these two, the out-breath and the up-breath, are indeed within this whole.
Furthermore, as to why he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup.

The third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas; it is so called by way of the Sāman, because the third pressing is called Vaiśvadeva. It is also so called by way of the Ṛc. Now, it is by way of the Yajus and by way of the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) that he draws this Mahāvaiśvadeva cup. 4.4.1. [12]
He draws that from the *pūtabhṛt* vessel.

The *pūtabhṛt* belongs to the All-Gods (*vaiśvadeva*), for from it they draw out [the soma] for the gods, from it for men, and from it for the ancestors; therefore the *pūtabhṛt* belongs to the All-Gods. 4.4.1. [13]
He draws that cup without a puroruk formula;

for he draws it for all the gods. All the gods are indeed everything—whatever Ṛg-verses, whatever Yajus-formulas, and whatever Sāman-chants there are. In that he draws it for all the gods, by that very act [he accomplishes his purpose].
This [cup] has a *puroruc* verse; therefore, he draws it without a *puroruc*.
4.4.1. Now, therefore, he draws it: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art good protection, thou art good standing. Indeed, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is good protection.
"Supratiṣṭhāna, homage to Bṛhadukṣa!"—Bṛhadukṣa is indeed Prajāpati; thus he says, "Homage to Prajāpati.

"For all the gods, thee! This is thy womb; for all the gods, thee!"—with these words he deposits [the cup], for he draws it for all the gods. Then, having gone forward, he sits down facing the east. 4.4.1. [15]
When the Hotṛ recites this verse:
"With one and with ten, O self-existent one; with two for the sacrifice, and with twenty;
with three, and with thirty yoked horses, O Vāyu—unharness them here," then [he does so] upon this [verse].
The vessels are released during the verse addressed to Vāyu; for cattle have Vāyu as their leader, and Vāyu is indeed breath, since it is by means of breath that cattle move. 4.4.1.
[16] He (Prajāpati) departed from the gods with the cattle.
The gods invited him at the morning pressing, but he did not turn back. They invited him at the midday pressing, but he still did not turn back. They invited him at the third pressing. 4.4.1. [17]
As he was about to turn back, he said:

"If I were to turn back, what would be mine from that? [The other replied: "These vessels shall be yoked by you alone, and they shall be unyoked by you alone. Thus, by this [formula], these vessels are yoked.

When he draws the cups beginning with that for Indra and Vāyu at the morning pressing, then these vessels are released by means of this [verse]: "O Vāyu, release those [horses] here with your teams (niyut). The teams are indeed cattle; thus, it is by means of cattle that he releases these vessels. 4.4.1.
[18] If he were to return to the morning pressing...

The morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī, and the Gāyatrī is the Brahman; thus the cattle would have remained among the Brāhmaṇas. Now, had they returned at the midday pressing—the midday pressing belonging to Indra and Indra being the Kṣatra—then the cattle would have remained among the Kṣatriyas.

If it had returned at the third pressing, they would have become cattle; for the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas, and all these Viśvedevas are this entire world—therefore, these cattle are found everywhere. He proceeds with the *caru* offering to Soma.

Soma is indeed the oblation of the gods; now this [rice] is made into an oblation for Soma himself, so that Soma is thus not separated [from his own portion]. It is a *caru* (porridge); for the *caru* is the food of the gods, since *caru* is boiled rice (*odana*), and boiled rice is manifest food. Therefore, it is a *caru*. 4.4.2.2.

Therefore, he does not proceed with it at the morning pressing, nor at the midday pressing; for these two pressings, the morning pressing and the midday pressing, belong exclusively to the gods, whereas Soma belongs to the Pitṛs as his deity. 4.4.2. [3]
If he were to proceed at the morning pressing or at the midday pressing,
he would indeed cause a conflict between the gods and the ancestors; therefore, he proceeds at the third pressing, for that belongs to the Viśvedevas.

Likewise, the third pressing causes exhilaration; he does not recite an invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), for the ancestors have departed once and for all, and therefore he does not recite an invitatory verse. 4.4.2.
[4] Then, having taken four ladlings of clarified butter (*ājya*).
Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice the ghee! and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Thus, he interposes this between those offerings which have been made prior to this; in this way, he creates a lack of conflict. Then, having spread a base of clarified butter—

He cuts off two portions of the *caru*, then pours clarified butter over it from above; having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Soma-oblation," and offers it at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter—

Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice the ghee! and offers it at the *vaṣaṭ*-call. Thus, he interposes this [offering] between those subsequent oblations which he is about to offer; in this way, he creates a state of non-contention. If he should so desire, he may perform the sacrifice on both sides; or if he should so desire, he may perform the sacrifice on only one side. 4.4.2. [7]
Now, there is a *pracaraṇī* ladle;

having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter into it, the Adhvaryu sprinkles the *dhiṣṇya* hearths with the *śālāka* sticks. As to why he sprinkles the *dhiṣṇya* hearths with the *śālāka* sticks—it is because when the gods [were about to depart], they...

They said, "At the third pressing, your offering shall consist of clarified butter (ghṛta) and not of Soma; for the Soma-draught has been taken away from you. Therefore, this Soma-offering does not reach you; at the third pressing alone does this offering of clarified butter reach you, and not that of Soma. And when he sprinkles the hearths (dhiṣṇya) with torches, he does so with these very sacrificial formulas (yajus), according to where they were strewn."
He performs the *vyāghāraṇa* libations as before, with the final one at the *mārjālīya* fire-altar.
Regarding this, some perform a second *āghāra* libation at the *āgnīdhrīya* fire-altar, thinking, "In this way the ritual will conclude toward the north.
However, one should not do so; the final libation should indeed be at the *mārjālīya*.
When the Adhvaryu sprinkles the hearths with the fire-sticks, at that moment the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the Pātnīvata cup.
Indeed, from the sacrifice offspring are born; being born from the sacrifice, they are born from a productive union.

Being born from a pairing, they are born at the end of the sacrifice; thus he causes them to be born from this pairing at the end of the sacrifice. Therefore, from this pairing at the end of the sacrifice, these creatures are born. That is why he draws the cup for the wives (pātnīvata). 4.4.2. [10]
Or he draws it with the upāṃśu cup;
if he should draw the Sāvitra draught with the upāṃśu cup, he should draw this one with the antaryāma cup; if [he should draw] the Sāvitra with the antaryāma cup—
He should draw this [cup] with the *upāṃśu* vessel, for these two, the *upāṃśu* and the *antaryāma*, are the same; they are indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*).
Now, what is the out-breath is also the up-breath (*udāna*). The out-breath is male, and the wife is female; thus a productive union is brought about.
He draws it without a *puroruk* verse.
"Vigor indeed is the *puroruc*; [he thinks], 'May I place vigor in women.
Therefore, he draws [the cup] without a *puroruc*.
Now, therefore, he indeed draws it."
"You are taken with a support; O divine Soma, of you who are pressed by Bṛhaspati"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman;

thus he says, "of you who are pressed by the Brahman, O divine Soma. "Of Indu, the possessor of power"—when he says "of Indu, the possessor of power," he means "of the one possessing heroic strength. "May I succeed in drawing the cups for the wives"—he does not say this immediately.
He takes [the butter] from the wives [of the sacrificer], thinking, "Lest I should place virility in women. Therefore, he does not take [butter] from the wives at this time.
Now, with whatever remains as residue in the *pracaraṇī* ladle, he mixes [the oblation] with it; he thereby makes it prosper.

While he propitiates the other *grahas*, he causes this one to waste away. Clarified butter (*ājya*) is indeed a thunderbolt; with this thunderbolt, the clarified butter, the gods struck the wives and deprived them of their power. Struck and deprived, they could not even claim for themselves, nor could they claim for their inheritance.
In the same way, this [sacrificer] now strikes the wives and deprives them of their power with this thunderbolt, the clarified butter; struck and deprived, they [cannot claim anything].
He does not master himself, nor does he master his inheritance. 4.4.2.[14] He unites [the worlds]: "I am above, I am below; that which is the intermediate space, that became my father.
I have seen the sun on both sides; I [know] the supreme secret of the gods. This is what he means by "I, I."
He thus sharpens it; he thereby bestows vigor upon the males.
Then he says, "O Āgnīdh, recite the offering prayer for the Pātnīvata.
The Āgnīdh is indeed a male and the wife is a female; this is a productive union.
"He offers it with the formula, 'O Agni, accompanied by thy wives! For Agni is male and the wife is female; thus a productive union is brought about.
"In harmony with the god Tvaṣṭṛ... [he says].

Tvaṣṭṛ indeed transforms the emitted seed; therefore, he (Agni) now transforms this emitted seed. He offers [the oblation] on the northern half [of the fire] with the words, "Drink the Soma, Svāhā! Those other oblations are the gods, while these are the wives;
for in this way the union is properly arranged, since the woman lies on the north side of the man.

The Adhvaryu brings a portion for the Agnīdhra; he says, "Adhvaryu, invite me! He should not respond with an invitation, for what response can there be for one who is slain and cast out? Yet he should indeed respond with an invitation, for they offer into his fire and they utter the *vaṣaṭ* call; therefore, he should indeed respond with an invitation. 4.4.2. [17]
Then he issues the command:
"O Agnīdh, sit in the lap of the Neṣṭṛ; O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife and have her look at the Udgātṛ;
O Unnetṛ, pour Soma into the Hotṛ’s cup following [the others], so that the Soma does not remain in excess," provided it is an Agniṣṭoma.
If it should be an Ukthya sacrifice, he should say: "Make the Soma swell. He... [should do so].
Bearing this very vessel, he sits down in the lap of the Neṣṭṛ. For the Āgnīdhra is, in essence, Agni;
the Neṣṭṛ is a woman; and the Āgnīdhra is a man. Thus, a productive union is brought about.
The Neṣṭṛ leads up the wife; he makes her look at the Udgātṛ, saying, "Thou art Prajāpati, the bull, the depositor of seed."
"Place seed in me," [he says]. Prajāpati is indeed the Udgātṛ, and the wife is the woman; thus this procreative union is brought about.
The meters of the gods are indeed cattle. 4.4.3. [1]
Just as yoked animals carry burdens for humans,
so do the meters (candāṃsi), when yoked, carry the sacrifice to the gods. When the meters had thus satisfied the gods, then the gods [became] the meters.

He satisfied them completely; therefore, it was previously that the *chandasyas*, being yoked, carried the sacrifice to the gods, because he had fully satisfied them. 4.4.3 [2] Then he draws the *hāriyojana* cup.
The *hāriyojana* cup is indeed the meters; it is thus the meters that he satisfies. Therefore, he draws the *hāriyojana*.
He draws it as an additional offering.

For when they have called for the *śamyu*-formula, he then draws this [cup]; for the gods are this [earth], then the meters are redundant, then humans are redundant, and then cattle are redundant; therefore, he draws it as something redundant. He draws it in the *droṇakalaśa*.

Soma was indeed Vṛtra. When the gods slew him, his head rolled away; it became the *droṇakalaśa*. Whatever amount of juice flowed into it, that was excessive. This cup is indeed excessive; thus, he places this excess into that excess. Therefore, he draws [the Soma] into the *droṇakalaśa*. 4.4.3. [5]
He draws that cup without a *puroruc* verse;
for he draws it for the metres. In that he draws it for the metres, thereby this cup of his comes to possess a *puroruc*. Therefore, he draws it without a *puroruc*. 4.4.3. [6]
Then he draws [the cup]: "Thou art taken with a support;
thou art the bay, the yoker of bays; for thee, with the two bays! For the two bays are indeed the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*;
it is with the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman* that he draws this [cup]. 4.4.3. [7]

Then he pours in the parched grains with the formula, "Ye are the parched grains for the two bay steeds, together with Soma, for Indra. Thus, whatever here is both measured and unmeasured, that entire thing he consumes. 4.4.3. [8]

The Unnetṛ causes the announcement to be made. Or rather, the Unnetṛ is an extra; for he does not cause the announcement to be made for anyone else. This cup is an extra; thus, being an extra himself, he places this extra [cup] as an extra. Therefore, the Unnetṛ causes the announcement to be made. 4.4.3. [9]
Having placed [the ladle] upon the head [of the sacrificer], he causes [the announcement] to be heard.

For this is its head. Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the *dhānāsoma*s. Having caused the announcement to be heard, he says, "Prompt for the *dhānāsoma*s that have been set forth. At the *vaṣaṭ* call he offers, and at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* call.
Then they desire to eat the parched grains (dhānā) for consumption.

Regarding this, some carry the *droṇakalaśa* over to the *hotṛ*, saying, "It is the portion for the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*. One should not do so; for while the other portions are according to the cups (*yathācamasa*), this [portion] is different.

Therefore, in this [offering], there is a share for all; hence they desire the *dhānās* for the sake of eating. They should not chew them with their teeth, thinking, "These are indeed animals; let us not cause injury to the animals," but rather [they should consume them] by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

They consume that which is your food, the winner of horses; that which is your food, the winner of cattle—for these are indeed cattle—therefore he says, "that which is your food, the winner of horses; that which is your food, the winner of cattle. [He says], "of you, whose *yajus* have been offered, whose *stomas* have been praised"—for the *yajus* have indeed been offered and the *stomas* have been praised—"of you, whose *ukthas* have been recited"—for the *ukthas* have indeed been recited—"of you who have been invited, [I am] invited."
"For I shall eat"—thus he eats when invited, for he has indeed been invited. 4.4.3 [12].
They should not scatter those [remnants] into the fire, thinking, "Lest we offer what is impure into the fire"; rather, they pour them out upon the *uttaravedi* altar. Thus it is done.
They do not exist outside of the sacrifice.
4.4.3.[13] Then they touch the full vessels (*pūrṇapātra*).
Regarding those which some call the "Soma-offerings in water" (*apsuṣoma*), it is just as when [a draft animal] is harnessed.
"Let those who perform the office of the *ṛtvij* carry this [water] away; for even one who is yoked may wound himself or tear himself. Water is a pacifier and a remedy.
Whatever they wound themselves with here, or whatever they tear themselves, water is the pacifier; thus they appease it with water as a pacifier, and they heal it with water.
Therefore, they touch the full vessels together. (4.4.3)
They touch themselves [with the verse]:

"We have united with luster, with milk, with our bodies, and with a gracious mind. May Tvaṣṭṛ, the bounteous giver, bestow wealth upon us; may he smooth over whatever in our bodies is injured. Thus they mend whatever has been torn asunder. 4.4.3. [15]
Then they touch their faces.
There is a twofold reason why they touch their faces: water is indeed immortality;
thus they touch themselves with immortality, and they also place this very rite within themselves.
Therefore, they touch the openings [of the mouth]. These, indeed, are the nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations he offers; as to why he offers nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations, it is because there are nine...

These are the *stotriya* verses for the *bahiṣpavamāna*; this [virāj] is deficient on both sides for the sake of procreation. Indeed, from this procreative source which is deficient on both sides, Prajāpati created offspring—both those moving upwards from here and those moving downwards from there.
In the same way, he (the sacrificer) now creates offspring from this very procreative source which is deficient on both sides.
Upward from here and downward from here; the *hiṅkāra* is the tenth of the *stotriya* verses,
and the *svāhākāra* belongs to these— thus indeed this [sacrifice] of his becomes complete.
The Virāj consists of ten tens.
Now, as to why they are called the Samiṣṭayajus offerings.

Or rather, whatever deities he invokes by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed, all of them indeed have then been fully satisfied (*samiṣṭā*). Since he offers these oblations when all of them have been fully satisfied, they are therefore called *samiṣṭayajūṃṣi*. 4.4.4 [4]

Now, as to why he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations: the self of one who has sacrificed becomes, as it were, emptied; for whatever he possesses, that he gives away. Therefore, with these three [oblations], he replenishes that very self once again. 4.4.4. [5]
Now, as for the three subsequent oblations which he offers:
whatever deities he invokes by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed,
they indeed remain waiting, thinking, "Let them now offer these *samistayajus* oblations for us."
He thus releases them according to their proper order, following wherever their course lies.
Now, as for those three final oblations which he offers:
having generated this sacrifice when he performed its expansion (*atanat*), he now [offers these].

He establishes it in that upon which it is established; therefore, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations. He offers: "O Indra, lead us together with mind and with cattle. By saying "with mind," he replenishes what has been depleted by means of the mind;
by saying "with cattle," he replenishes what has been depleted by means of cattle. "Together with the patrons, O Maghavan, together..."

"By well-being, together with the prayer (*brahman*) that is made by the gods—by that *brahman*. By this he causes that which was emptied by the *brahman* to swell again. "Together in the good-will of the gods worthy of sacrifice, Svāhā! 4.4.4 [8] Together with splendor!"

"With milk, with our bodies"—by saying "with luster," he causes that which has been depleted of luster to swell; by saying "with milk," since milk is indeed sap, he causes that which has been depleted of sap to swell. "We have gone forth with a gracious mind; may Tvaṣṭṛ, the bounteous giver, bestow wealth upon us; may he smooth over whatever in our bodies is injured"—thereby he joins together what has been torn asunder. 4.4.4 [9]

"May Savitṛ enjoy this; may Prajāpati, the god who guards the treasure, Agni, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu, being in harmony with offspring, bestow wealth upon the sacrificer—Svāhā! By saying this, he indeed replenishes again that which had been emptied.
"Bestow wealth upon the sacrificer; Svāhā! (4.4.4).
"O gods, we have made paths easy for you who have come here, enjoying this libation. Thus, O gods, the paths for you are easy.
"Those who come to the dwellings for other rites, enjoying this libation"—this is what he says.

"Bearing and bringing the oblations"—thereby he dismisses the deities. "Let those who are without vehicles go bearing [the offerings], and let those who have vehicles go bringing them"—this is what he says; therefore he says, "bearing and bringing."
"O Vasus, bestow upon us these oblations and riches; Svāhā!
(4.4.4.11) "O divine Agni, send forth those gods whom you have brought hither, to their own dwelling place"—whether he says this regarding Agni himself, or "Bring those gods hither!
Bring those gods hither!", he thereby says: "Send forth those gods whom you have already brought."

"Wherever their foot has gone, after that—having eaten and having drunk, all. For they have indeed eaten the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is the animal; and "having drunk," for they have indeed drunk King Soma.
Therefore he says: "Having eaten and having drunk, all, do ye ascend to the life-breath, the Gharma, and the light—Svāhā!"
In that very way, he releases the deities:
"For we have chosen you here, O Agni, as the Hotṛ-priest in this proceeding sacrifice; may our prayers be successful."
"Separately you have been appeased; knowing, come to the sacrifice, O wise one—Svāhā! With this [verse], he releases Agni himself;
he dismisses Agni. "O gods, you who know the way... [he says].
"For the gods are finders of the way; having found the way," by saying this he means "having found the sacrifice.

"Having gone the way," with this he releases [the sacrifice] according to its proper course. "O Lord of the Mind, O God, place this sacrifice in the wind, Svāhā!"—this wind that blows here is indeed the sacrifice; having thus gathered this sacrifice together, he places it in this sacrifice.
He establishes sacrifice by means of sacrifice; he joins sacrifice together. Therefore he says: "Svāhā! Place [it] in the wind! (4.4.4).
"O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice; go to your own womb, svāhā!"
Thus, he establishes this sacrifice, which is already established, in its own womb.

With the words, "This is thy sacrifice, O lord of the sacrifice, accompanied by the *sūktavāka* and all-heroic; enjoy it, Svāhā!"—he thereby finally establishes for the sacrificer that sacrifice, which is already established, as being accompanied by the *sūktavāka* and all-heroic. 4.4.5. [1]
He indeed goes down to the *avabhṛtha* bath. As for why he goes down to the *avabhṛtha*:
whatever essence of his there was, that he has generated from the oblations; now this is merely a body, and there is no essence in it, so it should not be cast away.
They pour water over it; for water is indeed sap, so he places that sap in it;
he unites him with that sap and thus brings him forth from there. Once born, he causes him to be born again.
Because they pour water over it, it is called the *avabhṛtha* (the purificatory bath). 4.4.5. [2]
Then he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations;

for the *samiṣṭayajus* are indeed the conclusion of the sacrifice. Having offered the *samiṣṭayajus*, they go together toward the *cātvāla* pit with whatever is on both sides of that [altar]. He [takes] the black antelope horn...
And he throws the girdle into the *cātvāla* pit with the formula:
"May you not be a snake, may you not be a viper.
Indeed, this [immersion in water] is the formal act of self-consecration (*svagākāra*) for the *ṛjīṣa*.
They consume [it], and this indeed is its *svagā*-formula: for snakes are like ropes, and the abodes of snakes are like wells.

There is indeed a mutual rivalry between humans and snakes; lest it [the food] should come into contact with that [rivalry], he therefore says: "May you not become a *mahiṣ* (buffalo), may you not become a *pṛdāku* (viper). 4.4.5. [4]
Then he causes [the sacrificer] to recite:

"For the king Varuṇa has made wide for Sūrya a path to follow, so that this path may be wide, free from fear, and free from destruction for Sūrya; even so may this [path] be wide, free from fear, and free from destruction for me."
"Let there be a path," this is what he says.
"He has made feet for him to step upon where there was no footing.
For even if one is without feet, it is indeed sufficient for taking a step.
"He becomes a cleanser, piercing even the heart"—thus he releases him from every sin and evil that has entered his heart.
Then he says, "Sing the Sāman! 4.4.5 [6]

"Recite the *sāman*," he says; or rather, one should say, "Sing it," for they indeed sing the *sāman*. Now, the reason he sings the *sāman* is so that the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā rakṣāṃsi*) may not injure this body outside the sacrifice; for the *sāman* is the repeller of the destructive spirits and the *rakṣases*. 4.4.5. [7]
He sings in the Agneyī metre;
for Agni is the repeller of the Rākṣasas. He sings in the Aticandas metre; this Aticandas indeed comprises all the metres; therefore he sings in the Aticandas metre. 4.4.5 [8]
He sings: "Agni burns, he strikes back, ahāva! ahāva!"—thereby he indeed drives away the destructive spirits and the *rakṣas* from here.
They go out toward the north.

They go by way of the *cātvāla* and in front of the *āgnīdhra* shed, toward whichever direction the waters are located; they proceed there. Now, there may be a pool among flowing waters that remains still.

He should descend into darkness; for those waters which do not flow among the flowing ones are seized by Varuṇa, and the *avabhṛtha* rite belongs to Varuṇa, so it serves to remove the state of being seized by Varuṇa.
If he cannot find such waters, he may descend into whatever waters he can find. 4.4.5. [11]
While causing him to step down into the darkness, he makes him recite:
"Homage to Varuṇa! Overstepped is the noose of Varuṇa. Thereby he releases him from every noose of Varuṇa and from everything pertaining to Varuṇa. 4.4.5 [12]
Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter and having cast a fuel-stick [into the fire], he makes an offering:
"The face of Agni has entered the waters; O Son of the Waters, as Lord, protect the divine power. In every house, you shall sacrifice the fuel-stick, O Agni; may your tongue [be ready] for you."
"May the ghee rise up with the cry of Svāhā! (4.4.5).
For indeed, the gods, however much they caused Agni to enter into the waters, did so lest the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*) [should seize him] from there.
"The Rakṣases are rising up; for Agni is the slayer of the Rakṣases; him he kindles with this fuel-stick and with this oblation, thinking, 'When he is kindled, I shall offer to the gods. 4.4.5.
[14] Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter—
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the *samidhs*.
He performs four *prayāja* offerings excluding the *barhis*. The *barhis* is indeed offspring, and the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) belongs to Varuṇa;
[he does this] so that Varuṇa may not seize the offspring. Therefore, he performs four *prayāja* offerings excluding the *barhis*. 4.4.5. [15]
Now, there is a cake on one potsherd for Varuṇa.

Whatever essence had been in him, or whatever was produced from his oblations—that he has generated; but this body contains no essence. The cake, indeed, is essence; thus, he places that essence into it.
He places it; thus he unites him with this essence and brings him forth from there. Once he is born, he causes him to be born.
Therefore, there is a cake on one potsherd for Varuṇa.
Having spread a layer of clarified butter—

While cutting portions from the *puroḍāśa*, he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Varuṇa. Regarding this, some cut twice from the *ṛjīṣa*; however, one should not do so in that manner, for it becomes a mere body and is not fit for an oblation. He cuts twice, pours clarified butter over it once, and anoints the two places of cutting. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Varuṇa," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 4.4.5. [17]
Then, having spread a layer of clarified butter, while placing a portion of the sacrificial cake upon it, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni and Varuṇa.
This is for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. As for why he does not say "for Agni," it is so that Varuṇa may not seize Agni. Then, as for the subsequent part of the *soma*-dregs...
He should cut off twice; then, if he does not care for it here, he cuts off once.

Then, from above, he pours clarified butter over it twice. Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Agni and Varuṇa," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation.
Now, these indeed are six oblations; for there are six seasons in the year, and Varuṇa is the year; therefore there are six oblations.
This is the course of the Ādityas.

"These sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) belong to the Ādityas," they say. He should desire to perform it exactly as he intends, provided that his own will is so inclined; however, if the sacrificer should tell him to do it otherwise, then he should do it otherwise.

He should offer these very four fore-offerings (prayāja), omitting the one for the sacrificial grass (apabarhiṣaḥ); [he should offer] two butter-portions (ājyabhāgau), and [sacrifices to] Varuṇa and Agni-Varuṇa.
There are two after-offerings (anuyāja) without the *barhis* grass; that makes ten. The *virāj* indeed consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is the *virāj*;
thus he brings this sacrifice into correspondence with the *virāj*.
This is the path of the Aṅgirases.

Having performed one of these two rites, he causes that jar in which the *ṛjīṣa* (the dregs) is contained to float away with the formula, "Into the ocean is thy heart; into the waters. The ocean is indeed the waters, and the waters are sap;
thus he places this sap within it and unites it with this sap; and from this [he delivers it].

"He generates him; as soon as he is born, he generates him. With the words, "May the plants and the waters enter into you," he bestows both kinds of essence upon him: that which is in the plants and that which is in the waters. With the words, "O Lord of the Sacrifice, may we worship thee with the recitation of hymns and the utterance of homage, with 'svāhā'," he offers whatever in the sacrifice is auspicious.

He thus places that very thing here in this [fire]. 4.4.5. Then, having released [the fire], he worships it with the mantra: "O divine waters, this is your embryo. For this [fire] is indeed the embryo of the waters; [he offers it] well-pleased.

"Support him well, support him!"—thus he entrusts him to the waters for protection. "O divine Soma, this is your place"—for water is indeed his place—"in that place, speak for us and protect us on all sides!"—by saying this, he means:
"In that place, be a source of well-being for us and guard us from all afflictions. 4.4.5 [22]
Then he causes him to bathe with the verse:

"O purifying bath, O Nicumpuṇa, you are a gliding one, O Nicumpuṇa; through the gods, may I wipe away the sin committed against the gods; through mortals, may I wipe away the sin committed against mortals. Thus he wipes it away.

"Thus indeed has this sin committed by the gods against the gods departed through King Soma; thus indeed has this sin committed by mortals against mortals departed through the cattle and the rice-cake, O God, protect me from the injury of Purūravas"—by this he says, "Protect me from all calamities. 4.4.5 [23]
Then, having approached and bathed, they run after one another's backs; putting on other two garments, they emerge.
Just as a snake would cast off its skin, so he is released from all evil; in that [state], there is no...

He remains free from sin for as long as he does not eat while still a youth; he returns by the same way by which he went out, and having returned, he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Thou art the kindler of the gods. By this act, he kindles the sacrificer himself, for it is after the kindling of the gods that the sacrificer is kindled. 4.5.1. [1]
He proceeds with the *caru* for Āditya as the concluding offering (*udayanīya*).

As to why there is this *caru* for Āditya: when the gods said of her, "Thine alone shall be the introductory offering (*prāyaṇīya*), thine alone the concluding offering (*udayanīya*)," he thereby makes that very one her share at both ends. 4.5.1. [2]

When he performs that sacrifice here while intending to go and purchase the King (Soma) there, it is therefore called the *Prāyaṇīya* (Introductory). And when he performs this sacrifice here after rising from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), it is therefore called the *Udayanīya* (Concluding). Indeed, these two are essentially the same.
The *prāyaṇīya* offering belongs to Aditi, and the *udayanīya* offering belongs to Aditi; for this earth is indeed Aditi.
He sacrifices first to Pathyā Svasti.
By means of speech alone, the gods thus regained their way when they were no longer able to discern their path.
For by speech alone is he bewildered; but when he has become wise, he acts as before.
4.5.1.[4] He first sacrifices to Agni, then to Soma, then to Savitṛ, then to Pathyā Svasti.
Then [he offers to] Svasti and Aditi; for Pathyā Svasti is speech and this Aditi is this very earth.
Thus the gods established speech upon this [earth], and so this speech speaks, being firmly established upon her. 4.5.1.
Then he immolates the barren cow (vaśā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa as the Anūbandhyā sacrifice.
This very sacrifice is performed as something distinct;
it is indeed the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), for the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings constitute the very end of the sacrifice.
Now, as to why there is a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa:
Or rather, whatever of the sacrificer’s sacrifice is well-offered, Mitra takes that of his;
whatever of his is ill-offered, Varuṇa takes that of his.
Regarding this they say: "Where has the sacrificer been? Since Mitra here takes what is well-offered of his, it is by means of this [offering] that he [restores it] to him.

Being pleased, Varuna releases him; and whatever ill-offered portion of his he takes, that he makes well-offered for him through this [offering], being pleased, and that he releases back to him. Thus this becomes his own sacrifice, his own good deed. 4.5.1. [8]
Now, as for the fact that there is a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa:
when the gods brought forth the seed that had been shed, they did so through the *āgnimāruta* hymn; it is explained therein how the gods [brought forth] that seed.
From that, they produced [heat], and from it coals (aṅgāra) came into being; from the coals came the Aṅgirases, and after them other animals.
Then, when the dust of these [animals] remained over, from that the donkey (gardabha) came into being; therefore, where—

"It has become dusty, like the place where a donkey stands," they say. And when not a single drop of essence remained, from that this barren cow (vaśā) belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa came into being. Therefore, she does not bring forth offspring, for semen originates from essence, and from semen come animals. Since she came into being at the very end, therefore she is the end.
It follows the sacrifice; therefore, in this case, a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa is most appropriately prepared.
If one should not find a barren cow, even a barren ox may serve. Then the Viśve Devas desired to immolate the other [victim].
From that, the Vaiśvadevī arose, and then the Bārhaspatyā;
for Bṛhaspati is the end, indeed the end. He who would give a thousand or even more [cows], [should do so with these verses].
He should sacrifice all of these; for him who gives a thousand or more, everything has indeed been obtained and everything conquered. All of these are exactly as before:
