first the one dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, then the one dedicated to the Viśve Devās, and then the one dedicated to Bṛhaspati. 4.5.1. [12]
Moreover, those who should sit for a long sacrificial session—
for a year or more— should immolate all these [animals].
For everything is attained by them and everything is conquered by those who sit for a long sacrificial session— for a year or more.
All this is exactly as before. 4.5.1.[13] Then he performs the Udavasānīyā sacrifice. He offers a cake on five potsherds for Agni; of that—

The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses consist of five-footed *paṅkti* meters. Indeed, the sacrifice of one who has already sacrificed becomes exhausted; it turns away from him. Now, Agni is all sacrifices, for in Agni they perform all sacrifices—both the *pākayajñas* and the others. Thus, he takes hold of the sacrifice once again, and so his sacrifice is no longer exhausted.
Thus it becomes for us, and he does not turn away from us.
Now, as to why there is a cake on five potsherds:
the *ṛc*s used as invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) consist of five-footed *paṅkti* meters; [the sacrifice] is fivefold.
This is indeed the sacrifice; thus he takes up the sacrifice again. In this way his sacrifice becomes free from weariness, and likewise it does not turn away from him.
Its sacrificial fee is gold.

This sacrifice indeed belongs to Agni; gold is the seed of Agni, therefore gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Or rather, it is an ox, for he belongs to Agni by his power of drawing; for his power of drawing is as if scorched by fire.
Then, having taken clarified butter in four ladlings, he offers it with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely; make wide room for our dwelling.
O you whose source is clarified butter, drink the clarified butter; further and further extend the lord of the sacrifice, svāhā! For the sacrifice is indeed...

Viṣṇu thus begins that very sacrifice anew; in this way his sacrifice becomes free from weariness, and likewise it does not turn away from him. In that regard, he should give whatever he is able to give, for they say, "An oblation should not be without a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then, when this *udavasānīyā* sacrifice is completed, he offers the evening oblation; at that very time, he offers the morning oblation as well. 4.5.2. [1]
He immolates a barren cow. Having immolated it, they quiet it; having quieted it, he says, "Extract the omentum.
Having extracted the omentum, he should say, "Search for the embryo," touching it as he speaks. If they do not find one, what regard would they pay? And if [they do find one]...

In that case, they find atonement; an expiation is performed. But it is certainly not appropriate that, while thinking there is only one [deity], they should proceed with only one [offering], or while thinking there are two, [they should proceed with only one].
They should proceed as if with two [assistants]; he should instruct [them] to prepare both a cooking pot and a turban. 4.5.2.
[3] Then they proceed with the omentum. Just as is the procedure for that, having proceeded with the omentum, both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer—
Then that Adhvaryu said, "Extract this embryo. He should not, however, extract it from the belly; for they extract [an embryo] from the belly only when it is afflicted or dead.
When the embryo has fully developed, it then comes out backward through the birth canal. Having even torn open the hips, he should tell him to extract it backward. 4.5.2. [4]
He consecrates it as it is being brought down with the mantra:

"Let the ten-month-old embryo come forth together with the afterbirth. When he says, "Let it stir," he thereby bestows vital breath upon it; and when he says, "The ten-month-old," it is because when the embryo is fully developed, it stays for ten months.
Now, although he is ten-months-old, even though he is not yet ten-months-old, by means of this very *brahman*-formula, the *yajus*,
he makes him ten-months-old with the words, "Together with the afterbirth."

"Just as a ten-month-old fetus might fall together with the placenta—this is what he means when he says, 'As this wind moves, as the ocean moves'—he thereby bestows the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon him.
Just as a ten-month-old fetus might be delivered together with the placenta—this is what he means. 4.5.2. [6]
Regarding this they say: "How should one prepare this embryo? [Some say] one should cut portions from each of its limbs, just as the cutting of portions is performed for other sacrificial offerings.
However, one should not do it in that way; for indeed, this [embryo] has its limbs unformed. One should rather cut off the neck from below and [place it] upon this [altar].

They should let this sacrificial essence drip into the pot; for this sacrificial essence drips from all his limbs, and thus it becomes an offering taken from all of his limbs. They cut off the portions of the barren cow (vaśā) exactly according to the manner of their cutting.
They cook those [limbs] on the animal-cooking fire.
Having wrapped that very sacrificial essence (medha) in a turban, they place the embryo at the side of the animal-cooking fire; when it is cooked, then—
He offers only the *samudya* oblations; they do not carry away this sacrificial essence (*medha*), nor that animal; rather, it is precisely this sacrificial essence they carry away.
They carry it behind the *cātvāla* pit, between the sacrificial post and the fire.

Having placed [the vessel] to the south, the Pratiprasthātṛ makes the portions; then he spreads an underlayer in the two ladles. Then he calls for the recitation for the Manotā deity regarding the oblation.
They make the portions of the portions of the cow (vaśā) in the same manner as the portioning of those [other sacrificial animals]. 4.5.2. [9]

Now, there is a *pracaraṇī* ladle; into it the Pratiprasthātṛ spreads a base of clarified butter for the fat portion, cuts off two portions, pours clarified butter over them once, and then anoints the two places from which the portions were cut. Then he gives the call, and having caused the *āśrāvaya*, he says, "Prompt! (*preṣya*), at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
The Adhvaryu offers the oblation; following the Adhvaryu’s offering, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers. [He offers] with the verse:
"O thou whose embryo is worthy of sacrifice...
Embryos are indeed unworthy of sacrifice; therefore, he makes them worthy of sacrifice by means of this very Brāhmaṇa-formula.
He makes it fit for sacrifice with the words, "Whose womb is golden. For when they carry it away, they tear apart its womb;

gold is immortal life. Thus he makes that womb of hers immortal. With the words, "I have united his limbs, which are uninjured, with their measure, Svāhā!"—if it be a male, or if it be a female—the limbs are indeed uninjured.

"To her whose measure I have united, Svāhā!"—if the embryo is unrecognizable, he should nevertheless offer the oblation with the masculine formula, for embryos are indeed male, "whose limbs are uninjured, him whose measure I have united, Svāhā!
For they make that [embryo] turn away from its mother when they draw it out; thus he now [unites it] by means of this very Brahman-formula, the Yajus.
Having made it equal in the middle of the sacrifice, he brings it back together with its measure.
4.5.2.[11] Then the Adhvaryu proceeds with the Vanaspati offering. Having proceeded with the Vanaspati, those portions which were in the Upabhṛt—

While bringing those [portions] together, he says, "Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," and the Pratiprasthātṛ steps across; he takes up that entire sacrificial essence (medha), then pours clarified butter over it twice from above, and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt! at which the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
The Adhvaryu offers the oblation; following the Adhvaryu’s offering, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers. [He offers] with the verse:
"O Indu, many-favored, multiform.
By saying "many-favored" (*purudasma*), he means "one who gives much"; by saying "multiform" (*viṣurūpa*), he means the same.
"For the embryos are indeed of diverse forms; the wise one has measured out his greatness within," [so it is said]. For he (the Soma) is indeed attached within the mother.

With the words, "May they spread along the worlds—one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed, eight-footed—Svāhā! he thus causes her to expand. Having sacrificed with the eight-footed [verse], he indeed conquers more abundantly.
Regarding what has been said concerning the eightfold [altar]:
they ask, "Where should one place this embryo? They should indeed hang it upon a tree.
For embryos have the intermediate space as their abode; and since a tree is, as it were, the intermediate space, he thus establishes it in its own proper abode. And so, indeed...

They say that if someone were to speak ill of him there, saying, "They shall lift up this dead man like a tree," it would surely happen exactly so. 4.5.2. [14] They should carry him down into water; for water is the support of all this, and thus they place him in water itself.
He establishes it. Regarding this, they say: "If someone were to speak ill of him there, saying, 'He will die in water,' so indeed it shall be.
They should scatter it upon a molehill.
This indeed is the foundation of all this; he thus establishes him upon this very foundation.
Regarding this, they say: "If someone were to utter a curse against him there, saying, 'Soon they will prepare a burial mound for him when he is dead,' it would surely happen exactly so. 4.5.2 [16]
One should offer it to the Maruts on the very animal-cooking fire;
for the Maruts are the non-eaters of oblations among the gods, and this [fetus] is like an unoffered oblation when it is not cooked. Furthermore, it has been brought from the Āhavanīya fire.
He says that the cooking of the sacrificial animal does not take place outside the sacrifice, nor as if directly in the Āhavanīya fire; for the Maruts are indeed the gods [of the air].
Thus, he establishes it among the Maruts themselves.
Having offered the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations, [he proceeds].

When the coals have first subsided, he takes up this embryo together with its turban; standing facing the east, he offers it with a verse addressed to the Maruts: "O Maruts, mighty ones of heaven, you who drink in whose dwelling—he is the most well-guarded person. He does not utter *svāhā*, for the Maruts are the eaters of the unoffered among the gods.
That which is offered without the *svāhā* call is like an oblation cast into excrement; since the Maruts are indeed the gods, he thereby establishes him among the Maruts alone.
Then he fans [the fire] with embers.
"May Heaven and Earth, the broad earth, mix this sacrifice for us; may they fill us with nourishments.
(4.5.3) Indra, indeed, is the *ṣoḍaśin*.
Now, the beings surpassed that Indra alone; for the beings are indeed creatures, and they seemed to become his equals. 4.5.3.
Indra, indeed, reflected.
"How indeed might I transcend all this? May all this remain below me.
He saw this cup; he drew it. He transcended all this, and all this remained below him. Truly, all this [is]...
All this that exists becomes subordinate to him who, knowing thus, has this cup drawn for him. Therefore, this has been declared by the Seer: 4.5.3. [3] Therefore, this has been declared by the Seer:
"The sky did not equal your greatness when you stood upon the earth with one hip"—for indeed, that sky did not even equal one of his hips;
thus he stood over all this, and all this became inferior to him; for indeed, everything...
All this indeed remains beyond him, and all this comes into being from him, for whomsoever, knowing thus, they draw this cup.
He draws it with a verse addressed to the Haris.
They praise with verses containing the word *hari*; he recites the *anuçamsana* with verses containing the word *hari*.
For *hara* (the golden power) is indeed vigor; Indra appropriated the *hara* of the Asuras, his rivals. In the same way, this sacrificer now appropriates the *hara*, that vigor, from his rivals.

Therefore, he draws [the cup] with a verse containing the word *hari*; they praise with verses containing the word *hari*; he recites the *anuçamsana* with verses containing the word *hari*. 4.5.3. [5]
Or rather, he draws it with an *anuṣṭubh* verse.

The morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī*, the midday pressing to the *triṣṭubh*, and the third pressing to the *jagatī*; but the *anuṣṭubh* is redundant, and thus he thereby causes it to flow out.
Therefore, he draws [the cup] with an *anuṣṭubh* verse (4.5.3).
He indeed draws it with a four-cornered vessel;
for these worlds are three, and thus by means of three [verses], he [grasps] these very worlds.
By means of the corners he attains him; by means of the fourth corner he causes him to overflow. Therefore, one draws [the draught] with a four-cornered vessel.
One should indeed draw it at the morning pressing.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa cup, he lets it rest from the time it was drawn at the morning pressing; thus he causes all the pressings to exceed that [cup].
Or rather, one should draw it at the midday pressing.

Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, this is the deliberation: he should draw it at the morning pressing itself; having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, once it has been drawn at the morning pressing, it remains lying there from that time until [the later occasion]. 4.5.3. [9]
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:

"Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra; your two bay steeds have been yoked by prayer. May the pressing-stone turn your mind hitherward with its sound. You are taken with a base; for Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin, this is yours."

"Thou art the womb for Indra, for thee, the *ṣoḍaśin*. Or with this [verse]: "Yoke indeed thy two long-maned, bay steeds, the vigorous ones that fill the girth-bands; then, O Indra, drinker of Soma, come to the hearing of our songs. Thou art taken with a support; for Indra, for thee, the *ṣoḍaśin*. This is thy womb; for Indra, for thee."

"Regarding the *ṣoḍaśin*," [it is said]. 4.5.3.[11] Then, having approached, he introduces the chant (*stotra*) with the words, "Soma has overflowed; come back! By this, he indeed causes him (Soma) to overflow. Him—
Verily, he performs the introductory rite before sunset and recites the concluding praise after sunset; thus he joins together day and night.
Therefore, he performs the introductory rite before sunset and recites the concluding praise after sunset.
All the gods, indeed, [are present].
In the beginning, they were all alike and all meritorious; among all those who were alike and all meritorious, three desired: "May we be pre-eminent"—namely Agni, Indra, and [Viṣṇu].
They moved about performing worship and exerting themselves.
They saw these *atigrāhya* cups; they drew them over [the others].

Because they drew them over [the others], they are called *atigrāhya*. They became standing still (*atiṣṭhāvan*), just as these [cups] stand still here. Indeed, he becomes one who stands still for whom these cups are drawn by one who knows thus. 4.5.4. [3]
Verily, in the beginning, there was no luster in Agni.
That luster which is now in him, he desired: "May this luster be in me.
He saw this cup; he drew it. Then that luster came to be in him. 4.5.4. [4]
In the beginning, indeed, there was no such strength as this in Indra. That strength which is now in him, he desired: "May this strength be in me.
He saw this cup; he drew it, and then that strength came to be in him. 4.5.4. [5]
In the beginning, indeed, there was no radiance in this sun; that which is now its radiance did not exist in it. He desired, "May there be this radiance in me.
He saw this cup and drew it; then this radiance came to be in him—these [are they].
Verily, he who knows this and for whom they draw these cups deposits these splendors and powers within himself.
One should indeed draw them at the morning pressing;
having drawn the Āgrayaṇa—the Āgrayaṇa being the self, or rather, the manifold—[one should draw them]. 4.5.4 [6]
This [cup] is one more than each of these [other cups]: the *kloman* and the heart belong to you alone.
One should draw it at the midday pressing.

Having drawn the Ukthya cup, or when about to perform the Upakarana rite for the Pūtabhṛt vessel—this Ukthya is indeed his unexpressed (anirukta) self; this is merely a deliberation: he should draw these [cups] at the morning pressing itself, after having drawn the Āgrayaṇa. 4.5.4. [8]
These [oblations] are offered following the oblation to Mahendra alone.
Indeed, this cup for Mahendra is Indra’s exclusive (niṣkevalya) draught; for him, too, there is this exclusive chant (stotra) and exclusive recitation (śastra), for Indra is [the deity].
These [cups] are drawn for the sake of the sacrificer’s desire; therefore, they are offered following the offering of the cup for Mahendra.
Now, therefore, he draws [the cups].
O Agni, purify yourself, you who are skillful; bestow upon us luster and heroic vigor, granting me wealth and prosperity.
You are taken with a support; I take you for Agni, for luster. This is your womb; I take you for Agni, for luster. 4.5.4 [10] Arising with strength...
Having drunk together, you shook your jaws, O Indra, after the Soma pressed in the vessels. You are taken with a support;
for Indra, for you, [I take you] for power. This is your seat; for Indra, for you, [I place you] for power.
4.5.4.[11] His banners have become visible.

The rays [shine] forth among the people, shining like fires. "Thou art taken with a support; for Sūrya, thee, for splendor! This is thy womb; for Sūrya, thee, for splendor! 4.5.4.[12] Their consumption [is as follows]:
O Agni, radiant one, you are radiant among the gods; may I be radiant among men. O Indra, most powerful one, you are most powerful among the gods;
may I be most powerful among men. O Sūrya, most brilliant one, you are most brilliant among the gods; may I be most brilliant.
"May I become among men"— these indeed are the splendors, these are the powers, which he places within himself for whomsoever,
knowing thus, they draw these cups.
One should draw them during the Pṛṣṭhya six-day period.

In the first three days, one takes [the draughts] for Agni on the first day, for Indra on the second, and for Sūrya on the third; in this very manner, day after day. Some, however, take them during the latter three days.
One should not do it in that way; rather, one should take them during the first three-day period.
If one intends to take them during the latter three-day period, one should first take them during the first three-day period and then take them during the latter three-day period.
In this very manner, according to the prior sequence, they are taken only in the Viśvajit, the one-day sacrifice (ekāha) consisting of all the *pṛṣṭhas*. 4.5.5. [1]
This indeed is Prajāpati;
it is this sacrifice which is being performed, from which these creatures were born, and even now they are born after following it. 4.5.5. [2]
The goats are born after the Upāṃśu vessel;
that very [vessel] is employed again in the sacrifice, and therefore these creatures are born again and again in return. 4.5.5. [3]
They are born following the very cup of the Antaryāma;
that [cup] is indeed employed again in the sacrifice, and therefore these creatures are born again and again. 4.5.5. [4]

Now, because he offers the *upāṃśu* oblation first while both of these [goats] are together, therefore, when both goats and sheep are together, the goats go first and the sheep follow behind them. 4.5.5. [5]
Now, because he wipes upwards after having offered the *upāṃśu* oblation, therefore these goats go as if stepping upon the other [cows]. 4.5.5. [6]
Now, because he wipes downward after having offered the Antaryāma cup, therefore these sheep go as if digging with their heads turned downward;
for goats and sheep are the most manifest forms of Prajāpati, and therefore they [are sacrificed] three times.
Being born throughout the year, they produce two or three [offspring].
Human beings are born after the *śukra* cup;
indeed, that very [cup] is employed again in the sacrifice.
Therefore these creatures are born again and again. That which shines yonder is indeed the bright one (*śukra*);
he is also Indra. Man is indeed the lord of cattle; therefore he rules over cattle.
Following the cup for the seasons (*ṛtupātra*), the single-hoofed animal is born.

That indeed is employed again in the sacrifice; therefore these creatures are born again and again. Or rather, it is as if the *ṛtupātra*, as if the head of the one-hoofed animal, the *āgrayaṇapātra*, the *ukthyapātra*, and the *ādityapātra*—after these very vessels cows are born. These, indeed, are they.
Furthermore, because they are employed at the sacrifice, these offspring are born again and again.
Now, as for the goats: since they are born after the smallest vessels, therefore they are born three times in the year.
When giving birth, they produce two or three; for the youngest [cattle] are born after the smallest vessels. And as for cows:
since they are born after the greatest number of vessels, therefore they give birth only once a year.
Giving birth, they produce each one individually; for indeed, most abundantly do vessels multiply after them. 4.5.5 [11]. Now, regarding the *droṇakalaśa*:
finally, he draws the *hāriyojana* cup. The *droṇakalaśa* is indeed Prajāpati. It...
These creatures turn toward him; he protects them and he smells them. Indeed, he becomes this very thing when he procreates them.
There are, however, only five vessels after which these creatures are born.
The procedure for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups is the same; [the others are] the Śukra cup, the Ṛtu cup, the Āgrayaṇa cup, and the Ukthya cup.
There are five seasons of the year, and the year is Prajāpati; Prajāpati is the sacrifice. But if there are six seasons of the year, then the Āditya cup is the sixth of these. 4.5.5. [13]

But there is indeed one single cup: that cup from which these creatures are born after [the sacrifice]. It is the Upāṃśu cup, for the Upāṃśu is breath; and Prajāpati is breath, for everything here follows Prajāpati. 4.5.6. [1]

This indeed is Prajāpati—the sacrifice which is being performed, from which these creatures were born, and even now they are born after it. Having drawn the Āśvina cup, he causes the Avakāśas to be recited. 4.5.6. [2]
He causes the Upāṃśu cup to flow first in a whisper:
"For my out-breathing, you who grant splendor, flow pure for splendor";
then the Upāṃśusavana stone: "For my through-breathing, you who grant splendor, flow pure for splendor."

"Flow on!"—thus [he draws] the Antaryāma cup, with the formula: "For my out-breath, flow on, bestowing splendor for the sake of splendor. Then the Aindravāyava cup: "For my speech, flow on, bestowing splendor for the sake of splendor. Then the Maitrāvaruṇa cup: "For my will and skill, flow on, bestowing splendor for the sake of splendor. Then the Āśvina cup: "For my hearing, flow on, bestowing splendor for the sake of splendor. Then...
"O Śukra and Manthin, you two who bestow splendor upon my eyes, purify yourselves for the sake of splendor! (4.5.6.3).
Then the Āgrayaṇa:
"O giver of splendor, purify yourself for the sake of splendor for me. Then the Ukthya: "O giver of splendor, [purify yourself] for the sake of vigor for me."

"For luster, flow clear," [he says]; then for the *dhruva* cup: "Give me luster; for luster, flow clear. Then for the two *ambhṛṇa* cups: "For all my offspring, you two who give luster, flow clear for luster. The two *ambhṛṇa* cups belong to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*), for from there they draw for the gods, from there for men, and from there for the ancestors; therefore the two *ambhṛṇa* cups belong to the All-gods. 4.5.6. [4]
Then, regarding the *droṇakalaśa* [vessel]:

"Who are you? Which one are you?"—"Ka" (Who) is indeed Prajāpati; "Of whom are you?"—"Ka" by name are you?—"Ka" by name is indeed Prajāpati. "Whose name we have meditated upon for you"—for he indeed meditates upon his name, "you whom..."

"May we satisfy ourselves with Soma"—for he indeed satisfies him with Soma. Having drawn the Āśvina cup, he invokes a blessing upon his own limbs, saying, "May I be rich in offspring through my offspring"; thereby he invokes offspring.
"May I be rich in heroes through my heroes"; thereby he invokes heroes. "May I be rich in nourishment through my nourishments"; thereby he invokes prosperity. 4.5.6 [5]
One should not leave them out entirely;

rather, one should leave out someone who is well-known, or someone dear to him, or someone learned in the Vedas who can reach them through his recitation. Having drawn the Āśvina cup, he thus brings forth the entire sacrifice.
Having generated that entire sacrifice, he places it within himself; he makes it his own self.

These, indeed, are the thirty-four *vyāhṛtis* known as expiations (*prāyaścitti*). This Prajāpati is indeed this very sacrifice which is being performed, from whom these creatures were born, and even now they are born after him.
There are eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, these very two, heaven and earth, as the thirty-third,
for there are thirty-three gods, and Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth; thus he makes him into Prajāpati— this indeed.
This which is immortal indeed exists; that which is immortal indeed exists. And this which is mortal—this is Prajāpati.
Prajāpati is indeed everything; thus he makes him into Prajāpati. Therefore, there are these thirty-four utterances (vyāhṛtis) called expiations (prāyaścittis). 4.5.7 [3]
Now, some call these the "limbs of the sacrifice," for they are indeed the joints of the sacrifice; this very sacrifice, being extended, proceeds becoming these very deities. 4.5.7.
[4] Now, if the cow that yields the *gharma* milk should stumble, ...
They might go to another [cow]; at whatever time they used to milk her previously, at that very time he should place her facing north, or facing east in front of the hall.
Now, those two [fires] which are on both sides—

The two crest-bones are the top-knot; in that which is the right of those two, he offers these thirty-four oblations of clarified butter. For as many as these thirty-four *vyāhṛti*s are, so great indeed is the entire sacrifice. Thus, he places the whole sacrifice in its entirety within this [top-knot]. This is the [explanation].
Therefore, one should cause the *gharma* to overflow; this is the expiation performed in that case.
Now, if the sacrifice should stumble, having observed that [the point of failure], one should offer an oblation in the *āhavanīya* fire during the *dīkṣā* and *upasad* rites, and in the *prasuta*.
In the Āgnīdhra shed, a joint of the sacrifice is indeed severed when it spills. Whatever deity is present there at that time, by that very deity he heals it; by that very deity he joins it together.
Now, if it should spill...

He should pour water over it, for by water all this is pervaded; [he does so] for the attainment of everything. With a verse addressed to Viṣṇu and Varuṇa—whatever in this world one praises, Varuṇa alone causes all that to be attained. "Those two by whose might the regions were established, who are most heroic in their valor, most powerful, who rule with unassailable strength—the two Viṣṇus."
"O Agni and Varuṇa, at the first invocation..."—Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he praises him with this verse. Varuṇa is the one who inflicts injury.
Thus, for whichever deity he praises and whichever deity inflicts the injury, by means of both of them he heals and by means of both he joins together. 4.5.7 [8]
Then he should indeed touch it:
"The sacrifice has gone to the gods, to heaven; may wealth come to me from that. The sacrifice has gone to men, to the intermediate space; may wealth come to me from that."

"To the fathers, to the earth, to Agni the sacrifice has gone; may wealth come to me from that; to whatever world the sacrifice has gone, from that may prosperity be mine"—this is what he thereby says.
Regarding this, Āruṇi indeed said:

"Would he be performing a sacrifice who, through the failure of the sacrifice, would consider himself worse off—or who would think, 'Through the failure of the sacrifice, may I become better off'? He said this regarding the fact that one approaches these prayers for blessings (āśis).

Now, when one gives a thousand [cows] at this three-night sacrifice, it is thereby made "thousandfold. On the first day, he leads away three hundred and thirty-three; in exactly the same way, on the second day, he leads away three hundred and thirty-three.
In this same manner, on the third day, he leads three hundred and thirty-three; and thus this [number] exceeds one thousand.
Regarding this, they say: "It should indeed be of three forms."
"For this [cow] is, as it were, its most perfect form," they say; however, it should be a reddish-brown cow with black spots, for that indeed is its most perfect form.
It should be one that has not been mated.
This thousand-versed *Ayātayāmnī* is speech by its very origin;
for this speech is indeed *Ayātayāmnī* (unexhausted) and unconfined. Therefore, it should be unconfined.
On the first day, one should lead it forth.
This thousand-fold [sacrifice] is, by its very origin, speech; this thousand is born from that speech.

This [speech] goes first, and the offspring follows after it. On the last day, one should lead it forward; then the offspring goes before it, and it follows after. This is the investigation, and it is indeed the highest.
Thus he leads her forward; first she goes toward what has been born for her, and then she follows after it.
To the north of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, to the south of the *āgnīdhra*, he makes her smell the *droṇakalaśa*; for the sacrifice is indeed...
The *droṇakalaśa* indeed shows this [earth] as the sacrifice itself.
"Smell the jar; let the drops enter thee abundantly"—for he who has poured out [the Soma] becomes, as it were, emptied. 4.5.8. [6]
"He gives a thousand; he thus replenishes him who was emptied when he says: 'Smell the jar;
may the drops enter thee abundantly. 'Return with strength. 4.5.8 [7] "Return with strength."
He causes that which has been emptied to swell again when he says, "Return with vigor," and "May you milk for us a thousandfold."
When he says, "May she milk for us a thousandfold," he causes her, who was emptied by that thousandfold [offering], to swell again; [and when he says],
"May the wide-streamed, milch-cow-like wealth enter me again."
He causes that which was emptied to swell again when he says, "May wealth enter me again.
Then he whispers into his right ear.

"O Iḍā, Rantī, Havyā, Kāmyā, Candrā, Jyotī, Aditi, Sarasvatī, Mahī, Viśrutī—these, O inviolable one, are your names. Speak for me to the gods that I am a doer of good; say 'So be it,' or at least these are her names among the gods.
By those names of yours among the gods, speak for me to the gods that I am a doer of good."
"Speak!"—this is what he thereby says.
They drive her away.
If she should go forward while unapproached by men, one should know that this sacrificer has succeeded.

"If it moves toward the north, one should know: 'The sacrificer will become superior in this world'; if it moves toward the west, one should know: 'He will be like a *tilvila* of grain, full of grain'; if it moves toward the south, one should know: 'The sacrificer will depart quickly from this world. These are the signs. 4.5.8 [12]

Now, those three sets of thirty-three that exist above—into these they incorporate this [Virāj]. For they indeed tear asunder this Virāj when they dissect it; this Virāj is torn asunder when it is divided. It consists of ten syllables.
He thereby unites the entire Virāj with the Virāj; he should give that to the Hotṛ, for the Hotṛ is associated with the thousandfold [sacrifice];
therefore, he should give it to the Hotṛ.
He should appoint two Unnetṛs.

Whichever of those two does not cause [the announcement] to be heard, to him one should give this [virāj]; for that Unnetṛ who, being an officiating priest, does not cause it to be heard, is unsuccessful; and that Virāj which is deficient is unsuccessful. Thus, he bestows what is unsuccessful upon one who is unsuccessful. 4.5.8. [14]
Regarding this, they say: "One should not give anything in addition to a thousand, for by means of a thousand alone one obtains all desires.
To this Āsuri said: "One may indeed give according to one's desire; for by means of a thousand one obtains all desires, and by means of desire everything else becomes given to him. 4.5.8 [15]
Now, if he intends to give a harnessed chariot,
or if he should give it when the omentum of a barren cow has been offered, or at the Udavasānīyā sacrifice; 4.5.8 [16].

When leading away the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā), he should lead them in groups of ten without deficiency. If he intends to give one [cow] to someone, he should assign her from among those ten; if he intends to give two to someone, he should assign them from among those five.
He should turn over a decade to one who intends to give three; he should turn over a decade to those three.
He should turn over a decade to two who intend to give five; he should turn over a decade to those two.
Thus up to a hundred. In this way, his Virāj, being not deficient, becomes a cow of plenty in yonder world.
It occurs thus: 4.5.9.[1] Now, when he performs this sacrifice with the twelve-day rite arranged according to the meters (*vyūḍhacandas*),
then he arranges the cups (*graha*) and the Udgātṛ priest arranges them.

The Hotṛ and the *candas*—this very [set] is already well-known as the first three-day period (*pūrvastryaha*), with its *candas* arranged in the *samūḍha* order; therein he draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu.
Then, on the fourth day, he performs the *vyūha*.
They transpose the *grahas* and the *chandases*; then he draws the cups beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*.
This fourth day belongs to Prajāpati; the *āgrayaṇa* is indeed the self (*ātman*), and Prajāpati is the self. Therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*. 4.5.9 [3]

Having taken it, he does not set it down. The cups (grahas) are indeed the vital breaths; [he thinks], "Lest I should confuse the vital breaths. For he would indeed confuse the vital breaths were he to set it down. They wait upon it while holding it fast. Then he draws the cups; then, when he has drawn the cups—

Then, at whatever time it is appropriate for this [cup], he draws it and, having uttered the *hiṃ* sound, sets it down. Now, that fifth day is indeed well-known; on that day, he draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu. Then, on the sixth day, he performs the rearrangement (*vyūhati*).
They arrange the planets and the meters; he draws the cups beginning with the Śukra.
This sixth day indeed belongs to Indra. He who shines yonder is indeed the Śukra, and he is also Indra; therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the Śukra.

Having taken it up, he does not set it down; for the cups are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), thinking, "Lest I should confuse the vital breaths. For were he to set it down, he would indeed confuse the vital breaths. They remain seated holding it up, and then he draws the cups; then, when he has drawn the cups...
Then, at whatever time it is appropriate for this [cup], he deposits it. 4.5.9.

[6] Now, on the seventh day, he rearranges [the cups]. They rearrange the cups; they rearrange the meters. Therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the *śukra*, or those belonging to the *bṛhatī* meter.
This is the seventh day. He who shines yonder is indeed Śukra, and he is also Bṛhan;
therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the Śukra.
Having drawn it, he does not set it down.
The cups (*graha*) are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); [he does this] thinking, "Lest I should confuse the vital breaths.
For if he were to set them down, he would indeed confuse the vital breaths; therefore, they wait upon him while holding [the cups]. Then he draws the cups.
Now, when he draws the cups, at that very time when it is its [proper] hour, he [draws] this one.
He deposits [the cups]; now, this eighth day is well known. On that day, he draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu. Then, on the ninth day, he performs the transposition (*vyūhati*);
they transpose the cups and the meters; on that day, he draws the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa, [which is] the Jāgata meter.
This ninth day is indeed the self; the Āgrayaṇa is the self, for this entire world is the self.
Therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa.
Having drawn it, he does not set it down.
The cups (grahas) are indeed the vital breaths; [he thinks], "Lest I should confuse the vital breaths.
For he would indeed confuse the vital breaths were he to set them down. They wait upon him while holding it up. Then he draws the cups.
Now, when he draws the cups, at whatever time that [cup] belongs, having uttered the *hiṃ* over it, he sets it down. 4.5.9. [10]
Regarding this they say: "One should not transpose the cups (*graha*), for the cups are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); one should not confuse the vital breaths.
Indeed, he would confuse the vital breaths if he were to transpose them; therefore, one should not transpose them.
However, one should indeed transpose them.
The limbs are indeed the *grahas*, for these limbs lie at will in various positions; therefore, one should indeed transpose them.
However, one should not transpose them at all.

"The *grahas* are indeed the vital breaths; 'I must not confuse the vital breaths,' [he thinks]. For he would indeed confuse the vital breaths were he to transpose them; therefore, he should not transpose them. What then, O Adhvaryu, in that case? 4.5.9. [13]
When the Udgātṛ and the Hotṛ transpose the meters, it is indeed the Adhvaryu who transposes them:
in that he draws the cups at the morning pressing with those for Indra and Vāyu first, at the midday pressing with the Śukra first, and at the third pressing with the Āgrayaṇa first. 4.5.10. [1]
If they should steal the Soma, he should say, "It runs away. If they find it, why should they care? But if they do not find it, an expiation is performed for that. 4.5.10. [2]

There are indeed two kinds of *phālguna* flowers: those with red blossoms and those with reddish-brown blossoms. One should press those *phālguna* flowers that have reddish-brown blossoms; for these reddish-brown *phālguna* flowers are indeed a limb of Soma.
Therefore, one should press the red flowers. 4.5.10.
[3] If they should not find red flowers, one should press those brought by a hawk; for it was there that Gāyatrī—

He discharged a soma-arrow at her; as she was bringing it back, a shoot of soma fell from it, and it became carried off by a hawk. Therefore, one should press the soma that has been carried off by a hawk. 4.5.10 [4]. If they should not find soma carried off by a hawk, [they should proceed otherwise].
One should press *ādāra* stalks for the soma. For when the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its essence that was scattered became the *ādāra* stalks; therefore, one should press *ādāra* stalks.
If one should not find *ādāra* stalks, [one may use other stalks].
One should press the red *dūrvā* grass; for the red *dūrvā* is indeed a part of Soma, therefore one should press the red *dūrvā*. If they should not find red *dūrvā*, [they may use other plants].

Even if one should press any green kuśa grasses whatsoever, there he should give only one cow; then, having emerged from the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he should undergo initiation again, for in that case the expiation is simply a repetition of the sacrifice. This is the rule for those whose soma has been stolen. 4.5.10. [7]
Now, regarding the breaking of the jar:

if the jar should break, he should say, "Do you seek to obtain [the water]? If they should obtain it—even if only as much as a handful or as much as a cupful—he should pour it back up along with the other *ekadhana* vessels.

They should proceed according to their respective capacity; however, if they should not obtain [the required vessels], they should pour out from the Āgrayaṇa vessel itself, fill other Ekadhana vessels, and proceed according to their capacity. If the pitcher should break while the sacrificial fees have not yet been led away, then one should give only a single cow; then, having emerged from the Avabhṛtha bath...
"One should undergo initiation again; for in that case, the sacrifice itself is the expiation"—thus [says] Kalaśadi Rāma 4.5.10.
Now, regarding the surplus Soma:
if it should exceed the Agniṣṭoma, one should perform the Ukthya from the *pūtabhṛt* vessel itself.
If the Ukthya should be exceeded, they should proceed to the Ṣoḍaśin; if the Ṣoḍaśin should be exceeded, they should proceed to the Night;
if the Night should be exceeded, they should proceed to the Day. Indeed, there is no such thing as exceeding [the sacrifice]. This Aṃśu cup is Prajāpati. 4.6.1. [1]

This is his very self, for this Prajāpati is indeed the self; thus they fashion this self for him when they draw these cups. Into that [self] he places these vital breaths (*prāṇa*), in accordance with how these cups, representing the vital breaths, are explained. Thus the sacrificer becomes possessed of his entire body in yonder world.
It comes into being like something that has a support;
for when they take it up, it is as if it has a support, but when they do not take it up, it is as if it has no support.
Therefore, he draws the *aṃśu* cup.
He draws it with a vessel made of *udumbara* wood;
for this [cup] is Prajāpati, belonging to Prajāpati.
Therefore, he draws [the Soma] with a cup made of *udumbara* wood.
He indeed draws it with a four-cornered cup;
for these worlds are three, and thus [he draws it] for these very worlds.
One attains the worlds by means of three [pressings]; Prajāpati indeed is the fourth beyond these worlds; thus, by means of the fourth, one attains Prajāpati himself.
Therefore, he draws [the Soma] with a four-cornered vessel.
He takes up the pressing-stone silently.
He pours in the shoots silently; he pours water upon them silently;
having lifted it up silently, he presses once; he offers this without pausing silently; thus he makes it Prajāpati. 4.6.1. [6]
Now, gold is bound to this [bowstring]; he smells it. Whatever he scratches here or whatever he licks off, gold is immortal life; thus he places that immortal life within himself. 4.6.1[7]
Regarding this, Rāma Aupatasvini said: "One may breathe at will and drink at will; for in that one offers silently, it is thereby that one makes him Prajāpati. 4.6.1. [8]
Now, gold is bound to this [cow];
he smells it. Whatever he scratches here or whatever he licks, that is immortal life-force (*amṛta-āyus*); gold is immortal life-force; thus he places immortal life-force within himself. 4.6.1. [9]
Regarding this, Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi said:
"One should draw [the Soma] having merely lifted it up; one should not press it.
For they do press [it] for other deities; thus he does otherwise than for those other deities. And then...
"Whatever he raises up, that alone becomes pressed for him," [so it is said].
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said:
"One should indeed press [the Soma]; the unpressed Soma does not exhilarate Indra."
"O Soma juices, you are not for one who is no Brahmin, O Maghavan"—thus it was declared by the seer. He does not press [the soma] even once for any other deity whatsoever;
he acts otherwise than that, as he does for other deities. Therefore, he should indeed press [it]. 4.6.1. [11]
Twelve first-born heifers are the sacrificial fee for this [rite]. There are indeed twelve months in a year;
Prajāpati is the year, and Aṃśu is Prajāpati; thus he makes him into Prajāpati. 4.6.1. [12]
They have twelve embryos;
they are twenty-four in number, for there are twenty-four half-months in a year.
Prajāpati is the year, and the sunbeam is Prajāpati; thus he makes him into Prajāpati. 4.6.1. [13]
Then Kaukūṣṭha gave as sacrificial fees these twenty-four first-calving four-year-old cows, a bull as the twenty-fifth, and gold; this indeed was what he gave. 4.6.1 [14]
Indeed, this [sacrificial cup] should not be taken from just anyone;

for it is his very self (ātman). It should be taken from one who knows it, or from one who is dear to him, or from one who is learned in the Vedas and might attain it through what has been studied. 4.6.1. [15]
It is to be taken at the *sahasra* [sacrifice];
for the *sahasra* is everything, and this [cup] is everything. It is to be taken at the *sarvavedasa* [sacrifice];
for the *sarvavedasa* is everything, and this is everything. It is to be taken at the *viśvajit* sacrifice with all the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]; for everything is indeed...

The Viśvajit, with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants, is to be drawn at the Vājapeya and the Rājasūya; for that [sacrifice] is everything. It is to be drawn at the *sattra*, for the *sattra* is indeed everything, and this [Viśvajit] is everything. These are the draughts. Indeed, they go toward this one. 4.6.2.1. They go toward this one.

That which shines with six months—that which they sit for a year—is declared according to the *Sāman*; its form is fashioned and declared according to the *Ṛc*. Then, this very thing is according to the *Yajus* and according to the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), namely that they take it up; by this very means they go unto him. 4.6.2. [2]
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"The rays bear aloft that god Sūrya, the Jātavedas, so that all may behold him.
Thou art taken with a support; for Sūrya, thee, for brilliance! This is thy womb; for Sūrya, thee, for brilliance! 4.6.3. [1]

Now, therefore, regarding the Paśvayana sacrifice itself: one should proceed with the eleven animal victims. He immolates the first victim for Agni, then one for Varuṇa, and then again one for Agni; in this very manner one should proceed with this set of eleven animals. 4.6.3. [2]
Moreover, one should sacrifice an animal every day specifically to Indra and Agni.
Agni indeed is all the deities, for into Agni they offer oblations to all the deities; and Indra indeed is the deity of the sacrifice; thus, this [sacrifice] satisfies all the deities.
He does not offend [the sacrifice], and he does not offend that deity of the sacrifice. 4.6.3.
Now, therefore, regarding the *stomāyana* (the progression of the *stomas*):
at the *agniṣṭoma*, one should offer an animal to Agni; for that is consistent with the proper order (*saloma*).

If it be an Agniṣṭoma, one should immolate an animal for Agni; if it be an Ukthya, one should immolate a second one for Indra and Agni, for the Ukthas belong to Indra and Agni; if it be a Ṣoḍaśin, one should immolate a third one for Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin belongs to Indra;
if it be an Atirātra, one should immolate a fourth one for Sarasvatī, for Sarasvatī is Speech, and Speech is indeed female.
The night is a woman of speech; it distinguishes the sacrificial rites according to their proper order. These are the three courses (ayana);

whichever of these one may desire, by that one should proceed. Two animals are to be immolated: on the Vaiṣuvata day, he immolates a solar animal, and on the Mahāvrata day, a Prājāpatya animal. 4.6.4. [1]
Now, therefore, concerning the Mahāvratīya [rite] itself.

When Prajāpati was creating the creatures, his joints gave way; with his joints dislocated, he was unable to hold himself together. Then the gods went about worshipping and toiling, and they found this [rite].
They saw him [as one] belonging to the Great Vow; they seized him with that [vow], and by it they set his joints together.
With his joints thus joined together, he rose up toward this food-eating, namely, this food-eating which belongs to Prajāpati.

Whatever is the food of men, that is the vow (*vrata*) of the gods. "Great indeed has this vow become, by which he has become so great"—therefore it is called the Mahāvrata. Thus indeed do these [days] come to be. 4.6.4 [3] Thus indeed do these [days] come to be.

Those who sit for a year do so just as Prajāpati sat when he was creating creatures; and just as Prajāpati rose up toward food at the end of the year, even so do they rise up toward food at the end of the year—those for whom this cup is drawn while they know thus. 4.6.4. [4]
Or rather, one should draw it for Indra Vimṛdh alone.

For all their adversaries (*mṛdh*) are indeed slain and everything is conquered by those who sit through the year-long rite; therefore [the verse is]: "O Indra, drive away our adversaries; strike them down."
O you who attack us! Whosoever seeks to harm us, send him down into the lowest darkness.
You are taken with a support for Indra.
"O you who crush the adversaries! This is your resting place; for Indra, who crushes the adversaries, you! And also: "For Viśvakarman.
For those [who perform this rite], every deed is accomplished and everything is conquered. 4.6.4. [5]
They sit for a year; therefore, for Viśvakarman, we shall invoke today for our protection Vācaspati, the all-maker, swift as thought, in this contest.
May he, who brings welfare to all and performs good deeds, graciously accept all our invocations for our aid.
"You are taken with a support; for Indra Viśvakarman you! This is your womb; for Indra Viśvakarman you! (4.6.4).
If, however, he should know an [offering] verse addressed to Indra Viśvakarman, he should take [the draught] in that same manner [with]: "O Viśvakarman, with the oblation..."
By means of Vardhana, you made Indra a protector who was invincible;
to him the ancient tribes bowed down, so that he might be the fierce one, worthy of invocation.
"You are taken with a support; for Indra Viśvakarman you! This is your womb;
for Indra Viśvakarman you!"—this indeed is the draught (graha). 4.6.5 [1]
That which shines yonder, by which all these creatures are seized—that is why they say, "We perform the *grahas*"; for they move about as those possessed by the *grahas*.
Speech itself is the *graha*.
"By speech indeed all this is grasped; what then is that which is the grasping of speech? "Name itself is the grasper.
For by name indeed all this is grasped; what then is that which is the grasper of name? [It is] many indeed..."
We know their names; therefore, they are not seized by us. 4.6.5. [4] Food indeed is the *graha* (seizing power).
For by food all this is seized; therefore, as many as eat our food, they...
All of us become seized; such is the established rule. 4.6.5 [5].
This which is the Soma-draught is indeed food. Whatever deity for whom one draws this draught, she [is pleased] for him.

The deity, seized by this cup, fulfills that desire for which one draws it. At sunrise or at sunset, he worships the sun, saying: "O Cup, seize so-and-so with this affliction; let so-and-so not attain this. Or, regarding one whom he hates, he says: "Let this desire not be fulfilled for him. And indeed, that desire is not fulfilled for him.
For he prospers for whom one thus pays homage. 4.6.6. [1] The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases; they said:
"Who will sit to our south? Then we shall perform the sacrifice from the north, in a place free from fear and free from destructive spirits.
They said, "He among us who is most heroic shall sit to the south; then we shall perform the sacrifice from the north, in a place free from fear and free from destructive spirits."
They said, "Indra is indeed the most heroic among us; let Indra sit on the south side, and then we shall perform the sacrifice from the north in a place free from fear and harm.
They then spoke to Indra.
"You are indeed the most powerful among us; you sit on the south, and we shall attend to the sacrifice from the north, in a place free from fear and danger.
He said, "What shall be mine from that? "The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin's *brahmasāman* shall be yours."
Therefore, they choose a Brāhmaṇa as the *brahmán* priest, saying, "Indra is the *brahmán*, he is the Brāhmaṇa. For this [priest] belongs to Indra;
thus Indra sits on the south side, and so they approach the sacrifice from the north, in a place free from fear and destruction.
Therefore, whoever may be the most heroic, he should sit on the south side, and they should approach the sacrifice from the north, in a place free from fear and destruction. Whoever...

Among the Brāhmaṇas, he who is the most learned in the Vedas is the most powerful of them. Now, as for the fact that whoever becomes a Brahman priest—some ask, "Does he sit silently?"—therefore, he who is the most powerful should sit on the south side.
Then, they should attend to the sacrifice from the north, in a place free from fear and free from destructive spirits. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas sit on the south side.
"In a place that is secure and free from danger, they attend to the sacrifice from the north. (4.6.6) When he says, "O Brahman, O Praśāstṛ, we shall chant the stotra," then the Brahman mutters:
"O divine Savitṛ, they have announced this sacrifice of yours to Bṛhaspati the Brahman; with that, protect the sacrifice, with that the lord of the sacrifice, with that..."

"Protect me; praise [him] at the impulse of Savitṛ"—this is the very same connection as before. Indeed, most people perform the rite with this one. However, one should rather perform it with this [other] one.
"O God Savitṛ, this; O Bṛhaspati, impel it. He approaches Savitṛ for instigation, for he is the instigator of the gods. "O Bṛhaspati, impel it"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman of the gods;
thus he says this to him who is the Brahman of the gods. Therefore he says, "O Bṛhaspati, impel it. 4.6.6. [8]
Then the Maitrāvaruṇa mutters:
"Impelled by the god Savitṛ, accepted by Mitra and Varuṇa. Thus he has recourse to Savitṛ for impulsion, for he is the impeller of the gods; [he is] accepted.

"To Mitra and Varuna"—for Mitra and Varuna are indeed the deities of the Maitrāvaruṇa; thus he addresses those very deities of the Maitrāvaruṇa, and therefore he says, "Acceptable to Mitra and Varuna. 4.6.7. [1] The triple science (trayī vidyā) is indeed [the Veda].

The *ṛcs*, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāmans*—this very thing is the *ṛcs*, for he who worships with it worships in this [earth]. Speech indeed is the *ṛcs*, for by means of speech he who worships worships. The intermediate space is the *yajus* formulas, and the sky is the *sāmans*. This threefold knowledge is employed in the Soma sacrifice. 4.6.7[2]
By means of the Ṛgveda one conquers this very world;

by means of the Yajurveda, the intermediate space; and by means of the Sāmaveda, the sky itself. Therefore, if someone has mastered even one of these sciences, he should desire to speak of the construction of the other two as being modeled after it—namely, that this very world is conquered by the Ṛgveda.
"The intermediate space triumphs by means of the *yajus*, the sky itself by means of the *sāman*.
This, indeed, is that: a thousandfold progeny of speech. Indra [obtained] two-thirds, Viṣṇu one-third; the *ṛc*s and *sāmans* belong to Indra, and the *yajus* belong to Viṣṇu.
Therefore, they perform the duties in the *sadas* with the *ṛc*s and *sāmans*, for the *sadas* belongs to Indra.
Then, with these sacrificial formulas (yajus), they carry this Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, as if in front; therefore it is called *puraścaraṇa*. 4.6.7 [5]
Speech indeed is the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants;

the mind alone is the Yajus-formulas. Wherever this speech was present, there everything was performed and everything was understood. But wherever the mind was present, nothing at all was performed there, nothing was understood—for it was not [speech].
"No one understands anyone who meditates with the mind.
Those gods said to Speech: "Go forward and make this known. She replied: "What would come of that for me?"

Whatever is offered in the sacrifice with the utterance of *svāhā* without the *vaṣaṭ*-call—that is this [Speech]. Therefore, whatever is offered in the sacrifice with the utterance of *svāhā* without the *vaṣaṭ*-call, that is Speech; she went forth eastward, and she made this known: "Do this! Do this! 4.6.7. [7]
Therefore, they indeed perform [the rites] with *ṛc*-verses in the Havirdhāna shed:
he recites the Prātaranuvāka, he recites the Sāmidhenī verses, and he praises the pressing-stones; for in this way, the two became yoked together. 4.6.7. [8]

Therefore, they indeed perform [these acts] in the *sadas*: they erect the *audumbarī* post, they construct the *sadas*, and they scatter the earth for the *dhiṣṇya* hearths; for in this way the two became united. 4.6.7. [9]
They enclose this very *sadas* for the sake of this union, thinking, "Let this union proceed as if in secret.
That union which another person looks upon is indeed unsuccessful; therefore, even when husband and wife engage in union, [they do so in private].

Moving about, they see; indeed, they run toward it and commit a transgression. Therefore, one should say to anyone looking at the *sadas* through a place other than the door, "Do not look! For it would be as if one were looking at a couple engaged in sexual intercourse;
yet one may look through the door at will, for that is a door made by the gods. 4.6.7. [10]

In this very way they enclose the *havirdhāna* shed, thinking, "May this couple perform their union as if in secret. That couple which another person looks upon is indeed deprived of its potency; therefore, even if it be husband and wife...

If they were to see them moving about in union, they would surely run away and commit a transgression; therefore, one should say to anyone looking toward the *havirdhāna* shed through a non-door, "Do not look! For it is just as if one were to see a couple engaged in union.
However, one may look through the door at will, for the door was made by the gods. 4.6.7. [11]
This *sāman* is indeed a bull, and it approaches the *ṛc*, which is a female, in the assembly;
from that union Indra was born. From the brilliance of both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, indeed, this brilliance was born, who is called Indra—Indra, indeed, is he who shines yonder. 4.6.7 [12]

Now, this Soma is the male, and the waters are the female; he approaches them in the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*). From that union, the moon was born. Indeed, that food which is born from the waters and from Soma is the moon; for the moon is the food of him (the sacrificer).

This [sun] shines; thus he causes the sacrificer to be born and produces food for him. He causes the sacrificer to be born from both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, and he produces food for him from both water and *soma*. 4.6.7. [13] By means of the *yajus*, indeed, the gods...

In the beginning, they performed the sacrifice with the *ṛc* and then with the *sāman*; even now, they perform the sacrifice first with the *yajus*, then with the *ṛc*, and then with the *sāman*. For that which is called "yajus" is indeed the sacrifice (*yajña*). 4.6.7 [14] Wherein, indeed, the gods...

These sciences milked out desires; among them, the science of the Yajus milked out the most desires. It was indeed the most highly refined, and the other sciences did not equal it, nor did the intermediate world equal the other two worlds. 4.6.7 [15]
Those gods desired:
"How indeed might this [earthly] knowledge correspond to the other two forms of knowledge? How might the intermediate world correspond to the other two worlds? 4.6.7 [16]

They said, "Let us perform with the Yajus formulas in a whisper; then this science will counterbalance the other sciences, and then the intermediate world will counterbalance the other two worlds. They performed in a whisper.

He thereby caused them to swell; from that, this knowledge stood facing the other knowledges, and from that, the intermediate world stood facing the other two worlds. Therefore, the *yajus* formulas, though being defined, are undefined;
therefore, this intermediate world, though being defined, is undefined. 4.6.7 [18]

He who performs with the *yajus* formulas in a low voice truly causes them to swell; they, being swollen, cause him to swell. But he who performs aloud truly parches them; they, being parched, parch him.
Harsh things cause harshness.
(4.6.7.19) Speech indeed is the *ṛc*s and the *sāman*s; the mind alone is the *yajus*. Those who proceed by means of both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, [proceed] by means of speech.
Now, those who perform with the *yajus* become the mind;

therefore, nothing whatsoever is done by the *adhvaryu* unless he has been prompted. Only when the *adhvaryu* says, "Recite! and "Sacrifice!", do they perform those things which are performed with the *ṛc*. And only when the *adhvaryu* says, "The Soma is being purified... [do they act].

"Turn back!"—thus they act; for those who perform it with the *sāman* do not speak with their voice until they have first reached [the goal] through reflection. That, indeed, is this mind of the *adhvaryu*.
He moves as if he were in a city; therefore it is called *puraścaraṇa*. Indeed, he who knows this becomes like a city in prosperity and fame.
This, indeed, is that very *puraścaraṇa*.
He who shines yonder should perform his duties according to the procedure of that very [sun];
having taken up the draught, he should turn back according to the procedure of that very [sun]; after responding to the call, he should turn back according to the procedure of that very [sun];

having offered the draught, he should turn back according to the procedure of that very [sun]. For he is indeed the sustainer; and whoever, knowing this, is able to act according to the procedure of that [sun], [he attains success].
He is indeed able to perform [the rite] and support his wives.

That which is the consecration (*dīkṣā*) is the session-sitting (*niṣad*); that is the sacrificial session (*sattra*). Therefore they say of them, "They sit" (*āsate*), and then they extend the sacrifice from there.
They go toward that; he who is the leader leads them, therefore they say, "They go toward it.
That which is the consecration (*dīkṣā*) is the session (*niṣat*);

that is the sacrificial session (*sattra*), that is the journey (*ayana*), that is the sacrificial session-journey (*sattrāyaṇa*). Now, as for that which follows from there, it is the conclusion of the sacrifice (*udṛc*).

"Having gone, they rise up; that is their rising. Therefore, they say, 'They have caused them to rise. Thus is the introductory section (purastādvadana). 4.6.8. [3] Now, those who are about to undergo initiation settle together.
If they are intending to build a fire-altar...
Having consigned the fires into the kindling woods, they go together to where they are about to sacrifice with the animal victim dedicated to Prajāpati;
having churned the fire, added fuel, and drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, they sacrifice with this animal victim dedicated to Prajāpati. 4.6.8 [4]
They place his head [on the fire].
If their consecration (dīkṣā) does not coincide on that day, they should consign the fires into the kindling woods (araṇis), return each to his own place, and offer the oblations. 4.6.8. [5]
Then, on the day their consecration comes together,
they mount the fires onto the kindling woods (*araṇi*) and proceed to the place where they are to be consecrated; the householder himself churns first toward the middle of the hall.

Then half of the others sit down to the south and half to the north; having churned fire and added fuel, they each take a single firebrand and approach together. Having drawn out the Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya of the householder himself, they undergo initiation. For them, the Āhavanīya is common.
The consecration and the Upasad rites may be performed with separate Gārhapatya fires. Then, on the day their purchase takes place,
he piles up the Gārhapatya layer for himself, and then for the others.
On the day of preparation (upavasatha), at the time of the Vaisarjina offerings for the hearths (dhiṣṇya), the wives come forward from the east;
they abandon these other fires once the Vaisarjina has been offered.
He leads forth the King (Soma).

This Āgnīdhrīya fire is already kindled; then, each of them taking a single firebrand (*ulmuka*), they go out to their respective hearths (*dhiṣṇya*). With those very firebrands of theirs, they strike [the fires].
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said: "Those who do so [act incorrectly]. This, indeed, is one way of proceeding. 4.6.8. [8]
Now this is the second [case]:
having consigned the fires into the kindling woods themselves, they go to where they are about to sacrifice with the animal victim dedicated to Prajāpati;
having churned the fire, added fuel, and drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, they sacrifice with this [rite].
With an animal sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati (prājāpatya-paśu),
they place its head [on the altar].
If their consecration (dīkṣā) does not coincide on that day, they should consign the fires into the two kindling woods (araṇis).
They offer the oblations in reverse order as appropriate. 4.6.8.
Now, on the day their initiation (dīkṣā) comes together, they mount the fires onto the kindling-wood (araṇi) and proceed to the place where [the sacrifice is to be performed].

They are about to undergo initiation. The householder himself churns first; then the others, having sat down around him, churn. As each fire is produced, they cast it into the Gārhapatya fire of the householder.
Having drawn out the Āhavanīya from the householder’s very Gārhapatya, they undergo initiation. For them, the Āhavanīya is common, and the [Gārhapatya] is common.
The Gārhapatya fire [is used] during the consecration and the Upasad days (4.6.8). Now, on the day their purchase takes place, on that day he piles up the Gārhapatya layer, and then for the others.
On the day of preparation (upavasatha), at the time of the Vaiśarjina offerings, the wives approach from the east;
they abandon this other fire once the Vaiśarjina offering has been performed. [4.6.8] He leads forth the King (Soma).

This Āgnīdhrīya fire is indeed already kindled; then, each of them taking a single firebrand, they go out to their respective hearths (dhiṣṇya). They thus create a conflict, for it is through conflict that he finds them; they become eager, and he finds even that half through conflict.
Regarding that purpose for which they sacrifice in such a manner...
Now this is the third [case]:
they take counsel regarding the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) of the householder alone; those who depart from here—this is the second way (*ayana*).
Now this is the third [formula]:
"The two forest fires of the householder itself converse: 'That fire which shall be born from here—let that be common to us;
what we shall win by this sacrifice, by this animal-binding, let that be common to us; let our good deeds be common to us.'"

"Even so, the evil belongs to him alone"—having said this, the householder first causes [the fires] to ascend, then he causes them to ascend for the others, or they cause them to ascend themselves; they come to where they are about to sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Prajāpati. Having churned [the fire], added fuel, and drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, they sacrifice with this.
With an animal sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati (4.6.8.15),
they place its head [on the altar].
If their consecration (*dīkṣā*) does not coincide on that day, they should instead cause the fires to ascend into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*).
They offer oblations, having turned [the fire] in whatever way is appropriate. 4.6.8.
[16] Now, on the day when their consecration (*dīkṣā*) comes together, they converse regarding the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) belonging to the householder alone, [saying]: "He who from here..."

"Fire shall be born; may it be ours in common, whatever we shall win by this sacrifice, whatever by this sacrificial session—that be ours in common. May our good deeds be in common; but whatever evil one may do, let that belong to him alone. Having spoken thus, the *gṛhapati* first causes the fires to ascend [into the kindling woods], then he causes them to ascend for the others, or they cause them to ascend themselves.
They come to where they are about to undergo initiation; having churned [the fire], added fuel, and drawn out the *āhavanīya* fire, they undergo initiation.
For them, the *āhavanīya* is common and the *gārhapatya* is common during the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) and the *upasads*. Now, on the day their purchase [of Soma] takes place...
On that day, he piles the Gārhapatya altar; then, on the Upavasatha day, he piles the Dhiṣṇya altars for the others.
At the time of the Vaisarjina offerings, the wives come forward from the east;
they abandon this other fire once the Vaisarjina has been offered. 4.6.8. [18]
He leads the king forward.
This fire of the Āgnīdhra is already prepared; then, each of them taking a single firebrand, they go away to their respective hearths. That which was done there is not undone.

In that they have separate hearths, there will be more ample space for their movement; and in that they have separate sacrificial cakes, there will be more of the oblation remaining for the sake of completion. Now, regarding the sacrificial session (*sattra*) by which the gods [attained their goal]...

They quickly struck away evil; they won this victory, for this is their victory. Therefore, when it is prepared, the gods indeed had a single householder, a single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and a single fire-hearth (*dhiṣṇya*);
they quickly struck away evil and were swiftly procreated. And so it is for him [who performs this rite].
Having a single householder, a single sacrificial cake, and a single hearth, they quickly strike away evil and quickly procreate.
Now, in that former case, there is a hall with its rafters pointing northward.
In that human rite, the Āhavanīya fire is common [to all], while the Gārhapatyas are separate; that is a deviation.

Only at the Gārhapatya of the householder do they perform the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives with the tail of the victim (*jāghanī*), while the others remain seated performing their respective offerings with clarified butter (*ājya*); that is a deviation. 4.6.8. [21]
Now, in this case, there is a hall with its sacred beam directed towards the east.

Thus, among the gods, the Āhavanīya fire is common, the Gārhapatya fire is common, and the Āgnīdhrīya fire is common; this sacrificial session is as successful as a one-day sacrifice (ekāha) is successful.
Thus he has no failure; this very thing is his common increase, for whatever is other than the *dhiṣṇya* hearths [belongs to him]. 4.6.9.
The gods, indeed, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), thinking:
"May we attain prosperity, may we be glorious, may we be eaters of food. To them—
This food had been won; the cattle were about to depart, for cattle are indeed food.
They wished to depart from them [the gods], thinking, "If these [cattle] are exhausted, they will not harm us; how indeed will they be able to overcome us? 4.6.9 [2]
They offered these two oblations in the Gārhapatya fire.
The Gārhapatya is indeed the home; the home is indeed the foundation.
Thus they settled them right within the home, and so the food they had won did not depart from them. 4.6.9. [3]
In the same way, those who sit for a sacrificial session (sattra) do so thinking, "May we attain prosperity, may we have glory, may we be eaters of food.
For them, this conquered food—which is indeed cattle—desires to depart; for cattle are food, and cattle are [the essence].

For they wish to depart from these very people, thinking, "Lest these men, being exhausted, should harm us; how indeed will they be able to endure us? 4.6.9 [4] They offer two oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire; for the *gārhapatya* is the household, and the household is the foundation.

Therefore, they keep it within the very houses; thus this food, once won by them, does not depart from them. And so too, this food brought to him desires to go away from him—[if he thinks], "May this [food] not [depart] from me. 4.6.9. [5]
"How indeed might he not injure me? [He thinks].
Therefore, he first eats only a small amount from the other side;
thus he presses it down, and so he knows: "Surely..."

It was just as I thought: "May he not harm me. Therefore, one approaches him [with this thought]. He who, knowing this, is able to observe this vow, truly becomes a lover of food and an eater of food. 4.6.9.
Now, on the tenth day, the rising from the sacrificial session (*sattrasthāna*) is performed; among them, each one remains restrained in speech.

They cause their speech to swell; with that speech, made full and not exhausted, they perform the subsequent day's rite. Then the others are dismissed—either to fetch firewood or for Vedic study—and there they eat. 4.6.9 [8] In the afternoon, they assemble.
Having touched water, they enter the wife’s hall (*patnīśālā*).
While they are holding on to one another, he offers these two oblations: "Here is delight; here do ye rejoice; here is steadfastness; here is self-steadfastness, svāhā!
This he says concerning cattle; it is cattle indeed that they thus secure for themselves. 4.6.9. [9]
Then he offers the second oblation with the verse:
"Licking the support from his mother"—by this he says, "Licking Agni from the earth";
"the supporter, sucking the mother"—by this he says, "Agni sucking the earth"; [grant] "abundance of wealth among us."
"May he maintain [it] with 'Svāhā'! Cattle indeed are the increase of wealth; thus they secure cattle for themselves.
They go out toward the east;
they enter the two *havirdhāna* sheds from behind, facing eastward, for [the sacrifice] is indeed in front.

Turning back, they are about to sit down; then, at the conclusion of the sacrificial session (*sattra*), they sing the *sāman* on the rear *kūbarī* (pole) of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, [with the words] "The success of the sacrificial session."

They rise up toward this very success, either from the northern hip of the high altar or more specifically from the northern part of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, [saying]: "We have gone to the light; we have become immortal. (4.6.9) [12]

"Light indeed they become, they become immortal, who sit for a sacrificial session (*sattra*)."—for those who sit for a sacrificial session do indeed ascend from earth to heaven. "We have found the gods"—for they find the gods. "The light of heaven"—thus they perform the *trirnidhana*; for they are indeed the light of heaven.
Whatever indeed is the form of this *sāman*, that very thing becomes those who sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
They crawl beneath, beneath the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, just as a snake [slips] from its skin.

Thus one would be released from all evil; they are released. They glide along with the *aticandas* [meter]. This *aticandas* indeed is all the meters; thus evil does not overtake them. Therefore they glide along with the *aticandas*. 4.6.9. [14] They glide along.
O Indra and Parvata, you who fight in the van, strike down each one who would attack us; strike him down with your thunderbolt, strike him down, whoever he may be.
Let him fall far away, even if he seeks refuge in a dense thicket—let him perish from among our enemies.
"O Hero, may the destroyer pierce the enemies on all sides; may he pierce them from every direction. (4.6.9) They go out toward the east;
they enter the *sadas* hall from the front, facing westward, for [the sacrifice] is indeed behind them.
Then, as they are about to praise [the sun], facing eastward, at the conclusion of the sacrificial session (satrotthāna),
they sit down according to their respective hearths (dhiṣṇya). Indeed, the essence of speech, once conquered by the gods, desired to depart from them.
He made this very [earth] turn away as it was about to slip away; for this earth is indeed Speech, and the plants and the trees are its essence.

They reached him by means of this *sāman*, and having been reached, he turned back toward them. Therefore, on this [earth], plants grow upward and trees grow upward. And in the same way, this essence of Speech is won from these [beings].

"If he intends to step aside, he wishes to slip away from this very [earth]. This earth is indeed speech; its essence is the plants and the trees. They reach it by means of this *sāman*. Having reached it, it turns back toward them.
Therefore, upon this [earth], the plants grow upward and the trees grow upward. 4.6.9. [17]
They praise with the verses of the Queen of Serpents (*sarparājñī*).
This earth, indeed, is the Queen of Serpents;
thus, by means of her, they obtain all this. It is self-praised and not sung after, so that it may not be like another.

If another were to chant the *prastāva*, he would cause an excess; if another were to sing the *upagīti*, he would cause an excess; if another were to listen, he would cause an excess. Therefore, it should be chanted by oneself, without being sung by another. 4.6.9. [18] The Hotṛ priest recites the Caturhotṛ formulas.
This very thing is praised; he commends it: "If the Hotṛ does not know [the response], the Gṛhapati should explain it; however, the explanation belongs to the Hotṛ alone. 4.6.9.
[19] Now follows the Adhvaryu's response (pratigara).

"These sacrificers have succeeded; it has turned out well for them"—thus he utters this auspicious word of human speech. Then they engage in the *brahmodya*, the theological debate, within the *vākovākya*.

Everything indeed is obtained by them, everything is conquered, who perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*). They have moved about with the *yajus* formulas; they attained that, they secured it. They have recited the *ṛc* verses; they attained that, they secured it.
They have chanted the *sāman* hymns.

By means of the *sāman*s they obtained those [worlds] and secured them; however, that which among these is the *vākovākya* and the *brāhmaṇa* remains unobtained and unsecured by them. It is precisely this that they obtain and secure by means of this [rite]. 4.6.9.
Having approached the *audumbarī* post, they restrain their speech.

Those who perform the sacrifice with mere speech indeed pierce and drain the sacrifice, for the sacrifice is speech. Therefore, before this [day], each one of them sits restraining his speech, swelling it up; with that speech thus swollen and made free from weariness, they perform the subsequent day. Now, on this [day], all speech is entirely obtained.
She becomes released; all those who have restrained their speech cause her voice to swell.
With that voice, now swollen and not exhausted, they perform the Atirātra sacrifice.
They sit holding onto a post made of Udumbara wood.
The udumbara is indeed food and strength; by means of strength they thus cause speech to swell. 4.6.9 [23].
When the sun has set, they go out toward the east.
They sit behind the Āhavanīya fire and in front of the two Havirdhāna carts.

The one who restrains his speech stands facing them while they likewise restrain their speech; he carries the *vasatīvarī* waters around them. They should release their speech with whatever desire they may have held while sitting [in session]. For indeed, the ancient seers used to sit in sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) according to their desires, saying, "This is our desire; may it be fulfilled for us.
If, however, they have many desires—whether desiring the world, offspring, or cattle—they should release their speech accordingly.
Or rather, they should release their speech with this very formula:
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. By means of this, they truly make their speech successful through truth.
With that prosperity they invoke blessings, thinking, "May we be rich in offspring through our children"—thus they invoke offspring;
"rich in heroes through our heroes"—thus they invoke heroes; "rich in nourishment through our nourishments"—thus they invoke nourishment. Then the householder calls the Subrahmaṇyā.

Or whatever the householder may say: "Some indeed invoke the *subrahmaṇyā* separately, but the householder himself should invoke the *subrahmaṇyā*"; or whatever the householder may say: "Having sought permission from him, they place the fuel-sticks upon the fire."
